28113.e: The round bronze coin with a square hole was called the ban liang. This shape stayed in use in China for over 2000 years.
28113.m: Chinese coins were round and had a square hole.

28114.q: What did Qin Shi Huang have destroyed in 213 BC to silence criticism?
28114.e: In the burning of the books, mainly the writings of philosophers and history books of other states were destroyed. Books on medicine, farming and fortune-telling were spared.
28114.m: Qin Shi Huang had many books burned.

28115.q: How did Qin Shi Huang rule his empire?
a: With strict laws and harsh punishments
With votes by all the people
With the help of an elected parliament
28115.e: The first emperor relied on clear laws and harsh punishments. Anyone who did not obey them could expect serious consequences.
28115.m: Qin Shi Huang ruled very strictly.

28116.q: What did Qin Shi Huang search for tirelessly towards the end of his life?
28116.e: He sent out scholars and expeditions to find an elixir of life. Even so, he died on a journey in 210 BC.
28116.m: The first emperor searched in vain for eternal life.

28117.q: Which modern name probably goes back to the state of Qin?
28117.e: Many researchers think that the word “China” comes from “Qin” (pronounced “chin”). The Chinese themselves call their country Zhongguo.
28117.m: The name China probably comes from the state of Qin.

28119.q: Near which Chinese city is the Terracotta Army?
28119.e: The pits are at Lintong, east of Xi’an in Shaanxi province.
28119.m: The Terracotta Army is near Xi’an.

28120.q: Roughly how many figures does the Terracotta Army include?
28120.e: Researchers estimate the number of warriors, horses and chariots at about 8000 figures. Many of them have not been dug up yet.
28120.m: The Terracotta Army has about 8000 figures.

28121.e: Terracotta comes from Italian and means baked earth. It refers to fired clay without a glaze.

28122.q: What did the terracotta warriors originally look like?
28122.e: The figures were painted in bright colours. In the air, the paint often flakes off quickly after they are dug up.
28122.m: The terracotta warriors were once brightly painted.

28123.q: What was the Terracotta Army meant for?
a: To protect the emperor in the afterlife
To entertain children in the palace
To serve as an offering to the gods
28123.e: The army guards the tomb of the first emperor of China. It was meant to protect him after his death.
28123.m: The clay warriors were meant to guard the emperor in the afterlife.

28124.q: What is still true today of the emperor’s actual burial mound next to the Terracotta Army?
a: It has not been opened yet
It is a museum you can go into
28124.e: The burial mound has not been excavated so far. People do not want to damage the tomb and are looking for gentle methods.
28124.m: The tomb of the first emperor is still unopened.

28125.q: What stood at regular distances along the Great Wall of China?
28125.e: There were many watchtowers on the wall. From there, soldiers kept a lookout and passed on warning signals.
28125.m: There were many watchtowers on the Great Wall of China.

28126.q: How old are most of the parts of the Great Wall of China that can be seen today?
28126.e: The well-preserved sections made of bricks and stone were mainly built between 1368 and 1644 under the Ming dynasty. Older parts have often fallen into ruin.
28126.m: The best-known parts of the wall are a few hundred years old.

28127.q: What was the Great Wall of China mainly meant to protect against?
28127.e: Nomadic peoples such as the Xiongnu kept raiding Chinese lands. The wall made their raids more difficult.
28127.m: The wall protected China from horse-riding peoples from the north.

28128.q: According to an official survey from 2012, how long are all the sections of the Great Wall of China added together?
28128.e: In 2012 the Chinese authority for cultural heritage came to about 21,196 kilometres. All sections of the wall from different periods were added together.
28128.m: All the sections of the Great Wall of China together are over 20,000 km long.

28129.q: Is it true that you can see the Great Wall of China from the Moon with the naked eye?
28129.e: The wall is very long, but only a few metres wide. From the Moon it cannot be seen with the naked eye.
28129.m: You cannot see the Great Wall of China from the Moon.

28130.q: How did the guards on the Great Wall of China pass on warnings?
28130.e: Signal fires were lit from tower to tower, and during the day the smoke could be seen. In this way a message travelled quickly over long distances.
28130.m: The wall guards warned each other with smoke and fire.

28131.q: What material were many early sections of the Great Wall of China made of?
28131.e: For early walls, earth was filled in layers between boards and pounded firm. This way of building is called rammed earth.
28131.m: Early parts of the wall were made of rammed earth.

28132.q: With which great empire did the Han dynasty in China exist at roughly the same time?
28132.e: The Han ruled from 206 BC to AD 220. During this time the Roman Empire in the West was at its height.
28132.m: The Han dynasty ruled at the same time as the Roman Empire.

28133.q: Which famous trade route to the West came about at the time of the Han dynasty?
28133.e: Trade along the Silk Road began under the Han. Along this route, silk and other goods from China reached the Mediterranean.
28133.m: The Silk Road came about in Han times.

28134.q: Which important invention comes from China at the time of the Han dynasty?
28134.e: Paper was made in China in Han times. Around AD 105 the official Cai Lun improved the way it was made. Gunpowder only came much later.
28134.m: Paper was invented in China in Han times.

28135.q: What do you call a series of rulers from the same family, such as the Han in China?
28135.e: In a dynasty, power is passed on within one family, usually from father to son. The Han dynasty ruled China for over 400 years.
28135.m: A ruling family is called a dynasty.

28136.q: Which teaching did Emperor Wu of Han make the basis of the state?
28136.e: Emperor Wu promoted the teaching of Confucius and founded an academy for future officials. After that, Confucianism shaped China for about 2000 years.
28136.m: Under the Han, Confucianism became the state teaching.

28137.q: Which is China’s largest ethnic group that still bears the name of this dynasty today?
28137.e: China’s largest population group is named after the Han dynasty. Chinese characters are also called hanzi.
28137.m: Most Chinese people call themselves Han after the Han dynasty.

28138.q: How did the earthquake detector from Han times show that an earthquake had happened?
a: A ball fell out of a dragon’s mouth
28138.e: In the year 132 the scholar Zhang Heng built a vessel with eight dragons. During an earthquake, a ball dropped into the mouth of a toad and so showed the direction.
28138.m: In the Han earthquake detector, a ball dropped when there was an earthquake.

28139.q: Why do people speak of the Western and Eastern Han?
a: Because the capital was later further east
Because two emperors ruled at the same time
Because China was split into two countries
Because the Han later moved to Japan
28139.e: The early Han ruled from Chang’an. After a short break, they moved the capital to Luoyang, which lies further east.
28139.m: The Eastern Han ruled from a capital further east.

28140.q: Why is the Silk Road called that?
a: Because valuable silk from China was traded along it
Because the road was covered with silk
Because all traders had to wear silk clothes
28140.e: Silk from China was an expensive luxury in the West. The name Silk Road was only invented in 1877 by the German geographer Ferdinand von Richthofen.
28140.m: The Silk Road is named after Chinese silk.

28141.q: Which parts of the world did the Silk Road link?
28141.e: The trade routes led from China through Central Asia to the Mediterranean. In the 2nd century BC the Chinese envoy Zhang Qian was one of the first to explore the lands in the West.
28141.m: The Silk Road linked China with the Mediterranean.

28142.q: Which feared desert did the caravans on the Silk Road have to go round to the north or south?
28142.e: The Taklamakan in the Tarim Basin is one of the largest sand deserts on Earth. The caravans travelled from oasis to oasis along its edges.
28142.m: The Silk Road led around the Taklamakan Desert.

28143.q: Which important oasis city on the Silk Road is in Uzbekistan today?
28143.e: Samarkand was a rich trading city of the Sogdians. Today, with its buildings, it is a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
28143.m: Samarkand was an important stop on the Silk Road.

28144.q: Which sought-after goods did China under the Han get from the Fergana Valley?
28144.e: The Han wanted strong horses for their cavalry against the nomads. They were called “heavenly horses”.
28144.m: China got heavenly horses from Fergana via the Silk Road.

28145.q: How did goods usually travel along the whole of the Silk Road?
a: Passed on from trader to trader
28145.e: Hardly any trader travelled the whole way. The goods were sold on at markets and so taken step by step to the west or east.
28145.m: Goods on the Silk Road passed from trader to trader.

28146.q: Which religion came from India to China along the Silk Road?
28146.e: From the 1st century AD, monks and traders brought the Buddha’s teaching to China. Cave temples were built along the route.
28146.m: Buddhism came to China along the Silk Road.

28147.q: Which ancient people paid a lot of money for silk from China?
28147.e: In Rome, silk was an expensive luxury. The Romans only knew of China from hearsay and called the people there the Seres, meaning the silk people.
28147.m: The Romans bought expensive silk from China.

28148.q: In which modern country was the heartland of the Kingdom of Kush?
28148.e: Kush lay in Nubia on the middle Nile, south of Egypt. Most of this area is part of Sudan today.
28148.m: The Kingdom of Kush lay in today’s Sudan.

28149.q: What role did kings from Kush play in Egypt in the 8th and 7th centuries BC?
a: They built the Pyramid of Khufu
28149.e: The kings of Kush conquered Egypt and formed the 25th dynasty. They are often called the black pharaohs.
28149.m: Kings from Kush ruled Egypt as pharaohs.

28150.q: In which direction did the kings of Kush march to conquer Egypt?
28150.e: Kush lay south of Egypt. The kings marched with their armies down the Nile to the north and conquered Egypt around 730 BC.
28150.m: Kush lay south of Egypt on the Nile.

28151.q: Which river was the lifeline of the Kingdom of Kush?
28151.e: Like Egypt, Kush lay on the Nile. The river provided water for the fields and was an important trade route.
28151.m: The Kingdom of Kush lay on the Nile.

28152.q: What is remarkable about the pyramids in the area of ancient Kush?
a: There are more than in Egypt
They are taller than at Giza
28152.e: There are over 200 pyramids in Sudan, more than in the whole of Egypt. They are smaller and have steeper sides.
28152.m: There are more pyramids in Sudan than in Egypt.

28153.q: Which buildings did the kings of Kush put up for their tombs, like the pharaohs?
28153.e: The kings of Kush were buried in pyramids. These are smaller and steeper than the pyramids of Giza.
28153.m: The kings of Kush also built pyramids.

28154.q: Which craft was Meroë known for in ancient times?
28154.e: Large heaps of iron slag were found at Meroë. The city was an important centre of iron-making in Africa.
28154.m: Meroë was a centre of iron-making.

28155.q: Who else could be at the head of the state in the Kingdom of Kush?
28155.e: Strong queens ruled in Kush again and again. One of them even waged war against the Romans.
28155.m: Powerful queens also ruled in Kush.

28156.q: On the territory of which modern countries did the Kingdom of Aksum lie?
28156.e: Aksum lay in the highlands of the Horn of Africa. The city of Aksum is in Ethiopia today.
28156.m: The Kingdom of Aksum lay in today’s Ethiopia and Eritrea.

28157.q: Which religion did King Ezana of Aksum adopt in the 4th century?
28157.e: Ezana became a Christian around AD 330 to 340. This makes Aksum one of the first Christian states in the world.
28157.m: Aksum became Christian under King Ezana.

28158.q: What happened in 2005 to a large stele that Italy had taken from Aksum in 1937?
a: It went to a Swiss museum
28158.e: The granite stele, about 24 metres tall, stood in Rome for almost 70 years. In 2005 it was given back and later put up again in Aksum.
28158.m: The Aksum stele returned from Rome in 2005.

28159.q: How did Aksum show its power as a trading empire?
a: With bars of salt as a coat of arms
28159.e: Aksum minted its own coins of gold, silver and bronze. Only a few states in ancient times did this, for example Rome and Persia.
28159.m: Aksum was one of the few empires to mint its own gold coins.

28160.q: What is the ancient city of Aksum in Ethiopia especially well known for?
28160.e: In Aksum there are tall, decorated stone pillars called steles. They marked the graves of kings.
28160.m: Aksum is famous for its tall stone steles.

28161.q: Across which sea did the Kingdom of Aksum trade with India and Rome?
28161.e: Aksum lay close to the Red Sea. From there, ivory, gold and frankincense went to India and the Roman Empire.
28161.m: Aksum traded across the Red Sea.

28162.q: What was the Kingdom of Aksum in the 3rd century AD?
a: One of the most powerful empires in the world
28162.e: Aksum was rich and powerful through trade. A scholar of that time counted it among the four greatest empires in the world, along with Rome, Persia and China.
28162.m: In the 3rd century Aksum was one of the greatest empires in the world.

28163.q: In which region did the Olmecs live?
a: On the Gulf coast of Mexico
28163.e: The Olmecs lived in the humid lowlands on the Gulf of Mexico. The area lies in today’s states of Veracruz and Tabasco.
28163.m: The Olmecs lived on the Gulf coast of Mexico.

28164.q: What are the Olmecs often seen as for later cultures such as the Maya and the Aztecs?
28164.e: Many features such as the ball game, the calendar and images of gods first appear among the Olmecs. That is why they are often called the mother culture of Mesoamerica.
28164.m: The Olmecs are seen as the mother culture of Central America.

28165.q: Roughly when did Olmec culture flourish?
28165.e: Olmec culture existed from about 1200 to 400 BC. That makes it much older than classic Maya culture.
28165.m: The Olmecs lived long before the Maya and the Aztecs.

28166.q: What do the huge stone heads of the Olmecs show?
28166.e: The colossal heads show human faces with helmet-like headgear. It is thought that they are rulers. Today 17 such heads are known.
28166.m: The stone heads of the Olmecs probably show rulers.

28168.q: Which green stone did the Olmecs especially value for figures and masks?
28168.e: The Olmecs carved precious figures, masks and axes from jade. The green stone probably stood for water, plants and fertility.
28168.m: The Olmecs carved precious figures from jade.

28169.q: Which animal plays a particularly important role in Olmec art?
28169.e: Many figures show creatures that are half human and half jaguar. The jaguar was seen as a powerful, sacred animal.
28169.m: The jaguar was a sacred animal for the Olmecs.

28170.q: Which great event did the Huns set off around AD 375 when they moved west?
28170.e: The Huns defeated the Alans and the Ostrogoths. As a result, many Germanic peoples fled into the Roman Empire.
28170.m: The advance of the Huns set off the Migration Period.

28171.q: Which weapon made the Hun horsemen so feared?
28171.e: The short recurve bow made of wood, horn and sinew was very powerful. The Huns could even shoot it from a galloping horse.
28171.m: The Huns fought on horseback with the recurve bow.

28172.q: In which area was the centre of the Hunnic Empire in the 5th century?
28172.e: The Huns settled on the plain along the Tisza, in today’s Hungary. From there they attacked the Eastern and Western Roman Empires.
28172.m: The Hunnic Empire had its centre in today’s Hungary.

28173.q: Which horse-riding people did Attila rule over?
28173.e: From 434 Attila was king of the Huns. The Huns were a horse-riding people who came to Europe from the steppes of Asia.
28173.m: Attila was the king of the Huns.

28174.q: Which great empire did Attila attack with his Huns?
28174.e: Attila invaded Gaul and Italy with his army; at that time they belonged to the Roman Empire. In 451 he was stopped by the Romans and the Visigoths.
28174.m: Attila attacked the Roman Empire with the Huns.

28175.q: Who travelled to meet Attila in Italy in 452, shortly before he withdrew?
28175.e: Pope Leo I met Attila with a delegation in northern Italy. Shortly afterwards Attila withdrew, probably also because of disease and hunger in his army.
28175.m: A pope met Attila in Italy in 452.

28176.q: Which nickname did Christian writers later give Attila?
28176.e: Christian writers saw his attacks as a punishment from God. That is where the nickname “Scourge of God” comes from.
28176.m: Attila was called the Scourge of God.

28177.q: In which famous medieval heroic poem does Attila appear as King Etzel?
28177.e: In the Nibelungenlied, King Etzel marries the widow Kriemhild. Behind this character is the Hun king Attila.
28177.m: In the Nibelungenlied, Attila is called King Etzel.

28178.q: Which year is traditionally seen as the start of the Migration Period?
28178.e: Around 375 the Huns defeated the Ostrogoths by the Black Sea. This year is seen as the starting point of the great migrations.
28178.m: By tradition, the Migration Period begins in the year 375.

28179.q: Which Germanic military leader deposed the last Western Roman emperor in 476?
28179.e: Odoacer was the leader of Germanic mercenaries in Italy. He sent the imperial insignia to Constantinople and then ruled Italy as king.
28179.m: Odoacer ended the rule of the Western Roman emperors in 476.

28180.q: Which horse-riding people from Asia did Attila lead?
28180.e: Attila was King of the Huns. Around 450 he attacked Gaul and Italy with his army, but in 451 he was stopped by Romans and Germanic peoples.
28180.m: Attila was King of the Huns.

28181.q: Who defeated a large Roman army at Adrianople in 378?
28181.e: The Goths had fled from the Huns into the Roman Empire and then rose up. At Adrianople they defeated the Romans, and even the emperor was killed.
28181.m: The Goths defeated the Romans at Adrianople in 378.

28182.q: What did the Visigoths do in the year 410 that shook the whole Roman world?
a: They sacked the city of Rome
They founded the city of Venice
28182.e: Under their king Alaric, the Visigoths captured Rome in 410 and plundered the city for three days. Rome had not been taken by enemies for 800 years.

28183.q: On which peninsula did the Visigoths have their kingdom in the end?
28183.e: The Visigoths moved on from Gaul to what is now Spain and Portugal. Their kingdom lasted there until 711.
28183.m: In the end the Visigoths ruled in Spain.

28184.q: Which group of peoples did the Visigoths belong to?
28184.e: The Goths were a Germanic people. They split into Visigoths and Ostrogoths and moved through Europe during the Migration Period.
28184.m: The Visigoths were a Germanic people.

28185.q: Who conquered the Visigothic kingdom in Spain from 711 onwards?
28185.e: In 711 Muslim troops crossed from North Africa to Spain and defeated the Visigothic king Roderic. Within a few years they conquered almost the whole Iberian Peninsula.
28185.m: With the Muslim conquest from 711, the Visigothic kingdom came to an end.

28186.q: Which book did the Gothic bishop Wulfila translate into the language of the Goths in the 4th century?
28186.e: Wulfila even invented his own Gothic script for it. A famous copy is the “Silver Bible”, which is kept in Sweden today.
28186.m: The Bible was translated into Gothic as early as the 4th century.

28187.q: Which religion did the Goths adopt in the 4th century?
28187.e: Missionaries converted the Goths to Christianity. However, their form of the faith differed from the teaching of the Roman Church, which led to disputes.

28188.q: Which Germanic people did Theodoric the Great lead?
28188.e: Theodoric became King of the Ostrogoths in the 470s. Under him they set up a kingdom in Italy.
28188.m: Theodoric the Great was King of the Ostrogoths.

28189.q: Which city was the capital of Theodoric’s kingdom in Italy?
28189.e: Theodoric ruled from Ravenna, where the last Western Roman emperors had already lived. His tomb still stands there today.

28190.q: Roughly when did Theodoric the Great live?
28190.e: Theodoric lived from about 451 to 526. He ruled Italy at the beginning of the Middle Ages.
28190.m: Theodoric the Great lived around AD 500.

28191.q: Under which name does Theodoric live on in German heroic legends?
28191.e: In the legends Theodoric is called Dietrich von Bern. “Bern” here means the Italian city of Verona, not the Swiss capital.
28191.m: Dietrich von Bern is Theodoric’s name in legend.

28192.q: Which empire had collapsed in Italy shortly before Theodoric’s rule?
28192.e: In 476 the last Western Roman emperor was deposed. After that, Germanic kings such as Theodoric ruled Italy.
28192.m: After the end of the Western Roman Empire, Theodoric ruled Italy.

28193.q: What did Theodoric have built in his capital Ravenna?
28193.e: Churches from Theodoric’s time still stand in Ravenna today. Their walls are decorated with shining mosaics.
28193.m: Theodoric had churches with mosaics built in Ravenna.

28195.q: Which group of peoples did the Vandals belong to?
28195.e: The Vandals were a Germanic people. During the Migration Period they moved through Gaul and Spain as far as North Africa.
28195.m: The Vandals were a Germanic people.

28196.q: Which famous city did the Vandals sack in the year 455?
28196.e: In 455 the Vandals sailed from Africa to Italy and plundered Rome for two weeks.

28197.q: Which city did the Vandals capture in 439 and make their capital?
28197.e: Carthage in what is now Tunisia was one of the richest cities of the Western Roman Empire. From there the Vandal fleet controlled the western Mediterranean.
28197.m: Carthage became the capital of the Vandals.

28198.q: Which modern word for pointless destruction comes from the name of the Vandals?
28198.e: The term was coined in France in 1794. It referred to the sack of Rome by the Vandals, who were imagined as especially destructive.

28199.q: Which country did the Lombards move into in the year 568?
28199.e: In 568 the Lombards migrated from Pannonia to northern Italy. This event is often seen as the end of the Migration Period.
28199.m: The Lombards came to Italy in 568.

28200.q: Which mountain range did the Lombards cross to reach Italy?
28200.e: In 568 King Alboin led his people over the Alps into Italy and conquered large parts of the north.
28200.m: The Lombards came to Italy over the Alps.

28201.q: Which Italian region still bears the name of the Lombards today?
28201.e: The name Lombardy comes from “Langobardia”, the land of the Lombards. Its capital today is Milan.
28201.m: Lombardy is named after the Lombards.

28202.q: Which ruler conquered the kingdom of the Lombards?
28202.e: Charlemagne besieged the Lombard capital Pavia and conquered the kingdom in 774.

28203.q: According to tradition, what does the name “Langobards” (Lombards) mean?
28203.e: According to a legend told by the historian Paul the Deacon, the name came from the men’s long beards. Other researchers explain it differently, but “long beards” is the best-known explanation.
28203.m: According to legend, Langobards means “long beards”.

28204.q: Which additional title did Charlemagne take after his victory over the Lombards?
28204.e: After capturing Pavia in 774, Charlemagne also called himself King of the Lombards.
28204.m: Charlemagne also became King of the Lombards.

28205.q: What happened to Desiderius, the last King of the Lombards?
a: He had to spend the rest of his life in a monastery
28205.e: Desiderius lost his kingdom to Charlemagne in 774. He was taken prisoner and then lived in a Frankish monastery.
28205.m: Desiderius was the last Lombard king.

28206.q: What did the Lombard king Rothari have written down in the year 643?
28206.e: The Edict of Rothari is written in Latin. It recorded the legal customs of the Lombards, which until then had only been passed on by word of mouth.
28206.m: King Rothari had Lombard law written down.

28207.q: Which people did Clovis I lead as king?
28207.e: Around 500 Clovis was King of the Franks. He united many Frankish groups into one large kingdom.
28207.m: Clovis was King of the Franks.

28208.q: According to a legend, what is Clovis said to have promised in a dangerous battle?
a: To become a Christian if he won
To go on pilgrimage to Rome
28208.e: According to the story, Clovis prayed in his need to the God of his Christian wife. After the victory he was baptised.
28208.m: Clovis was baptised after a victory.

28209.q: Which country today bears the name of Clovis’s people?
28209.e: Clovis was King of the Franks. The name France comes from their name.
28209.m: France is named after the Franks.

28210.q: Which German first name developed from “Chlodwig”, the German form of Clovis?
28210.e: In German, Chlodwig became Ludwig, and in French it became Louis. That is why many French kings bore this name.
28210.m: The name Ludwig, like Louis, comes from Clovis.

28211.q: Which Merovingian king united the Franks and was baptised around 500?
28211.e: Clovis I defeated other rulers and became king of all the Franks. With his baptism the Franks also became Christians.
28211.m: Clovis I was the most important Merovingian king.

28212.q: Which outward sign was seen as a mark of royal dignity among the Merovingian kings?
28212.e: The Merovingian kings wore their hair long and were therefore called the “long-haired kings”. Anyone who was deposed often had his hair shorn.
28212.m: Among the Merovingians, long hair was a sign of the king.

28213.q: Which ruling family replaced the Merovingians as kings of the Franks?
28213.e: In 751 Pepin the Short became King of the Franks. His family is called the Carolingians after his son Charlemagne.
28213.m: The Merovingians were followed by the Carolingians.

28214.q: Which mayor of the palace defeated an Arab army between Tours and Poitiers in 732?
28214.e: Charles Martel stopped an advance of the Muslims from Spain towards the north. His nickname “Martel” means “hammer”.
28214.m: Charles Martel won at Tours and Poitiers in 732.

28215.q: Which people did the Merovingians rule over?
28215.e: The Merovingians were the first royal family of the Franks. Their kingdom lay in what is now France, Belgium and western Germany.
28215.m: The Merovingians were kings of the Franks.

28216.q: Among the Merovingians, what often happened to the kingdom when a king died?
a: It was divided among his sons
It was given to the pope
The people elected a new king
28216.e: Among the Franks, all the sons inherited part of the kingdom. That is why smaller kingdoms and quarrels between brothers kept arising.
28216.m: The Merovingians divided their kingdom among their sons.

28217.q: According to the sources, how did the Romans present react when the pope placed the crown on Charlemagne’s head?
28217.e: According to the Frankish Royal Annals, the whole Roman people acclaimed Charlemagne as emperor. By Roman custom, this acclamation was part of raising someone to emperor.
28217.m: At the coronation the Romans proclaimed Charlemagne emperor.

28218.q: In which church did Charlemagne’s coronation as emperor take place?
28218.e: The coronation took place in the old Basilica of St Peter in Rome. In the 16th century this building was replaced by today’s St Peter’s Basilica.
28218.m: Charlemagne was crowned in Old St Peter’s Basilica.

28219.q: Why did Pope Leo III seek help from Charlemagne in the year 799?
a: He had been attacked in Rome
He needed money for a church
He wanted to travel to America
28219.e: The pope fled from Rome and met Charlemagne in Paderborn. The meeting paved the way for the later coronation as emperor.
28219.m: The threatened pope sought protection from Charlemagne in 799.

28220.q: Which empire saw Charlemagne’s coronation as a presumption, because it saw itself as the only empire?
28220.e: In Constantinople there was still an emperor who saw himself as the successor of the Roman emperors. This is therefore called the problem of the two emperors.
28220.m: At first Byzantium refused to recognise Charlemagne’s title of emperor.

28221.q: What does Charlemagne’s biographer Einhard report about the coronation as emperor?
28221.e: Einhard lived at Charlemagne’s court and wrote the story of his life. He reports that Charlemagne was surprised by the coronation.
28221.m: According to Einhard, Charlemagne was surprised by the coronation.

28222.q: Whom did Charlemagne have crowned as co-emperor in 813?
28222.e: Shortly before his death, Charlemagne himself made his son Louis co-emperor. Louis, later called “the Pious”, became sole ruler in 814.
28222.m: Louis the Pious became his father’s co-emperor in 813.

28223.q: On which Zurich church does a seated figure on the tower recall Charlemagne?
28223.e: According to a legend, Charlemagne founded the Grossmünster. The original stone figure is now in the crypt, and a copy sits on the south tower.
28223.m: Charlemagne sits enthroned as a stone figure on the Grossmünster in Zurich.

28224.q: What shape is the floor plan of the Palatine Chapel in Aachen?
28224.e: The Palatine Chapel is an eight-sided central building with a dome. It is still the heart of Aachen Cathedral today.
28224.m: The Palatine Chapel in Aachen is built as an octagon.

28225.q: Among other things, what attracted Charlemagne to Aachen?
28225.e: Aachen has hot thermal springs that the Romans already used. According to Einhard, Charlemagne liked to bathe in them often.
28225.m: The warm springs made Aachen attractive to Charlemagne.

28226.q: In which year did Charlemagne die in Aachen?
28226.e: Charlemagne died on 28 January 814 in his palace. He was buried in the Palatine Chapel on the same day.

28227.q: Which important list is Aachen Cathedral on today?
a: The list of the tallest churches in the world
The list of the Wonders of the Ancient World
The list of the oldest bridges
28227.e: In 1978 Aachen Cathedral was one of the very first buildings to be put on the UNESCO World Heritage List. It is an especially valuable witness to the time of Charlemagne.
28227.m: Aachen Cathedral is a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

28228.q: Which piece of furniture from Charlemagne’s time still stands in the Palatine Chapel in Aachen?
28228.e: The throne is made of plain marble slabs and stands in the gallery. From 936 to 1531 more than 30 German kings were crowned in Aachen and then sat on this throne.
28228.m: Many German kings sat on the marble throne in Aachen.

28229.q: What is the golden shrine called in which Charlemagne’s bones lie in Aachen Cathedral?
28229.e: The Shrine of Charlemagne was completed in 1215. It is decorated with figures of emperors and kings.
28229.m: Charlemagne’s bones rest in the Shrine of Charlemagne.

28230.q: Roughly how long did Charlemagne’s Saxon Wars last?
28230.e: The wars began in 772 and only ended around 804. Again and again the Saxons rose up against Frankish rule.
28230.m: The Saxon Wars lasted from 772 to 804.

28231.q: Which people did Charlemagne rule as king?
28231.e: Charlemagne was King of the Franks. With the Saxon Wars he enlarged his Frankish kingdom towards the north.
28231.m: Charlemagne was King of the Franks.

28232.q: How did Charlemagne’s Saxon Wars end?
a: The Saxons became part of the Frankish kingdom
The Saxons conquered the Frankish kingdom
Charlemagne was captured by the Saxons
28232.e: After more than 30 years of war the Saxons were defeated. Their land now belonged to the Frankish kingdom, and they became Christians.
28232.m: At the end of the Saxon Wars the Saxons belonged to the Frankish kingdom.

28233.q: How did Charlemagne deal with uprisings in the Saxon Wars?
a: He left the Saxons in peace
He gave them back their land
28233.e: After uprisings Charlemagne had many captured Saxons executed, for example at Verden in 782. He wanted to break their resistance.
28233.m: Charlemagne dealt harshly with the Saxons.

28234.q: Under Charlemagne’s law, what punishment threatened Saxons who refused to be baptised?
28234.e: Charlemagne wanted to make the Saxons Christians by force. Anyone who refused baptism or kept up old customs could be punished with death.
28234.m: Charlemagne forced the Saxons to be baptised with harsh punishments.

28235.q: Where did the Saxons mainly live in the time of Charlemagne?
a: In the north-west of present-day Germany
In the present-day German state of Saxony
28235.e: The old land of the Saxons was roughly in present-day Lower Saxony and Westphalia. The present-day state of Saxony only got its name much later.
28235.m: The old Saxons lived in north-west Germany.

28236.q: What did the missionary Boniface want to achieve among the Germanic peoples?
28236.e: Boniface travelled through Germania and preached the Christian faith. At that time many people still worshipped the old Germanic gods.
28236.m: Boniface spread the Christian faith among the Germanic peoples.

28237.q: Which country did the missionary Boniface come from?
28237.e: Boniface was born around 673 in the south-west of England. He was a monk there before he went to the Continent.
28237.m: Boniface came from England as an Anglo-Saxon monk.

28238.q: Which sacred tree did Boniface cut down near Geismar in Hesse in 723?
28238.e: By cutting down the oak dedicated to the god Donar, Boniface wanted to show that the old gods were powerless. He is said to have built a chapel from the wood.
28238.m: Boniface cut down Donar’s Oak near Geismar.

28239.q: Which title of honour does Boniface bear?
28239.e: Boniface founded dioceses and monasteries and organised the Church in the Frankish kingdom. That is why he is called the “Apostle of the Germans”.
28239.m: Boniface is regarded as the Apostle of the Germans.

28240.q: Among which people was Boniface killed on a missionary journey in 754?
28240.e: Boniface was killed by robbers near Dokkum in what is now the north of the Netherlands. He was already around 80 years old.
28240.m: Boniface died in 754 as a missionary among the Frisians.

28241.q: In which town is Boniface buried?
28241.e: His body was taken to the monastery of Fulda, which his pupil Sturm had founded. His grave is now in Fulda Cathedral.

28242.q: What did Boniface found to spread the Christian faith for good?
28242.e: Boniface founded monasteries such as Fulda and organised dioceses. So the Church had fixed places where priests and monks worked.

28243.q: What is Boniface said to have built from the wood of the felled Donar’s Oak?
28243.e: According to the legend, Boniface built a chapel from the wood of the oak. In this way the sacred tree of the Germanic peoples became a Christian place.
28243.m: A chapel is said to have been made from Donar’s Oak.

28244.q: What could a great vassal do with parts of his fief?
a: Pass them on to his own followers
Nothing, he had to farm everything himself
28244.e: Great vassals passed parts of their fief on to their own followers. These sub-vassals are called rear vassals.
28244.m: Vassals could pass on parts of their fief.

28245.q: Who divided the Frankish kingdom among themselves in the Treaty of Verdun in 843?
28245.e: After the death of Charlemagne’s son Louis, his three sons quarrelled over the inheritance. At Verdun they came to an agreement and divided the great kingdom into three parts.
28245.m: Charlemagne’s grandsons divided the Frankish kingdom in 843.

28246.q: Who received East Francia in the Treaty of Verdun?
28246.e: Louis received the lands east of the Rhine. Later the Holy Roman Empire developed from them.
28246.m: Louis the German received the eastern kingdom.

28247.q: From which part of the Frankish kingdom divided in 843 did France later develop?
28247.e: The kingdom was divided into a western, a middle and an eastern part. The west later became France, and the east became the Holy Roman Empire.

28248.q: Into how many parts was the Frankish kingdom divided in the Treaty of Verdun in 843?
28248.e: The three brothers each received one part: West Francia, Middle Francia and East Francia.
28248.m: In 843 the Frankish kingdom was divided into three parts.

28249.q: Which present-day region is named after King Lothair II, a son of Lothair I?
28249.e: Lorraine comes from “Lothair’s kingdom” (Lotharingia). This means the northern part of Middle Francia, which Lothair II inherited from his father.

28250.q: Why did two Frankish kings swear loyalty to each other in Strasbourg in 842 in two different languages?
a: So that both armies understood the oath
So that nobody understood the oath
28250.e: In the west the soldiers spoke an early form of French, in the east an early form of German. That is why the oaths were sworn in both languages.
28250.m: The Oaths of Strasbourg were sworn in Old French and Old High German.

28251.q: Where is the area of Angeln, where some of the Anglo-Saxons came from?
28251.e: The Angeln peninsula lies on the Baltic Sea in the north of Germany. From there many people crossed the North Sea to Britain.
28251.m: The Angles came from what is now Schleswig-Holstein.

28252.q: Which faith did the Anglo-Saxons gradually adopt?
a: The religion of the ancient Egyptians
28252.e: At first the Anglo-Saxons worshipped Germanic gods. From about 600 missionaries came from Rome and Ireland, and the Anglo-Saxons became Christians.
28252.m: The Anglo-Saxons became Christians from about 600.

28253.q: Which of the following was an Anglo-Saxon kingdom?
28253.e: There were several Anglo-Saxon kingdoms in England, such as Wessex, Mercia, Northumbria and Kent. Wessex later became the most powerful of them.
28253.m: Wessex was an important Anglo-Saxon kingdom.

28254.q: Which part of the Roman Empire carried on for almost 1,000 years after 476?
28254.e: In the west the last emperor was deposed in 476. The Eastern Roman Empire, with its capital Constantinople, lasted until 1453.
28254.m: The Eastern Roman Empire lasted almost 1,000 years after the end of the Western Empire.

28255.q: Across which river did the Romans let the Goths into their empire in 376?
28255.e: Fleeing from the Huns, the Goths asked to be let into the empire. They crossed the Danube but were treated badly by Roman officials and rose up.
28255.m: In 376 the Goths crossed the Danube into the Roman Empire.

28256.q: Which city was the capital of the Eastern Roman Empire?
28256.e: Emperor Constantine made the city on the Bosporus the capital. Today it is called Istanbul.
28256.m: Constantinople, today’s Istanbul, was the capital of the Eastern Roman Empire.

28257.q: Which Germanic people settled in what is now German-speaking Switzerland during the Migration Period?
28257.e: The Alemanni moved into the Swiss Plateau from the 5th century. The Alemannic language, from which Swiss German developed, comes from them.
28257.m: The Alemanni settled in what is now German-speaking Switzerland.

28258.q: On which continent did the Vandals found their kingdom?
28258.e: The Vandals moved through Spain to North Africa. They ruled there for about a hundred years, until an Eastern Roman army defeated them in 534.
28258.m: The Vandal kingdom was in North Africa.

28259.q: Across which strait did the Vandals cross from Spain to Africa in 429?
28259.e: At its narrowest point the Strait of Gibraltar separates Spain and Morocco by only about 14 kilometres. Around 80,000 people are said to have crossed with the Vandals.
28259.m: The Vandals crossed the Strait of Gibraltar in 429.

28260.q: What is the period called when the Vandals, Goths and many other peoples moved through Europe?
28260.e: From the 4th to the 6th century many Germanic peoples moved into the Roman Empire. This time is called the Migration Period.
28260.m: The Vandals moved through Europe during the Migration Period.

28262.q: What happened to Clovis’s kingdom after his death?
a: It was divided among his sons
It became part of the Roman Empire
It was conquered by the Vikings
28262.e: By Frankish custom, all the sons inherited a part. That is why Clovis’s four sons divided the kingdom among themselves.
28262.m: Clovis’s sons divided up his kingdom.

28263.q: Which French first name also comes from Clovis (in German “Chlodwig”)?
28263.e: In French, Clovis became Louis. Many French kings later had this name, for example Louis XIV.
28263.m: The name Louis goes back to Clovis.

28264.q: What are the late Merovingian kings often called, because they hardly had any power left?
28264.e: In the 7th and 8th centuries the kings ruled in name only. The real power lay with other men at court.
28264.m: The late Merovingians were only shadow kings.

28265.q: Why was the imperial throne considered vacant in the West in the year 800?
a: Because a woman was ruling in Constantinople
28265.e: In Constantinople, Empress Irene ruled alone. In the West people argued that a woman could not be emperor.
28265.m: Because Irene ruled as a woman, the imperial throne was seen as vacant in the West.

28266.q: In which century was the Treaty of Verdun concluded?
28266.e: The Treaty of Verdun dates from the year 843. That belongs to the 9th century, about 30 years after the death of Charlemagne.
28266.m: The Treaty of Verdun dates from the 9th century.

28267.q: What did a vassal receive from his feudal lord?
a: A piece of land, the fief
28267.e: The vassal received a fief, usually land, and in return promised loyalty and military service. In Carolingian times the fief was called “beneficium” in Latin.
28267.m: A vassal received a fief for his loyalty.

28268.q: Why did the Frankish kings give their warriors land instead of wages?
a: Because there was little money in circulation
Because warriors did not want money
28268.e: In the Early Middle Ages there were only a few coins. With the produce of the land the vassals could pay for a horse and armour for military service.
28268.m: In the Early Middle Ages land replaced wages for warriors.

28269.q: What happened to a fief if a vassal died without heirs?
a: It went back to the feudal lord
It was shared out among the peasants
28269.e: Because the land belonged to the lord, it came back to him if there was no heir. This is called escheat.
28269.m: Without heirs, the fief went back to the lord.

28270.q: What are vassals called who received their fief directly from the king?
28270.e: Tenants-in-chief included dukes, counts, bishops and abbots. They often passed land on to their own followers.
28270.m: Tenants-in-chief received their fief directly from the king.

28271.q: What were the unfree servants called who received fiefs in the High Middle Ages and rose into the lower nobility?
28271.e: Ministeriales were originally unfree, but served as administrators and mounted warriors. Many families of knights came from them.
28271.m: A large part of the knightly class came from the ministeriales.

28272.q: What had to happen when the feudal lord or the vassal died?
a: The fief had to be granted again
28272.e: The feudal relationship was tied to two particular people. If one of them died, the heir had to receive the fief again and swear loyalty.
28272.m: After a death, a fief was granted again.

28273.q: What did a vassal have to promise his feudal lord in return for the fief?
28273.e: The vassal swore loyalty to his lord and had to serve him with weapons in war. In return he was allowed to use the land.
28273.m: For the fief, the vassal owed loyalty and military service.

28275.q: Which language developed from the language of the Anglo-Saxons?
28275.e: Over many centuries the Old English of the Anglo-Saxons became today’s English. That is why English is related to German.
28275.m: English comes from the language of the Anglo-Saxons.

28276.q: How many Anglo-Saxon kingdoms make up the so-called Heptarchy?
28276.e: The term Heptarchy comes from the Greek word for seven. It means Northumbria, Mercia, East Anglia, Essex, Kent, Sussex and Wessex.
28276.m: The Heptarchy consisted of seven Anglo-Saxon kingdoms.

28277.q: What did Vikings raid in England in 793, which began the Viking Age?
28277.e: In 793 Vikings plundered the island monastery of Lindisfarne. Monasteries were rich and hardly protected, so they were often raided.
28277.m: The Viking Age began with the raid on a monastery in 793.

28278.q: What is the Eastern Roman Empire usually called in the Middle Ages?
28278.e: After the division of the Roman Empire, the eastern part carried on. Historians call it the Byzantine Empire.
28278.m: The Eastern Roman Empire is also called the Byzantine Empire.

28279.q: Which language became the main language of daily life and government in the Byzantine Empire?
28279.e: At first Latin was still the official language, but from the 7th century Greek became the language of state and Church.
28279.m: In the Byzantine Empire people mainly spoke Greek.

28280.q: Which city was the capital of the Byzantine Empire?
28280.e: Emperor Constantine enlarged the old city of Byzantion and called it Constantinople. Today it is called Istanbul.
28280.m: Constantinople was the capital of Byzantium.

28281.q: What is the split in the Church between East and West in 1054 called?
28281.e: In 1054 the Church of Rome and the Church of Constantinople separated. This split is called the East-West Schism or Great Schism.
28281.m: Since the schism of 1054 the Eastern and Western Churches have been separate.

28282.q: With which incendiary weapon did the Byzantines set enemy ships on fire?
28282.e: Greek fire even burned on water. Its exact recipe was a closely guarded secret and is still unknown today.
28282.m: Greek fire even burned on water.

28283.q: Which Christian Church developed mainly in the Byzantine Empire?
28283.e: The Eastern Church calls itself Orthodox, meaning “of the right belief”. Today it is widespread in countries such as Greece, Serbia and Russia.
28283.m: The Orthodox Church has its roots in the Byzantine Empire.

28284.q: What are icons in the Orthodox Church?
28284.e: Icons show Jesus, Mary or saints. In the Byzantine dispute over images there was a long argument about whether they may be venerated.
28284.m: Icons are holy pictures of the Eastern Church.

28285.q: In which century did the Byzantine emperor Justinian I reign?
28285.e: Justinian I ruled from 527 to 565. That is the middle of the 6th century.
28285.m: Justinian I was emperor in the 6th century.

28286.q: What did Emperor Justinian I have collected and organised?
a: All the maps of the world
The recipes of the imperial kitchen
28286.e: Justinian had Roman law collected in the Corpus Juris Civilis. This work still influences law in Europe today, including in Switzerland.

28287.q: What background did Theodora, the influential wife of Emperor Justinian I, come from?
28287.e: Theodora was not a princess but came from a humble background. As empress she advised Justinian on important questions.
28287.m: Empress Theodora had great influence on Justinian.

28288.q: Where did the Nika riots against Justinian I begin in Constantinople in 532?
a: At the chariot races in the Hippodrome
28288.e: The spectators at the chariot races shouted “Nika!”, meaning “Win!”. This turned into an uprising, which Justinian had bloodily crushed.
28288.m: The Nika riots began at the chariot races.

28289.q: Who was Belisarius to Emperor Justinian I?
28289.e: In 533 and 534 Belisarius defeated the Vandal kingdom in North Africa. After that he also fought in Italy.
28289.m: Belisarius was Justinian’s most famous general.

28290.q: What did Justinian I want to achieve with his wars in the West?
a: To convert the north of Europe
To find new trade routes to India
28290.e: Justinian wanted to win back the lost lands of the Western Roman Empire. He conquered North Africa, Italy and parts of Spain.
28290.m: Justinian dreamed of renewing the Roman Empire.

28291.q: Which epidemic broke out in the empire of Justinian I from 541?
28291.e: The so-called Plague of Justinian killed a very large number of people around the Mediterranean. It greatly weakened the empire.
28291.m: The first great wave of plague struck under Justinian.

28292.q: In which present-day city is the Hagia Sophia?
28292.e: The Hagia Sophia is in Istanbul in Turkey. The city used to be called Constantinople.
28292.m: The Hagia Sophia is in Istanbul.

28293.q: What did the Hagia Sophia become in the 1930s under Atatürk?
28293.e: In 1934 the young Republic of Turkey declared the Hagia Sophia a museum. From 1935 visitors could tour it.
28293.m: Under Atatürk the Hagia Sophia became a museum.

28294.q: Which part of the building makes the Hagia Sophia especially famous?
28294.e: The dome has a diameter of more than 30 metres and seems to float above the room. For a long time it was one of the largest in the world.
28294.m: The enormous dome is the trademark of the Hagia Sophia.

28295.q: What did the Ottomans add to the outside of the Hagia Sophia?
28295.e: Four minarets were built one after another for the call to prayer.
28295.m: The four minarets of the Hagia Sophia were added by the Ottomans.

28296.q: Which Roman emperor is Constantinople named after?
28296.e: Emperor Constantine made the city the new capital in 330. Constantinople means “city of Constantine”.
28296.m: Constantinople is named after Emperor Constantine.

28298.q: What is the inlet of the sea called that served Constantinople as a natural harbour?
28298.e: The Golden Horn is a long arm of the sea on the Bosporus. Ships lay there in safety.
28298.m: The Golden Horn was the harbour of Constantinople.

28299.q: Which nickname did Constantinople have as the capital of the East?
28299.e: Constantinople was meant to replace old Rome as the capital. That is why it was called “New Rome”. “Eternal City” is the nickname of Rome itself.
28299.m: Constantinople was seen as the New Rome.

28300.q: In which city was the Prophet Muhammad born around 570?
28300.e: Muhammad was born in Mecca on the Arabian Peninsula. Today the city is the most important place of pilgrimage in Islam.

28301.q: What is Muhammad’s emigration from Mecca to Medina called?
28301.e: The Hijra took place in 622. The Islamic calendar begins with this year.
28301.m: The Hijra of 622 marks the beginning of the Islamic calendar.

28302.q: What is the holy book of Islam called?
28302.e: For Muslims, the Quran contains the revelations that Muhammad received.
28302.m: The Quran is the holy book of Islam.

28303.q: In which language is the Quran written?
28303.e: The Quran was handed down in Arabic. That is why the Arabic language spread widely with Islam.
28303.m: The Quran is written in Arabic.

28304.q: What is the cube-shaped shrine in Mecca called?
28304.e: The Kaaba stands in the courtyard of the Great Mosque of Mecca. Muslims pray facing towards it.
28304.m: Muslims pray facing the Kaaba in Mecca.

28305.q: How many pillars does Islam have?
28305.e: The five pillars are the declaration of faith, prayer, giving alms, fasting in Ramadan and the pilgrimage to Mecca.
28305.m: Islam is based on five pillars.

28306.q: In which year did the Prophet Muhammad die?
28306.e: Muhammad died in Medina in 632. After that, caliphs took over the leadership of the community.

28307.q: Which city was the capital of the Umayyad Caliphate?
28307.e: The Umayyads ruled their empire from Damascus in present-day Syria.

28308.q: Which religion did the Umayyad caliphs belong to?
28308.e: The Umayyads were caliphs, meaning successors of Muhammad at the head of the Muslims. From 661 they ruled over a large empire.

28309.q: Which famous building in Jerusalem did the Umayyads have built?
28309.e: The Dome of the Rock was completed around 691 under the caliph Abd al-Malik. Its golden dome dominates the city.
28309.m: The Dome of the Rock in Jerusalem was built by the Umayyads.

28310.q: Which country in Europe did Umayyad troops conquer from the year 711?
28310.e: In 711 Muslim troops crossed from Africa to Spain. Large parts of Spain then remained under Muslim rule for a long time.

28311.q: What were the gold coins called that the Umayyads had minted?
28311.e: Under Abd al-Malik, Islamic coins without pictures were made. The gold coin was called the dinar.
28311.m: The dinar was the gold coin of the caliphs.

28312.q: Which city in Spain became a magnificent capital under the Umayyads?
28312.e: In the 10th century Córdoba was one of the largest cities in Europe. Its huge mosque with many columns is famous.
28312.m: Córdoba was the capital of the Umayyads in Spain.

28313.q: Which religion did the Abbasid caliphs have?
28313.e: The Abbasids were Muslim rulers. As caliphs they were seen as successors of the Prophet Muhammad.

28314.q: Which city did the Abbasids found as their new capital in 762?
28314.e: Caliph al-Mansur had the city built from 762. It became one of the largest cities in the world.
28314.m: In 762 the Abbasids founded the capital Baghdad.

28315.q: What was the first layout of Baghdad called because of its plan?
28315.e: The centre of Baghdad was laid out in a perfect circle, with the palace and the mosque in the middle.
28315.m: Baghdad was planned as a round city.

28316.q: Which Abbasid caliph appears in the stories of “One Thousand and One Nights”?
28316.e: Harun al-Rashid reigned from 786 to 809. In many tales he wanders through Baghdad in disguise.
28316.m: Harun al-Rashid is the caliph from “One Thousand and One Nights”.

28317.q: Which animal did an Abbasid caliph give to Charlemagne around 800?
28317.e: The elephant was called Abul Abbas and arrived in Aachen in 802. It was a sign of good relations.
28317.m: Charlemagne received an elephant from Baghdad.

28318.q: What was the most important task in the House of Wisdom?
28318.e: Scholars there translated works from Greek, Persian and Indian languages into Arabic and carried out further research.
28318.m: Knowledge was collected and translated in the House of Wisdom.

28320.q: Which mathematician in the House of Wisdom gave his name to the word “algorithm”?
28320.e: The Latin form of al-Khwarizmi’s name became “Algorismi” and later “algorithm”.
28320.m: The word algorithm goes back to al-Khwarizmi.

28321.q: Which language does the word “algebra” come from?
28321.e: “Algebra” comes from the Arabic “al-jabr” in the title of a famous maths book from Baghdad.
28321.m: The word algebra is of Arabic origin.

28322.q: Which Greek philosopher was translated especially often in Baghdad?
28322.e: Almost all the writings of Aristotle were translated into Arabic. Through these translations Europe later rediscovered many of his works.
28322.m: The works of Aristotle were translated in Baghdad.

28323.q: Which science was promoted in Baghdad with its own observatories?
28323.e: Caliph al-Mamun had observatories built. There the scholars observed the sun, moon and stars closely.
28323.m: In Baghdad scholars studied the stars in observatories.

28324.q: Which number symbols came to Europe, among other ways, through scholars from Baghdad?
a: The Roman numerals I, V and X
28324.e: The digits originally come from India. Scholars in Baghdad such as al-Khwarizmi spread them, and so they later reached Europe.
28324.m: Our digits came to Europe through Arab scholars.

28325.q: What does the name Al-Andalus refer to?
28325.e: Al-Andalus means the areas of the Iberian Peninsula that were under Muslim rule in the Middle Ages.

28326.q: In which year did Muslim troops cross from Africa to Spain?
28326.e: In 711 an army under Tariq ibn Ziyad landed in Spain and defeated the Visigothic kingdom.
28326.m: Muslim rule in Spain began in the year 711.

28327.q: Which rock is named after the military leader Tariq ibn Ziyad?
28327.e: Gibraltar comes from “Jabal Tariq”, which means “mountain of Tariq”.

28328.q: What is the great mosque of Córdoba called, which is a cathedral today?
28328.e: The Mezquita is famous for its forest of columns and red and white arches. After the Christian conquest a cathedral was built inside it.
28328.m: The Mezquita of Córdoba is both a mosque and a cathedral.

28329.q: Which religions often lived side by side in Al-Andalus?
28329.e: Muslims, Christians and Jews lived together in Al-Andalus. They exchanged knowledge, even though there were tensions again and again.
28329.m: Muslims, Christians and Jews lived in Al-Andalus.

28330.q: Which city in Al-Andalus was considered one of the largest cities in Europe in the 10th century?
28330.e: As the capital of the caliphate, Córdoba had many inhabitants, mosques, baths and libraries.
28330.m: In the 10th century Córdoba was a world city.

28331.q: What is the Christian reconquest of the Iberian Peninsula called?
28331.e: “Reconquista” is Spanish for reconquest. It lasted several centuries.
28331.m: The Reconquista was the Christian reconquest of Spain.

28332.q: In which year did the Catholic Monarchs conquer Granada, the last Muslim kingdom in Spain?
28332.e: On 2 January 1492 the last emir, Boabdil, handed over the city. That ended the Reconquista.
28332.m: Al-Andalus ended with the fall of Granada in 1492.

28333.q: What could you find in 10th-century Córdoba that hardly existed in many European cities at the time?
28333.e: Córdoba had paved streets that were lit at night, many baths and a huge library of the caliph. Many cities in the rest of Europe were much smaller and simpler at that time.
28333.m: Córdoba was a very advanced city in the Middle Ages.

28335.q: Which court of the Alhambra has a fountain held up by twelve stone figures?
28335.e: In the Court of the Lions, twelve stone lions hold up a fountain basin.
28335.m: Twelve lions hold up the fountain in the Court of the Lions.

28336.q: What especially shapes the gardens and courtyards of the Alhambra?
28336.e: In this dry region water was precious. The rulers had it flow through gardens and courtyards in channels, pools and fountains.
28336.m: Water plays a big part in the gardens of the Alhambra.

28337.q: What are the walls of the Alhambra mainly decorated with?
28337.e: In Islamic palaces the walls are usually decorated with geometric patterns, plant shapes and Arabic writing.
28337.m: The Alhambra is decorated with ornaments and writing.

28338.q: Roughly what does the Arabic name “Alhambra” mean?
28338.e: The name comes from the Arabic word for red. The walls of reddish clay and stone glow in the evening sun.

28339.q: Where were the digits we call “Arabic” originally developed?
28339.e: The digits came about in India. Arabs adopted them and later brought them to Europe.
28339.m: Our digits originally come from India.

28340.q: Which digit did not exist in the Roman number system?
28340.e: The Romans had symbols such as I, V and X, but no symbol for zero.

28341.q: What is a number system called in which the value of a digit depends on its position?
28341.e: In 352 the 3 means three hundreds, because it is in the hundreds place.
28341.m: In a place value system the position of the digit counts.

28342.q: How do you write the number 2024 in Roman numerals?
28342.e: 2000 is MM, 20 is XX and 4 is IV. Together that makes MMXXIV.
28342.m: In Roman numerals 2024 is written MMXXIV.

28343.q: How many different digits do you need in the decimal system?
28343.e: With the digits 0 to 9 you can write any whole number. That makes ten digits.
28343.m: The decimal system needs only ten digits.

28344.q: Which calculating device was often used in Europe before Arabic numerals?
28344.e: It is hard to do written sums with Roman numerals. That is why people calculated with stones or beads on an abacus.
28344.m: Before Arabic numerals people often calculated with an abacus.

28345.q: What is the Arabic name of Avicenna?
28345.e: Avicenna is the Latin form of Ibn Sina.
28345.m: In Arabic, Avicenna is called Ibn Sina.

28346.q: In which fields was Avicenna especially famous?
28346.e: Avicenna was a doctor and a philosopher. He wrote about illnesses, remedies and about thinking.
28346.m: Avicenna was a great doctor and philosopher.

28347.q: What is Avicenna’s most important medical work called?
28347.e: “The Canon of Medicine” summed up the medical knowledge of his time in five books.
28347.m: Avicenna’s main work is the Canon of Medicine.

28348.q: What was Avicenna’s medical book used for in Europe for a long time?
a: As a cookery book in monasteries
As a law book for kings
As a prayer book in churches
28348.e: The Canon of Medicine was translated into Latin. Students learned from it until the 17th century.
28348.m: Avicenna’s Canon was a textbook in Europe for a long time.

28349.q: Which part of the world did Avicenna come from?
28349.e: Avicenna was born around 980 near Bukhara. The city is in Central Asia, in present-day Uzbekistan.

28350.q: In which language did Avicenna write most of his works?
28350.e: His mother tongue was Persian, but for science he mostly wrote in Arabic.
28350.m: Avicenna mostly wrote his works in Arabic.

28351.e: Mehmed II was only 21 years old at the time of the conquest.

28352.q: Which empire came to an end with the conquest of Constantinople in 1453?
28352.e: Constantinople was the capital of the Byzantine Empire. After the city fell, this empire no longer existed.

28353.q: Which weapon helped the Ottomans to break through the city walls?
28353.e: The Ottomans had huge cannons cast, among others by the cannon founder Orban. They fired at the walls for weeks.
28353.m: Huge cannons blasted holes in the walls of Constantinople.

28354.q: How did the Ottomans get round the chain blocking the harbour in 1453?
28354.e: The Ottomans dragged dozens of ships over a hill on wooden tracks and put them into the water behind the chain.
28354.m: The Ottomans dragged their ships over land into the harbour.

28355.q: Which nickname did the sultan who conquered Constantinople receive?
28355.e: In Turkish he is called “Fatih”, which means “the Conqueror”.
28355.m: The victor of 1453 is called “the Conqueror”.

28356.q: Where did many Greek scholars flee after the fall of Constantinople?
28356.e: The scholars brought Greek manuscripts to Italy. This helped the Renaissance.
28356.m: Greek scholars brought their knowledge to Italy.

28357.q: Who is the Ottoman Empire named after?
28357.e: Around 1300 Osman I was the leader of a small principality. His successors called themselves Ottomans after him.
28357.m: The Ottoman Empire bears the name of Osman I.

28358.q: Where did the Ottoman Empire begin around 1300?
28358.e: Osman’s principality was in the north-west of Asia Minor, in present-day Turkey, on the border with Byzantium.
28358.m: The Ottoman Empire began in Anatolia.

28359.q: Which 16th-century sultan bears the nickname “the Magnificent”?
28359.e: Suleiman I reigned from 1520 to 1566. Under him the Ottoman Empire was especially powerful.
28359.m: Suleiman the Magnificent led the empire to its height.

28360.q: Which city did the Ottomans besiege without success in 1529 and 1683?
28360.e: Both sieges of Vienna failed. After that the Ottomans did not advance any further into Central Europe.
28360.m: The Ottomans failed twice at Vienna.

28361.q: What were the elite soldiers of the Ottoman sultans called?
28361.e: The Janissaries were an infantry force that served the sultan directly.
28361.m: The Janissaries were the elite troops of the sultans.

28363.q: In which Swiss city was the treaty concluded in 1923 that set the borders of the new Turkey?
28363.e: The Treaty of Lausanne replaced earlier peace terms. It is seen as the founding document of present-day Turkey.
28363.m: The Treaty of Lausanne set the borders of Turkey in 1923.

28364.q: What is the inside of the Hagia Sophia decorated with, made of little pieces of glass and gold?
28364.e: Mosaics are made of many small coloured stones. In the Hagia Sophia they show Christ, Mary and emperors, among others.
28364.m: Precious mosaics decorate the Hagia Sophia.

28365.q: What happened to the first dome of the Hagia Sophia in the year 558?
a: It burned down in a fire
28365.e: Earthquakes had damaged the dome, and in 558 it collapsed. After that it was rebuilt steeper and more stable.
28365.m: The first dome of the Hagia Sophia collapsed in 558.

28366.q: Since which year has the Hagia Sophia been used as a mosque again?
28366.e: In 2020 a Turkish court and a presidential decree changed its status. Since then people pray there again, but visitors are still welcome.
28366.m: Since 2020 the Hagia Sophia has been a mosque again.

28367.q: Where did the great chariot races take place in Constantinople?
28367.e: The Hippodrome had room for tens of thousands of spectators. The Colosseum and the Circus Maximus are in Rome.
28367.m: In the Hippodrome of Constantinople the people cheered the charioteers.

28368.q: What was the huge Basilica Cistern under Constantinople used for?
a: As a church for the emperor
28368.e: In the Basilica Cistern, hundreds of columns hold up the ceiling. It stored drinking water for the city.
28368.m: The Basilica Cistern supplied Constantinople with water.

28369.q: On which important trade link between Asia and Europe was Constantinople?
28369.e: Goods from China and India reached the Mediterranean along the Silk Road. Trade made Constantinople rich.
28369.m: Constantinople profited from trade on the Silk Road.

28370.q: Around 552, what did Justinian I have monks secretly bring from Asia into the empire?
28370.e: Monks smuggled silkworm eggs inside hollow canes. In this way Byzantium could make silk itself.
28370.m: Under Justinian the silkworm came to Byzantium.

28371.q: What are the Muslims called who regard Ali as Muhammad’s rightful successor?
28371.e: The name comes from “Shiat Ali”, the party of Ali. The dispute over the succession shaped the time of the Umayyads.
28371.m: The Shiites regard Ali as Muhammad’s rightful successor.

28372.q: Which material was made in Baghdad from the end of the 8th century, after it became known from China?
28372.e: At the end of the 8th century a paper mill was set up in Baghdad. Paper was cheaper than parchment and helped to spread books.
28372.m: Paper was already being made in Baghdad in the 8th century.

28373.q: What was Baghdad famous for in the time of the Abbasids?
28373.e: Scholars from many countries worked in Baghdad. They translated Greek books and did research in medicine, mathematics and astronomy.
28373.m: Under the Abbasids Baghdad was a centre of knowledge.

28374.q: Who used to live in the Alhambra?
28374.e: The emirs of Granada lived and ruled in the Alhambra. In 1492 the last emir handed the city over to the Christian monarchs.
28374.m: The Alhambra was the palace of the Muslim rulers of Granada.

28375.q: Which emperor had a Renaissance palace built in the Alhambra in the 16th century?
28375.e: From 1527 Emperor Charles V had a palace with a round inner courtyard built.
28375.m: The Palace of Charles V also stands in the Alhambra.

28376.q: How do you write the Roman numeral XLII in Arabic numerals?
28376.e: XL means 50 minus 10, so 40. Then comes II, so 2. Together that makes 42.

28377.q: Roughly how long did the Ottoman siege of Constantinople in 1453 last?
28377.e: The siege began at the start of April and ended on 29 May. That is about 53 days.
28377.m: The siege of 1453 lasted just under two months.

28378.q: Against which horse-riding people did Otto the Great win the Battle of Lechfeld in 955?
28378.e: For decades the Hungarians had carried out raids into East Francia. After their defeat at Lechfeld these raids stopped.
28378.m: At Lechfeld in 955 Otto defeated the Hungarians.

28379.q: Which title did Otto the Great receive in Rome in 962?
28379.e: In 962 Otto was crowned emperor by the pope in Rome. That was the beginning of the Holy Roman Empire.
28379.m: Otto the Great became emperor in 962.

28380.q: Who was the father of Otto the Great, who was king before him?
28380.e: Henry I was King of East Francia from 919. After his death in 936 his son Otto became king.
28380.m: Otto the Great followed his father Henry I on the throne.

28381.q: For which city did Otto the Great found an archbishopric in 968?
28381.e: Magdeburg was Otto’s favourite place. From there the lands east of the Elbe were to be Christianised.
28381.m: Otto the Great made Magdeburg an archbishopric in 968.

28382.q: Why does Otto bear the nickname “the Great”?
a: Because of his successes as a ruler
Because he was the eldest son
Because he built great churches himself
28382.e: Otto defeated the Hungarians, strengthened his kingdom and became emperor. Because of these successes he was called “the Great”.
28382.m: Otto was called “the Great” because of his successes.

28383.q: In which country did Otto the Great gain influence through his marriage to Adelaide?
28383.e: Adelaide of Burgundy was the widow of the King of Italy. Through the marriage in 951 Otto gained a say in Italy.
28383.m: Through Adelaide, Otto gained influence in Italy.

28384.q: From which empire did the princess come who married Otto’s son in 972?
28384.e: Princess Theophanu came from Constantinople. The wedding was meant to improve relations between East and West.
28384.m: Otto’s son married a princess from Byzantium.

28385.q: On whom did Otto the Great especially rely when governing, because they could not found families that inherited power?
28385.e: Clergy were not allowed to marry, so they could not pass on their offices. Otto gave them land and rights and so gained loyal helpers.
28385.m: Otto the Great governed with the help of bishops and abbots.

28386.e: Investiture comes from the Latin “investire”, to clothe. It means the solemn installation of a bishop or abbot in his office.
28386.m: Investiture means installing someone in an office.

28387.q: Which pope quarrelled with King Henry IV in the Investiture Controversy?
28387.e: Gregory VII wanted only the Church to appoint bishops. In 1075 he banned lay investiture and later excommunicated the king.
28387.m: Gregory VII was Henry IV’s great opponent.

28388.q: Which treaty ended the Investiture Controversy in 1122?
28388.e: At Worms the emperor and the pope reached an agreement. The Church installed the bishops spiritually, and the emperor granted the worldly rights.
28388.m: The Concordat of Worms in 1122 ended the Investiture Controversy.

28389.q: How did the Investiture Controversy end in the year 1122?
a: With a compromise between emperor and pope
With a complete victory for the emperor
28389.e: In the Concordat of Worms, Emperor Henry V and the pope reached an agreement. The Church installed the bishops spiritually, and the emperor granted the worldly rights.
28389.m: The Investiture Controversy ended in 1122 with a compromise.

28390.q: With which symbols was a bishop installed in his spiritual office?
28390.e: Ring and staff stood for the spiritual office of the bishop. For the worldly rights the king later used the sceptre.
28390.m: Ring and staff are the symbols of a bishop’s office.

28391.q: Which right did Pope Gregory VII claim in the year 1075?
a: That he could even depose emperors
That he could raise taxes throughout Europe
That he could become emperor himself
28391.e: In a document, the Dictatus Papae, Gregory VII stated that the pope may depose emperors. These claims made the dispute with the king worse.
28391.m: Gregory VII placed the pope above the emperor.

28392.q: What did the Church reformers want to achieve in the 11th century?
a: To free the Church from the influence of worldly lords
To place the Church under the emperor
To hold church services in German
28392.e: The reform movement, which started at the monastery of Cluny, wanted an independent Church. This paved the way for the Investiture Controversy.
28392.m: The Church reformers wanted a Church independent of princes.

28393.q: What did the Church reformers especially criticise before the Investiture Controversy?
a: That church offices could be bought
28393.e: Buying and selling church offices is called simony. The reformers saw it as a serious abuse.
28393.m: Church offices were not supposed to be bought.

28394.q: What did Henry IV want to achieve with his walk to Canossa?
28394.e: Because of the excommunication, the princes were threatening to depose him. Through his penance he forced the pope to take him back into the Church.
28394.m: Henry IV went to Canossa to get rid of his excommunication.

28395.q: For how many days is Henry IV said to have waited in penitent’s clothes in front of Canossa Castle?
28395.e: According to the reports, the king stood in front of the gate from 25 to 28 January 1077. Only then was he let in.
28395.m: Henry IV waited three days in front of Canossa Castle.

28396.q: What did Henry IV have to cross on the way to Canossa in the winter of 1076/77?
28396.e: The king travelled with a few companions over the Alps to Italy in the middle of winter. The journey was considered very dangerous.
28396.m: Henry IV crossed the Alps in winter to reach Canossa.

28397.q: Whom did Henry IV want to meet at Canossa Castle in 1077?
28397.e: Pope Gregory VII was staying at Canossa Castle. Henry IV wanted him to lift the excommunication.
28397.m: At Canossa Henry IV met the pope.

28398.q: What does the saying “to go to Canossa” mean today?
28398.e: The saying recalls the king’s penance. Anyone who goes to Canossa has to admit a mistake and ask for forgiveness.
28398.m: Anyone who goes to Canossa has to apologise humbly.

28399.q: Which politician said in the Reichstag in 1872: “We will not go to Canossa”?
28399.e: At that time Bismarck was in conflict with the Catholic Church in the so-called Kulturkampf. With this sentence he meant that he would not submit to the pope.
28399.m: Bismarck said that they would not go to Canossa.

28400.q: What is an anti-king, like the one the princes elected against Henry IV in 1077?
a: A second king who disputes the first one’s crown
A king of a neighbouring country
A king who rules for only one year
A servant who stands in for the king
28400.e: Many princes were unhappy with Henry IV. In 1077 they elected Rudolf of Rheinfelden as anti-king, so that there were two kings.
28400.m: An anti-king disputes the crown of the ruling king.

28401.q: How did Frederick Barbarossa die in 1190?
28401.e: On the way to the Holy Land the emperor drowned in a river in present-day Turkey. It is not certain whether he was bathing or crossing it.
28401.m: Barbarossa drowned in a river in 1190.

28402.q: On which crusade did Frederick Barbarossa die?
28402.e: After the loss of Jerusalem in 1187 several kings set off on the Third Crusade. Barbarossa never reached the Holy Land.
28402.m: Barbarossa died on the Third Crusade.

28403.q: What does the Italian nickname “Barbarossa” mean?
28403.e: “Barba” means beard and “rossa” means red. The Italians called Emperor Frederick I this because of his reddish beard.

28404.q: Which Italian city did Barbarossa have destroyed in 1162?
28404.e: Milan led the resistance of the Lombard cities. After a long siege the city surrendered and was destroyed.
28404.m: Barbarossa destroyed the city of Milan in 1162.

28405.q: With which powerful Welf duke did Barbarossa fall into a serious quarrel?
28405.e: Henry the Lion was Duke of Saxony and Bavaria. He refused to help Barbarossa and lost his duchies in 1180.
28405.m: Henry the Lion was Barbarossa’s great rival.

28406.q: Who crowned Frederick Barbarossa emperor in Rome?
28406.e: In the Middle Ages the emperors of the Holy Roman Empire were crowned by the pope in Rome. Barbarossa became emperor in 1155.

28407.q: Which relics were brought to Cologne in 1164 after the conquest of Milan?
a: The bones of the Three Kings
28407.e: Barbarossa’s chancellor Rainald of Dassel brought them to Cologne. The Shrine of the Three Kings, which stands in Cologne Cathedral today, was made for them.
28407.m: The relics of the Three Kings have been in Cologne since 1164.

28408.q: What happened to two of Barbarossa’s sons at his great court festival in 1184?
28408.e: Thousands of knights celebrated at the court festival in Mainz. The highlight was the knighting of the emperor’s two sons.
28408.m: At the court festival in 1184 Barbarossa’s sons were knighted.

28409.q: Which famous emperor was the grandfather of Frederick II?
28409.e: Frederick II was the son of Emperor Henry VI. Henry’s father was Frederick I, known as Barbarossa.
28409.m: Frederick II was a grandson of Barbarossa.

28410.q: On which island did Frederick II of Hohenstaufen grow up?
28410.e: His mother Constance was the heiress of the Kingdom of Sicily. Frederick spent his childhood in Palermo.
28410.m: Frederick II grew up on Sicily.

28411.q: Which Latin nickname, meaning “the wonder of the world”, was given to Frederick II?
28411.e: Frederick II spoke several languages and was interested in science. That is why the people of his time marvelled at him.

28412.q: Which subject did Frederick II write a famous book about?
28412.e: The book is called “De arte venandi cum avibus”, the art of hunting with birds. It contains careful observations of birds.
28412.m: Frederick II wrote a book about falconry.

28413.q: How did Frederick II win back Jerusalem for the Christians in the year 1229?
28413.e: Frederick II made a treaty with Sultan al-Kamil. In this way he obtained Jerusalem almost without fighting.
28413.m: Frederick II gained Jerusalem through negotiations.

28414.q: Why did Frederick II found a university in Naples in 1224?
a: To train officials for his kingdom
28414.e: Frederick II needed well-trained lawyers and officials for his kingdom. That is why he founded his own university.
28414.m: Frederick II founded a university for his officials.

28415.q: What did the law code that Frederick II issued for his Kingdom of Sicily in 1231 regulate?
a: The recipes of the court kitchen
28415.e: The law code reorganised administration and justice in the Kingdom of Sicily. It is seen as a very modern law code for its time.
28415.m: With a law code, Frederick II organised administration and the courts.

28416.q: To which valley in Central Switzerland did Frederick II grant a charter of freedom in 1240?
28416.e: The people of Schwyz had supported the emperor at the siege of Faenza. In the charter he placed them directly under the empire.
28416.m: Schwyz received a charter of freedom from Frederick II in 1240.

28417.q: What was the most important task of the prince-electors in the Holy Roman Empire?
28417.e: The prince-electors decided who became King of the Romans. The person elected could later be crowned emperor by the pope.

28418.q: According to the Golden Bull, how many of the prince-electors were archbishops?
28418.e: The spiritual prince-electors were the archbishops of Mainz, Cologne and Trier.

28419.q: Which king was one of the secular prince-electors?
28419.e: Besides the King of Bohemia, the Count Palatine of the Rhine, the Duke of Saxony and the Margrave of Brandenburg were secular prince-electors.
28419.m: The King of Bohemia was one of the prince-electors.

28421.q: What did the Golden Bull of 1356 mainly regulate?
a: The election of the king by the prince-electors
28421.e: The Golden Bull laid down that seven prince-electors elect the king. It remained a fundamental law of the empire until 1806.
28421.m: The Golden Bull regulated the election of the king by the prince-electors.

28422.q: Which emperor issued the Golden Bull?
28422.e: Charles IV of the House of Luxembourg was also King of Bohemia. He mostly lived in Prague.
