28422.m: Emperor Charles IV issued the Golden Bull.

28423.q: How did the Golden Bull get its name?
a: From the price of gold at the time
28423.e: A bull is a document with a seal. On important documents the seal was made of gold.
28423.m: The Golden Bull is named after its golden seal.

28424.q: According to the Golden Bull, in which city was the election of the king to take place?
28424.e: The Golden Bull named Frankfurt as the place of election. The king was then crowned in Aachen.
28424.m: The election of the king took place in Frankfurt am Main.

28425.q: Which title did William hold before he became King of England?
28425.e: William had been Duke of Normandy since he was a child. Only through the conquest did he become king.
28425.m: William the Conqueror was a duke first.

28426.q: In which church in London was William the Conqueror crowned?
28426.e: William had himself crowned in Westminster Abbey. Since then English kings have almost always been crowned there.
28426.m: William was crowned in Westminster Abbey.

28427.q: Which unflattering nickname did William have before his conquest?
28427.e: William was the illegitimate child of Duke Robert I. That is why he was first called “William the Bastard”.

28428.q: Which famous castle in London did William the Conqueror have built to secure his power?
28428.e: After 1066 William had a mighty stone tower built in London, the White Tower. It is the core of the Tower of London.
28428.m: William the Conqueror had the Tower of London built.

28429.q: Which long embroidered strip of pictures tells the story of the conquest of England in 1066?
a: The Picture Bible of St Gallen
28429.e: The Bayeux Tapestry is about 70 metres long. Like a comic, it shows how William crossed the English Channel and won the Battle of Hastings.
28429.m: The Bayeux Tapestry shows the conquest of England.

28430.q: Which language did the nobility in England speak after William’s conquest?
28430.e: The Normans spoke a form of Old French. That is why many English words come from French.
28430.m: After 1066 the English nobility spoke French.

28431.q: Which son succeeded William the Conqueror as King of England in 1087?
28431.e: William II was called “Rufus”, meaning “the Red”, probably because of his red hair. His elder brother Robert inherited Normandy.
28431.m: William II succeeded his father on the English throne.

28432.q: In which year did the Battle of Hastings take place?
28432.e: On 14 October 1066 William the Conqueror defeated the English army. After that he became King of England.
28432.m: The Battle of Hastings was in 1066.

28433.q: According to tradition, how is the English king said to have died at the Battle of Hastings?
a: From an arrow in the eye
From a fall from his horse
28433.e: That is how it is often told, and how the Bayeux Tapestry is interpreted. Whether it really happened like that is disputed among experts.
28433.m: According to legend, the English king was hit in the eye by an arrow.

28434.q: Who won the Battle of Hastings?
28434.e: William, Duke of Normandy, defeated the English army. That is why he is called William the Conqueror.

28435.q: What is the battle formation of the English at Hastings called, with shields held close together side by side?
28435.e: The warriors stood close together on a hill. Their shields formed a wall that was hard to break through.
28435.m: At Hastings the English fought in a shield wall.

28436.q: Which troops did the Normans have at Hastings that the English lacked?
28436.e: The Anglo-Saxons fought on foot. The Normans used armoured horsemen and archers.
28436.m: At Hastings the Normans had a strong cavalry.

28437.q: With which trick did the Normans lure English soldiers out of their position at Hastings?
a: With a false offer of peace
With a fire in the forest
28437.e: The horsemen pretended to flee. English warriors chased them, left the shield wall and were then surrounded.
28437.m: At Hastings the Normans faked a retreat.

28438.q: What did William later have built right on the battlefield of Hastings?
28438.e: Battle Abbey was built as penance for the many dead. The town there is simply called “Battle” today.
28438.m: Battle Abbey stands on the battlefield of Hastings.

28439.q: Across which sea did William’s army cross to England in 1066?
28439.e: The Normans came from Normandy in northern France. With many ships they crossed the English Channel to southern England.
28439.m: The Normans crossed the English Channel in 1066.

28440.q: In which region of France is the Bayeux Tapestry on display today?
28440.e: The tapestry is shown in a museum in the town of Bayeux. Bayeux is in Normandy.
28440.m: The Bayeux Tapestry is on display in Normandy.

28442.q: On which fabric were the pictures of the Bayeux Tapestry made?
28442.e: The base fabric is linen. It was embroidered with dyed woollen threads.
28442.m: The Bayeux Tapestry is made of wool on linen.

28443.q: In which country was the Bayeux Tapestry probably made?
28443.e: Many experts think it was embroidered in Canterbury in southern England. English embroiderers were famous at the time.
28443.m: The Bayeux Tapestry was probably made in England.

28444.q: How were the pictures put onto the Bayeux Tapestry?
28444.e: Although it is called a tapestry, it is really an embroidery. The pictures were embroidered on linen with coloured woollen threads.
28444.m: The Bayeux Tapestry is really an embroidery.

28445.q: What is noticeable about the end of the Bayeux Tapestry?
28445.e: The last piece has been lost. That is why we do not know exactly which scene the tapestry originally ended with.
28445.m: The end of the Bayeux Tapestry is missing.

28446.q: Roughly when was the Bayeux Tapestry made?
28446.e: It was made a few years after the events it shows. That is why it is an important source for history.
28446.m: The Bayeux Tapestry was made around 1070.

28447.q: Did King John keep to Magna Carta after 1215?
a: No, he soon had it declared invalid
Yes, he kept to it until his death
Yes, and he wrote it himself
No, he burned all the copies
28447.e: As early as August 1215, at John’s request, the pope declared the charter invalid. This led to war with the barons.
28447.m: King John did not want to keep to Magna Carta.

28448.q: What did the most famous clause of Magna Carta guarantee?
28448.e: No free man could be arrested or punished without the judgement of his equals or without the law. This idea still has an effect on today’s fundamental rights.
28448.m: Magna Carta forbade punishment without lawful judgement.

28449.q: In which language is Magna Carta written?
28449.e: In the Middle Ages important documents were usually written in Latin. Magna Carta is written on parchment.
28449.m: Magna Carta is written in Latin.

28450.q: Who forced King John to accept Magna Carta?
28450.e: The barons were unhappy with John’s high taxes and his defeats. They forced him to confirm their rights in writing.
28450.m: The barons forced the king to accept Magna Carta.

28451.q: Is part of Magna Carta still valid today?
a: Yes, some sentences are still valid in England today
No, it was only valid for one day
Yes, it is the constitution of Switzerland
28451.e: Most of the clauses were abolished over time. Some sentences, for example on protection from punishment without judgement, are still valid in England today.
28451.m: A few sentences of Magna Carta are still valid today.

28452.q: Under Magna Carta, what could the king no longer demand without the consent of the royal council?
28452.e: The king could only raise certain taxes, such as scutage, with the consent of the great men of the kingdom.
28452.m: The king needed the council’s consent for certain taxes.

28454.q: Against which country had King John lost a war shortly before Magna Carta?
28454.e: In 1214 John lost an important battle against the French king. After that he was weakened and the barons could put pressure on him.
28454.m: A defeat against France weakened King John.

28455.q: Between which two kingdoms was the Hundred Years’ War fought?
28455.e: It was mainly about the French throne and about lands in France that belonged to the English kings.
28455.m: In the Hundred Years’ War England and France fought each other.

28456.q: How many years did the Hundred Years’ War from 1337 to 1453 actually last?
28456.e: 1453 minus 1337 makes 116. But there were long truces in between.
28456.m: The Hundred Years’ War lasted 116 years.

28457.q: Who won the Battle of Agincourt in 1415, even though their army was much smaller?
28457.e: At Agincourt in northern France a small English army defeated a much larger French army of knights.
28457.m: The English won at Agincourt in 1415.

28458.q: Which weapon of the English foot soldiers was especially feared in the Hundred Years’ War?
28458.e: English archers could shoot quickly and far. In several great battles they hit many French knights.
28458.m: The English longbow was feared in the Hundred Years’ War.

28459.q: What was the Hundred Years’ War mainly about?
28459.e: The English king Edward III thought that the French throne belonged to him. This led to a long war over the crown and over lands in France.
28459.m: The Hundred Years’ War was about the French crown.

28460.q: Who won the Hundred Years’ War in the end?
28460.e: By 1453 England had lost almost all its lands in France. Only the town of Calais stayed English until 1558.
28460.m: France won the Hundred Years’ War.

28461.q: Which duchy was at times allied with England in the Hundred Years’ War?
28461.e: The dukes of Burgundy were in conflict with the French royal family. In 1435 they made peace with France again.
28461.m: Burgundy was at times allied with England.

28462.q: Which epidemic raged throughout Europe during the Hundred Years’ War?
28462.e: From 1347 the plague, the Black Death, spread across Europe. It also hit England and France hard and interrupted the fighting.
28462.m: The plague raged during the Hundred Years’ War.

28463.q: By which nickname is Joan of Arc known?
28463.e: She received this nickname after freeing the besieged city in 1429.
28463.m: Joan of Arc is called the Maid of Orléans.

28464.q: In which city was Joan of Arc burned at the stake in 1431?
28464.e: Rouen in Normandy was in English hands at the time. Her trial also took place there.
28464.m: Joan of Arc died in Rouen in 1431.

28465.q: What kind of family did Joan of Arc come from?
28465.e: Joan grew up in a peasant family in the village of Domrémy in eastern France. Even so, she later led an army.
28465.m: Joan of Arc was a peasant girl.

28466.q: Who captured Joan of Arc near Compiègne in 1430?
28466.e: The Burgundians, who were allied with England, captured her. Then they handed Joan over to the English for money.
28466.m: Joan of Arc was captured by the Burgundians.

28467.q: What did the court accuse Joan of Arc of at her trial?
a: Treason against the King of France
28467.e: A church court under English influence condemned her as a relapsed heretic. She was also accused of wearing men’s clothing.
28467.m: Joan of Arc was condemned for heresy.

28468.q: What is Joan of Arc for the Catholic Church today?
28468.e: Pope Benedict XV declared Joan of Arc a saint in 1920. In France she is also a national heroine.
28468.m: Joan of Arc is a saint.

28469.q: What happened in 1456, 25 years after the death of Joan of Arc?
28469.e: In a new trial the sentence was declared invalid. This is called the rehabilitation trial.
28469.m: In 1456 the sentence against Joan of Arc was overturned.

28470.q: Which office did Rudolf of Habsburg receive in the year 1273?
a: He became King of the Romans
28470.e: Rudolf was elected king in Frankfurt in 1273. He was the first king from the House of Habsburg.
28470.m: Rudolf of Habsburg became king in 1273.

28471.q: What was missing in the empire in the roughly 20 years before Rudolf of Habsburg was elected?
28471.e: During this time there was no king whom everyone recognised. It is called the Interregnum, meaning the period between reigns.
28471.m: With Rudolf of Habsburg the empire had a recognised king again.

28472.q: In which present-day Swiss region is the ancestral castle of the Habsburgs?
28472.e: Habsburg Castle stands near Brugg in the canton of Aargau. The family that later ruled Austria is named after it.

28473.q: How did Rudolf of Habsburg become king?
a: He was elected by the princes
He inherited the crown from his father
He bought the crown from the pope
28473.e: In the Holy Roman Empire the king was elected by the most powerful princes. In 1273 they elected Count Rudolf of Habsburg.
28473.m: In the empire the king was elected.

28474.q: Which duchy did Rudolf give to his sons, laying the foundation of Habsburg power?
28474.e: In 1282 Rudolf granted Austria and Styria to his sons as fiefs. The Habsburgs ruled there until 1918.
28474.m: Since Rudolf, Austria has belonged to the Habsburgs.

28475.q: How did the Swiss Confederates behave towards the power of the Habsburgs?
a: They chose them as their Landammänner
28475.e: Shortly after Rudolf’s death in 1291, Uri, Schwyz and Unterwalden joined together. In 1315 the Confederates defeated a Habsburg army at Morgarten.
28475.m: The Swiss Confederates resisted the rule of the Habsburgs.

28476.q: Why is Rudolf of Habsburg regarded only as a king and not as an emperor?
a: He was never crowned by the pope
28476.e: The title of emperor required a coronation by the pope in Rome. That never happened for Rudolf.
28476.m: Rudolf of Habsburg was never crowned emperor.

28477.q: Which noble title did Rudolf of Habsburg hold before he became king?
28477.e: Rudolf was a count with lands in Aargau, Alsace and on the Upper Rhine. That is why his election as king was a surprise.
28477.m: Before his election Rudolf of Habsburg was a count.

28478.q: Into how many parts was the farmland divided in the three-field system?
28478.e: A village’s farmland was divided into three large fields. One grew winter grain, one summer grain and one lay fallow.
28478.m: In the three-field system three fields changed their use every year.

28479.q: In the three-field system, what happened to the field that lay “fallow”?
a: It was not planted for a year
28479.e: The fallow field was not sown for a year so that the soil could recover. Cattle often grazed there, and their dung fertilised the soil.
28479.m: A fallow field rests for a year so that the soil can recover.

28480.q: Which grain was typically sown in autumn as winter grain in the Middle Ages?
28480.e: Rye and wheat were sown in autumn and spent the winter in the field. Maize and rice were not grown in medieval Europe north of the Alps.
28480.m: Rye is a typical winter grain that is sown in autumn.

28481.q: In the three-field system, which plant was typically grown in spring on the summer field?
28481.e: Oats, barley or pulses grew on the summer field. Potatoes and tomatoes only came to Europe after the discovery of America.
28481.m: Oats and barley were sown in spring as summer grain.

28482.q: Which farming system was replaced in many places by the three-field system in the High Middle Ages?
28482.e: In the older two-field system, half of the farmland lay fallow every year. Crop rotation only came in modern times.
28482.m: The three-field system replaced the older two-field system.

28483.q: What did “compulsory field use” mean in the three-field system?
a: All farmers had to farm their land in the same way
Every farmer could sow whatever he wanted
The fields were not allowed to be ploughed
Only the priest was allowed to enter the fields
28483.e: Because the farmers’ plots lay side by side as narrow strips in the fields, everyone had to sow and harvest the same thing at the same time. Otherwise, when ploughing, you would have destroyed your neighbour’s crops.
28483.m: Compulsory field use obliged all farmers to farm their land together in the same way.

28484.q: What was the advantage of growing both winter and summer grain in the three-field system?
a: If one harvest failed, there was still the other
The farmers did not have to pay taxes
28484.e: Winter and summer grain were sown and harvested at different times. If, for example, a wet summer spoiled one harvest, the other made sure there was food.
28484.m: In the three-field system two grain harvests spread the risk of a failed harvest.

28485.q: In Switzerland, what were the large fields of a village in the three-field system often called?
28485.e: In German-speaking Switzerland the three large fields were called Zelgen. The term still lives on today in field and street names such as “Zelgli”.
28485.m: In Switzerland the fields of the three-field system were called Zelgen.

28486.q: What is the unpaid work called that dependent peasants had to do for their lord?
28486.e: On certain days dependent peasants had to plough, harvest or carry loads on the lord’s fields. They received no wages for it.
28486.m: Labour service was unpaid work done by peasants for their lord.

28487.q: In the Middle Ages, who managed the manor farm on behalf of the lord?
28487.e: The steward, in German “Meier”, ran the manor farm, collected the dues and supervised the labour services. The surname Meier or Meyer goes back to this office.
28487.m: The steward managed the manor farm for the lord.

28488.q: What was the tax called for which farmers had to give a tenth of their harvest to the Church?
28488.e: The tithe was originally a church tax of a tenth of the harvest and the livestock. In many villages a “tithe barn” still reminds people of it.
28488.m: The tithe was a tax of a tenth of the harvest paid to the Church.

28489.q: What did it mean if a peasant in the Middle Ages was a “serf”?
a: He was not allowed to leave his lord’s land
He owned his land completely freely
He was free from all taxes
He was allowed to fight as a knight
28489.e: Serfs were personally dependent on their lord and bound to his land. They often even needed his permission to marry.
28489.m: Serfs were bound to their lord and his land.

28490.q: What is the land called that all the villagers used together as pasture or woodland?
28490.e: The common land, in Switzerland the “Allmend”, belonged to the village community and was used as cattle pasture, a source of wood or a watering place. In Switzerland there are still common lands today, and corporations that manage them.
28490.m: Common land was land that the whole village community used together.

28491.q: What is the lord’s land called that the lord had farmed directly from his manor farm?
28491.e: The demesne belonged directly to the manor farm. It was worked by farmhands and maids and by the labour services of the dependent peasants.
28491.m: The demesne was the lord’s land that belonged to the manor farm.

28492.q: What was a tithe barn, as you can still see in some villages, used for?
a: As a dance hall for festivals
As a church for the village
28492.e: The peasants had to give a tenth of their harvest. This grain was collected in the tithe barn.
28492.m: The peasants’ dues were stored in the tithe barn.

28493.q: At what age did a nobleman’s son usually begin his training as a page?
28493.e: At about 7 years old a boy went as a page to another noble’s court. There his long training to become a knight began.
28493.m: Knight training began at about 7 years old as a page.

28494.q: What was a young man called who served a knight from about the age of 14 and went into battle with him?
28494.e: At about 14 the page became a squire. He looked after his knight’s horse and armour and learned to fight with sword and lance.
28494.m: A squire served a knight and learned to fight.

28495.q: What is the body protection made of many small iron rings linked together called?
28495.e: Chain mail consisted of thousands of small iron rings and protected against sword blows. It was the usual armour of knights in the High Middle Ages, before plate armour came in.
28495.m: Chain mail is made of many small linked iron rings.

28496.q: Where was a page usually brought up in the Middle Ages?
a: At the court of another noble
With a farmer in the village
28496.e: Pages were usually sent to the court of a friendly or higher-ranking noble. There they learned riding, good behaviour, table manners and serving the lady of the house.
28496.m: Pages learned manners and riding at another noble’s court.

28497.q: What was one of a squire’s tasks?
a: Looking after his lord’s armour and horse
28497.e: The squire cleaned armour and weapons, looked after the horse and helped the knight put on his armour. In this way he learned everything a knight needed to know.
28497.m: A squire looked after his knight’s armour and horse.

28499.q: What did the knightly virtue of “mâze” mean?
a: Taking as much loot as possible
28499.e: “Mâze” meant moderation, finding the right measure in everything. A knight was supposed to be neither mean nor wasteful, neither cowardly nor reckless.
28499.m: The knightly virtue of “mâze” demanded moderation in everything.

28500.q: What did the knightly virtue of loyalty demand of a knight?
a: To stand by his lord and his word
To win as many tournaments as possible
To ride a new horse every day
Never to speak to other knights
28500.e: Loyalty, in Middle High German “triuwe”, was considered one of a knight’s most important duties. He was supposed to serve his feudal lord and keep his word.
28500.m: A loyal knight stood by his lord and his word.

28501.q: With which weapon did two knights ride towards each other in a joust?
28501.e: In a joust two riders tried to hit their opponent with the lance or knock him out of the saddle. It was the best-known part of a tournament.
28501.m: In a joust two knights on horseback fought with lances.

28502.q: What was the “coronel” at the tip of a tournament lance for?
a: It was a decoration for ladies
28502.e: The coronel was a tip with several short prongs. It spread the force of the blow and did not slip off, but caused less injury than a sharp point.
28502.m: The coronel made the tip of a tournament lance less dangerous.

28503.q: From the Late Middle Ages, what was the long wooden barrier between the two riders in a joust for?
a: To stop the horses from colliding
So that the audience could sit
So that the knights had to dismount
The lances were attached to it
28503.e: The barrier separated the two riding lanes. In this way the horses did not crash head-on, and the knights met at an angle.
28503.m: In a joust a barrier separated the two riders.

28504.q: How did the Church react to knights’ tournaments in the 12th century?
28504.e: Because many knights were injured or killed in tournaments, the Church banned them, for example at the Council of Clermont in 1130. The tournaments still went on.
28504.m: The Church banned tournaments but could not stop them.

28505.q: In which country did knights’ tournaments probably begin in the 11th century?
28505.e: The first tournaments are thought to have taken place in northern France in the 11th century. From there they spread across all of Europe.
28505.m: Knights’ tournaments probably began in France.

28506.q: In a joust, what showed that a hit was a good one?
a: The lance shattered on the opponent
28506.e: Tournament lances were made so that they broke on a powerful hit. Broken lances scored points, and knocking the opponent out of the saddle was even better.
28506.m: In a tournament a lance broken on the opponent counted as a good hit.

28507.q: Why did knights often fight with blunt weapons at tournaments?
a: So that nobody was badly injured
So that the fights lasted longer
28507.e: Tournaments were for practice and entertainment. Blunt weapons were meant to avoid injuries, but accidents still often happened.
28507.m: Blunt weapons were meant to prevent injuries at tournaments.

28508.q: What were coats of arms on a knight’s shield originally for?
a: Recognising the knight in full armour
28508.e: With his helmet closed, a knight could no longer be recognised. A sign on the shield showed friend and foe who was inside the armour.
28508.m: Coats of arms made knights in armour recognisable.

28509.q: What are figures such as two lions standing on the left and right of a coat of arms called?
28509.e: Supporters are people, animals or mythical creatures that hold up the shield from both sides. They are a decorative extra and not a required part of the coat of arms.
28509.m: Supporters hold up the shield of a coat of arms from the side.

28510.q: Which two colours count as “metals” in heraldry?
28510.e: Gold is usually shown as yellow and silver as white. Red, blue, black and green, on the other hand, count as colours.
28510.m: In heraldry gold and silver are the two metals.

28511.q: Which important rule about arranging colours applies in heraldry?
a: Never metal on metal or colour on colour
Never more than two animals on the shield
28511.e: Gold or silver should not be placed on gold or silver, and a colour should not be placed on a colour. In this way the coat of arms can be recognised easily even from far away.
28511.m: A coat of arms puts metal and colour next to each other so that it is easy to recognise.

28512.q: What does the Swiss coat of arms look like?
a: A white cross on a red background
A red cross on a white background
A white cross on a blue background
A golden cross on a red background
28512.e: The Swiss coat of arms shows a free-standing white cross on a red shield. It probably goes back to the battle flag of the people of Schwyz.
28512.m: The Swiss coat of arms shows a white cross on a red background.

28513.q: What were the men called in the Middle Ages who knew the coats of arms and announced the knights at tournaments?
28513.e: Heralds had to recognise all the coats of arms. The word heraldry, the study of coats of arms, also comes from them.
28513.m: Heralds were experts on coats of arms, hence the word heraldry.

28514.q: What is the decoration called that sits on top of the helmet in a full coat of arms?
28514.e: The crest was a figure made of feathers, horns or animals on the helmet. Together with the shield and helmet it is part of a full coat of arms.
28514.m: The crest decorates the helmet above the shield.

28515.q: From whose point of view are “right” and “left” decided in heraldry?
28515.e: The heraldic right side is the right side of the knight holding the shield. For the viewer it is therefore on the left.
28515.m: In heraldry right and left are seen from the shield bearer’s point of view.

28516.q: What were the middle-class song poets called who carried on the art of the minnesingers in guild schools in the Late Middle Ages and after?
28516.e: The Mastersingers were mostly craftsmen in cities such as Nuremberg and Mainz. Their best-known member is Hans Sachs.
28516.m: The Mastersingers carried on the song art of the minnesingers in the towns.

28517.q: In “high Minne”, to whom was the singer’s song addressed?
a: To the peasants in the village
28517.e: In high Minne the singer admired a high-ranking, often married lady. This love remained unfulfilled and was meant to make the singer a better person.
28517.m: High Minne sang of admiring an unattainable lady.

28518.q: Who is regarded as the most famous German-speaking minnesinger?
28518.e: Walther von der Vogelweide lived around 1200 and wrote love songs and political verses. His song “Under der linden” is still known today.
28518.m: Walther von der Vogelweide is the best-known minnesinger.

28519.q: In which city was the Codex Manesse, the most important collection of Minne songs, made around 1300?
28519.e: The Codex Manesse was written and painted in Zurich around 1300. It is named after the Manesse family of Zurich, who collected songs.
28519.m: The Codex Manesse was made in Zurich.

28520.q: What do the full-page pictures in the Codex Manesse mainly show?
28520.e: The codex contains 137 coloured pictures, each showing a poet, often with his coat of arms. The pictures are not real portraits but idealised images.
28520.m: The pictures in the Codex Manesse show the minnesingers.

28521.q: In which stage of the German language are the songs of the Minnesang written?
28521.e: The minnesingers wrote around 1200 in Middle High German. This stage of the language was spoken and written from about 1050 to 1350.
28521.m: Minne songs are written in Middle High German.

28522.q: Which poets and singers from southern France were models for the German Minnesang?
28522.e: From about 1100 the troubadours wrote love songs in the Occitan language in southern France. The German minnesingers took over their ideas of courtly love.
28522.m: The troubadours of southern France were models for the Minnesang.

28523.q: What does a “dawn song” in the Minnesang tell of?
a: Two lovers saying goodbye in the morning
28523.e: In a dawn song two lovers must part at daybreak, often woken by a watchman. It is a separate type of Minnesang.
28523.m: A dawn song tells of lovers saying goodbye at dawn.

28524.q: Which shape of arch is typical of Romanesque churches?
28524.e: Romanesque buildings have round arches over windows, doors and arcades. The builders took this shape from the ancient Romans.
28524.m: The round arch is the hallmark of the Romanesque style.

28525.q: How do Romanesque churches typically look from the outside?
a: Solid, with thick walls and small windows
Playful, with lots of gold decoration
Plain, made of steel and concrete
28525.e: The thick walls had to carry the heavy weight of the ceiling and vault. That is why only small windows were possible, and the inside stayed rather dark.
28525.m: Romanesque churches have thick walls and small windows.

28526.q: During which period was the Romanesque style mainly used for building in Central Europe?
28526.e: In Central Europe the Romanesque period lasted from about the year 1000 to around 1250. After that the Gothic style took over.
28526.m: Romanesque was the building style from around the year 1000 into the 13th century.

28527.q: Why is the building style called “Romanesque”?
a: Because it is reminiscent of Roman architecture
Because it was invented in Romania
Because it is named after a builder called Roman
Because it was only found in Rome
28527.e: The name was coined in the 19th century. Round arches, columns and vaults reminded researchers of Roman buildings.
28527.m: Romanesque is named after the architecture of the Romans.

28529.q: What is the Romanesque church of St Martin in Zillis (Grisons) famous for?
a: For its painted wooden ceiling with many picture panels
For the tallest church tower in Europe
For its organ made of ice
28529.e: The wooden ceiling in Zillis was made around 1110 and consists of 153 painted panels. It is considered one of the oldest surviving church ceilings painted with figures.
28529.m: The church in Zillis has a famous Romanesque picture ceiling.

28530.q: What is the underground room beneath the choir of many Romanesque churches called?
28530.e: Relics of saints or the graves of important people were often kept in the crypt. It usually lies beneath the raised choir.
28530.m: The crypt is a room beneath the choir of a church.

28531.q: Which shape of arch is the typical feature of Gothic architecture?
28531.e: The pointed arch directs the weight downwards more steeply than the round arch. So churches could be built taller and slimmer.
28531.m: The pointed arch is the hallmark of Gothic architecture.

28532.q: What were the flying buttresses on the outside of Gothic cathedrals for?
a: They carried the thrust of the vaults outwards
They served as stairs for craftsmen
They held the bells in place
28532.e: Flying buttresses and buttresses take the sideways thrust of the vault. As a result the walls needed less masonry and could have large windows.
28532.m: Flying buttresses support Gothic churches from the outside.

28533.q: What is the large round window with tracery radiating outwards on many Gothic churches called?
28533.e: The rose window often sits above the main entrance. Its colourful stained glass usually shows scenes from the Bible.
28533.m: The rose window is a large round window of Gothic churches.

28534.q: Which church near Paris is considered the first Gothic building?
28534.e: Around 1140 Abbot Suger had the choir of the Abbey Church of Saint-Denis built in the new style. From there Gothic architecture spread across the whole of Europe.
28534.m: Gothic architecture began around 1140 at Saint-Denis near Paris.

28535.q: Where does the name “Gothic” come from?
a: From the Goths, as an insulting label
28535.e: Italian scholars of the Renaissance scornfully called the style “Gothic”, meaning barbaric like the Goths. But the building style has nothing to do with the Gothic people.
28535.m: The name Gothic was originally meant as an insult.

28536.q: What are the stone figures on Gothic churches called, often shaped like mythical creatures, that carry rainwater away from the roof?
28536.e: Gargoyles carry the rainwater far away from the wall so that the masonry is not damaged. Many look like dragons, demons or animals.
28536.m: Gargoyles carry rainwater away on Gothic churches.

28537.q: In which year was Cologne Cathedral completed after more than 600 years of building?
28537.e: Building began in 1248 but stopped for centuries. Only in the 19th century was it continued according to the old plans and completed in 1880.

28538.q: What is the ceiling of Gothic churches called, in which stone ribs cross each other?
28538.e: In a rib vault, crossing ribs carry the weight. The load is directed onto a few points, so that thin walls and windows are possible in between.
28538.m: The rib vault is typical of Gothic churches.

28539.q: Who crowned himself Emperor of the French in Notre-Dame Cathedral in 1804?
28539.e: The pope was present at the coronation in December 1804, but Napoleon placed the crown on his own head. The event was painted by the artist Jacques-Louis David.
28539.m: Napoleon crowned himself emperor in Notre-Dame in 1804.

28541.q: Which special point is marked in the ground on the square in front of Notre-Dame?
a: Point zero of the roads of France
The grave of the first king
28541.e: A bronze plate in front of the cathedral marks “Point zéro”. Road distances from Paris to other places in France are measured from there.
28541.m: Point zero of the French roads lies in front of Notre-Dame.

28542.q: In which year did a huge fire destroy the roof of Notre-Dame?
28542.e: On 15 April 2019 the roof timbers burned down and the spire collapsed. The towers and the rose windows were mostly saved.

28544.q: After the fire in 2019, what happened to the collapsed spire of Notre-Dame?
a: It was rebuilt as it was before
It was replaced with a modern glass one
It was put on display in a museum
28544.e: France decided to rebuild the spire exactly as it had been before. Craftsmen worked with oak and lead to do this.
28544.m: The spire of Notre-Dame was rebuilt true to the original.

28545.q: Which famous relic was rescued during the fire at Notre-Dame in 2019?
28545.e: The Crown of Thorns, which is venerated as the crown of Jesus, belongs to the treasury of Notre-Dame. Firefighters brought it to safety during the fire.
28545.m: The Crown of Thorns of Notre-Dame was rescued from the fire in 2019.

28546.q: In which architectural style was Notre-Dame de Paris built?
28546.e: Notre-Dame is a Gothic cathedral. Typical features are pointed arches, high vaults and large rose windows.
28546.m: Notre-Dame is a masterpiece of Gothic architecture.

28547.q: Which country did Francis of Assisi come from?
28547.e: Francis was born around 1181 in Assisi in the Italian region of Umbria. He also died there in 1226.
28547.m: Francis of Assisi came from Italy.

28548.q: What was the job of Francis of Assisi’s father?
28548.e: His father, Pietro Bernardone, traded successfully in cloth. Francis gave up his family’s wealth to live in poverty.
28548.m: Francis of Assisi was the son of a rich cloth merchant.

28549.q: Which promise was at the centre of life for Francis of Assisi and his brothers?
a: A life at the royal court
28549.e: The brothers owned nothing and lived from work and alms. That is why these communities are called mendicant orders.
28549.m: Francis of Assisi wanted to live in complete poverty.

28550.q: What is the famous song called in which Francis of Assisi praises God for the sun, moon and water?
28550.e: Francis wrote the Canticle of the Sun shortly before his death. It is considered one of the oldest poems in the Italian language.
28550.m: In the Canticle of the Sun Francis of Assisi praises God for creation.

28551.q: Which awareness day is held on 4 October, the feast day of Francis of Assisi?
28551.e: Francis loved animals and is even said to have preached to the birds. That is why his feast day is also World Animal Day.

28552.q: Which order, besides the Franciscans, is also one of the mendicant orders?
28552.e: The Dominicans were founded in 1216 by the Spaniard Dominic and also lived in poverty. The Benedictines, Cistercians and Carthusians, by contrast, are monastic orders with large monasteries.
28552.m: Like the Franciscans, the Dominicans are a mendicant order.

28553.q: What is the order of women called that was founded by a companion of Francis of Assisi?
28553.e: Clare of Assisi joined Francis and founded a community of women who lived in poverty. These sisters are named after her as the Poor Clares.
28553.m: The Poor Clares go back to Clare of Assisi.

28554.q: Unlike many older monasteries, where did the mendicant orders usually settle?
28554.e: The mendicant orders wanted to be close to people, to preach and to care for the poor. That is why they built their friaries in the growing towns, for example in Zurich, Basel or Lucerne.
28554.m: Mendicant orders worked mainly in the towns.

28555.q: Which position did Hildegard of Bingen hold in her convent?
28555.e: Hildegard was a Benedictine nun and led her convent community as abbess. An abbess is the head of a convent.
28555.m: Hildegard of Bingen was the abbess of a convent.

28556.q: What is Hildegard of Bingen’s “Lingua ignota”?
28556.e: “Lingua ignota” means “unknown language”. Hildegard invented around 1,000 words of her own for it, and even her own letters.
28556.m: Hildegard of Bingen invented her own secret language.

28557.q: On which river is Bingen, where Hildegard founded her convent?
28557.e: Bingen is in Germany on the Rhine. Around 1150 Hildegard founded her own convent there on the Rupertsberg.
28557.m: Hildegard founded her convent near Bingen on the Rhine.

28560.q: Besides medicine and visions, what else is Hildegard of Bingen known for?
28560.e: Hildegard wrote more than 70 sacred songs and the musical play “Ordo Virtutum”. Her music is still performed today.
28560.m: Hildegard of Bingen was also a composer.

28561.q: Besides her visions, what did Hildegard of Bingen write a lot about?
28561.e: Hildegard described many plants and their healing effects. Her advice on herbs and diet is still known today.
28561.m: Hildegard of Bingen wrote about healing plants.

28562.q: With which emperor did Hildegard of Bingen exchange letters?
28562.e: Hildegard wrote letters to popes, princes and to Emperor Frederick I Barbarossa. In them she was not afraid to criticise powerful people.
28562.m: Hildegard of Bingen wrote letters to Frederick Barbarossa.

28563.q: In the Middle Ages, who granted a place the right to hold a market?
a: The king or the territorial lord
28563.e: The market right was a privilege that was originally granted by the king, and later also by princes and other territorial lords. A market brought income to the place and to the lord.
28563.m: The market right was granted by the king or the territorial lord.

28564.q: What did the “market peace” guarantee during a market?
a: Special protection from violence and quarrels
The same prices for all goods
28564.e: Anyone who used violence at the market was punished especially severely. A market cross or a sign often showed that the market peace applied.
28564.m: The market peace protected traders and buyers from violence.

28566.q: In Switzerland, what is the funfair with stalls and rides called that goes back to the church consecration festival?
28566.e: “Chilbi” comes from “Kirchweih”, the festival for the consecration of a church. Even in the Middle Ages, a market and entertainment were part of it.
28566.m: The Chilbi goes back to the church consecration festival.

28567.q: Why was a market valuable to the lord of a place?
a: He collected tolls and stall fees
He was allowed to keep all the goods
He got the traders as servants
He no longer had to pay taxes
28567.e: Traders had to pay fees for their stalls and tolls on their goods. This income went to the lord of the market.
28567.m: Markets brought the lord of the market income from tolls and fees.

28568.q: With which old measure of length was cloth measured at medieval markets?
28568.e: The ell was roughly the length of a forearm and differed from town to town. Often a measuring ell was fixed to the town hall or church so that nobody could cheat.
28568.m: In the Middle Ages cloth was measured with the ell.

28569.q: Where were dishonest traders put on public display at the market as a punishment?
28569.e: The pillory was a post or frame in the market square to which convicted people were tied. The shame in front of everyone was part of the punishment.
28569.m: Cheats were publicly shamed in the pillory.

28570.q: Which place in what is now the canton of Aargau was widely known for its great fairs in the Late Middle Ages?
28570.e: The Zurzach fairs drew traders from many countries to the Rhine. They were among the most important markets in the area of present-day Switzerland.
28570.m: Zurzach was a famous fair town in the Middle Ages.

28574.q: In Swiss towns such as Bern, Lucerne or Solothurn, what was the head of the town called?
28574.e: The Schultheiss presided over the council and led the town court. The title was used in some cantons until the 19th century.
28574.m: In many Swiss towns a Schultheiss led the town.

28575.q: On which river did the Zähringen family found the town of Fribourg?
28575.e: The Zähringen family founded Fribourg in 1157 on a rock above the Sarine. The river protected the town like a moat.

28576.q: Which small town by a lake in the canton of Fribourg has an almost completely preserved town wall that you can walk along?
28576.e: Most of Murten’s medieval ring wall has been preserved. Visitors can walk round a large part of the old town on the wall walk.
28576.m: Murten has a well-preserved medieval town wall.

28577.q: Which Bern landmark was originally a gate in the town fortifications?
28577.e: The Zytglogge was built around 1220 as the western town gate of Bern. As the town grew, it became a clock tower with the famous astronomical clock.
28577.m: Bern’s Zytglogge was once a town gate.

28578.q: Who called the knights to the First Crusade in the year 1095?
28578.e: In 1095, in a speech in France, Pope Urban II called for Jerusalem to be conquered. Many knights followed his call.
28578.m: The pope called for the First Crusade in 1095.

28579.q: Which call became the battle cry of the crusaders?
28579.e: The listeners are said to have answered the pope’s sermon with “Deus lo vult”, which means “God wills it”.
28579.m: The battle cry of the crusaders was “God wills it”.

28580.q: Which city did the crusaders capture in 1099 at the end of the First Crusade?
28580.e: After three years of travelling and fighting, the crusaders captured Jerusalem in 1099. They killed many of the city’s inhabitants.

28581.q: Who mainly set off on the so-called People’s Crusade of 1096?
28581.e: Even before the army of knights, thousands of ordinary people set off. They were poorly equipped, and the expedition ended in defeat in Asia Minor.
28581.m: On the People’s Crusade mainly ordinary people set off.

28582.q: From which empire did the request for help come that led to the First Crusade?
28582.e: The Emperor of Byzantium was under pressure from the Seljuks and asked the pope for soldiers. This turned into the crusade.
28582.m: A request for help from Byzantium was the start of the First Crusade.

28583.q: What are the territories called that the crusaders founded in the Middle East?
28583.e: After the First Crusade the crusaders founded several crusader states, for example the Kingdom of Jerusalem. They lasted about 200 years.
28583.m: The crusaders founded crusader states in the Middle East.

28584.q: Which holy city did Saladin win back from the crusaders in 1187?
28584.e: After his victory over the crusader army, Saladin captured Jerusalem in 1187. This led to the start of the Third Crusade.

28585.q: Which religion did Saladin belong to?
28585.e: Saladin was a Muslim ruler. He fought against the Christian crusaders in the Holy Land.

28586.q: What was Saladin respected for, even by his Christian enemies?
28586.e: Saladin was considered fair and generous. For example, he spared the inhabitants of Jerusalem when he captured the city.
28586.m: Saladin was seen as a generous and chivalrous ruler.

28587.q: Which ruler’s title did Saladin hold?
28587.e: Saladin was a sultan, a Muslim ruler. He ruled over Egypt and Syria.
28587.m: Saladin was Sultan of Egypt and Syria.

28588.q: Which English king did Saladin fight against in the Third Crusade?
28588.e: Richard the Lionheart led an army to the Holy Land in the Third Crusade. But he could not win back Jerusalem from Saladin.
28588.m: Saladin and Richard the Lionheart were enemies in the Third Crusade.

28590.q: What was the nickname “Lionheart” meant to say about King Richard?
28590.e: The lion is a symbol of courage and strength. Richard was known as a brave fighter.

28591.q: How did Richard the Lionheart get free from captivity?
a: In exchange for a large ransom
28591.e: Richard was captured on his way home from the crusade. Only in 1194 was he freed in exchange for a very large ransom.
28591.m: Richard the Lionheart was freed for a ransom.

28592.q: Which country did Richard the Lionheart rule as king?
28592.e: Richard I was King of England from 1189 to 1199. But he spent only a few months of his reign in the country.
28592.m: Richard the Lionheart was King of England.

28593.q: Which brother succeeded Richard the Lionheart as king in 1199?
28593.e: John Lackland became king in 1199. In 1215 he had to seal Magna Carta.
28593.m: John Lackland succeeded his brother Richard on the throne.

28594.q: In which city was the Order of the Knights Templar founded around 1120?
28594.e: Hugh de Payens and a few knights joined together in Jerusalem to protect pilgrims.
28594.m: The Order of the Templars began in Jerusalem.

28595.q: Whom were the Knights Templar originally supposed to protect?
a: Pilgrims on the way to Jerusalem
28595.e: Around 1120 a few knights joined together in Jerusalem. They wanted to protect Christian pilgrims on the dangerous roads of the Holy Land.
28595.m: The Templars protected pilgrims in the Holy Land.

28596.q: Where does the Order of the Templars get its name from?
28596.e: The knights were given lodgings on the Temple Mount, where the Temple of Solomon was believed to have stood.
28596.m: The Templars are named after the Temple of Solomon.

28597.q: Which sign did the Knights Templar wear on their white cloaks?
28597.e: The white cloak with a red cross was the mark of the knight brothers.
28597.m: The Templars wore a red cross on a white cloak.

28598.q: What happened to many Templars in France on Friday 13 October 1307?
a: They set off on a crusade
28598.e: The French king had the Templars arrested on that day. He owed the order money and wanted to get hold of its wealth.
28598.m: In 1307 the King of France had the Templars arrested.

28599.q: Why did the Templars become very rich over time?
a: They received many donations and managed money
They found gold treasure in the sea
They owned silver mines in America
28599.e: Many people gave the order land and money. The Templars also managed money for pilgrims and kings and so became a kind of bank.
28599.m: Donations and money dealings made the Templars rich.

28600.e: The Templars were an order of knights. Like monks, they took vows, and at the same time they fought as knights.
28600.m: The Templars were monks and knights at the same time.

28601.q: Which order received most of the Templars’ property after the order was dissolved?
28601.e: The pope decided that the Templars’ wealth should go to the Knights Hospitaller, who were also an order of knights.
28601.m: The Knights Hospitaller inherited most of the Templars’ property.

28602.e: After a fire, Henry the Lion refounded Lübeck and promoted trade across the Baltic Sea.
28602.m: Henry the Lion is regarded as the founder of Lübeck.

28603.q: What is the typical type of ship of the Hanseatic League called?
28603.e: The cog was a round-bellied sailing ship that could carry a lot of cargo across the North Sea and the Baltic.
28603.m: The cog was the most important trading ship of the Hanseatic League.

28604.q: What was the assembly called at which the Hanseatic towns made decisions together?
28604.e: At the Hanseatic Diet, envoys of the towns discussed trade, treaties and wars.
28604.m: The Hanseatic towns met at the Hanseatic Diet.

28605.q: In which Norwegian city did the Hanseatic League have an important trading post?
28605.e: At the trading post in Bergen the Hanseatic merchants traded mainly in stockfish. The Bryggen quarter is a UNESCO World Heritage Site today.
28605.m: The Hanseatic trading post in Norway was in Bergen.

28606.q: What was the salt from Lüneburg, which the Hanseatic League supplied to the Baltic region, mainly needed for?
28606.e: Herrings from the Baltic Sea went off quickly and were therefore salted in barrels. The salt came from Lüneburg via Lübeck to the north.
28606.m: Lüneburg salt preserved the herrings of the Baltic.

28607.q: Against which country did the Hanseatic League successfully wage war in the 14th century?
28607.e: The Danish king wanted to control trade in the Baltic Sea. The Hanseatic League defeated him and received extensive trading rights in 1370.
28607.m: The Hanseatic League won against Denmark in 1370.

28608.q: Which city was considered the most important city of the Hanseatic League?
28608.e: Lübeck on the Baltic Sea was called the “Queen of the Hanse”. Most Hanseatic Diets also took place there.
28608.m: Lübeck was the most important city of the Hanseatic League.

28609.q: What was the elected head of the Republic of Venice called?
28609.e: The Doge was elected for life and lived in the Doge’s Palace on St Mark’s Square.
28609.m: Venice was led by a Doge.

28610.q: Which animal is the heraldic animal of Venice?
28610.e: The winged lion is the symbol of St Mark the Evangelist, the patron saint of Venice.
28610.m: The Lion of St Mark is the symbol of Venice.

28611.q: How did the Republic of Venice mainly become rich in the Middle Ages?
28611.e: Venice’s ships brought spices, silk and other goods from the East to Europe. Trade made the city very rich.
28611.m: Venice became rich through sea trade.

28612.q: What was built in the Arsenal, the large state shipyard of Venice?
28612.e: In the Arsenal, galleys were built almost like on an assembly line. It was one of the largest workplaces in Europe.
28612.m: Venice’s fleet was built in the Arsenal.

28613.q: What is the famous old bridge over the Grand Canal in Venice called?
28613.e: The Rialto Bridge is one of the best-known bridges in Venice. The city’s trading centre lay around it.
28613.m: The Rialto Bridge crosses the Grand Canal.

28614.q: On which sea is the port city of Genoa?
28614.e: Genoa lies in north-western Italy on the Mediterranean. As a maritime republic, the city traded as far as the Black Sea in the Middle Ages.
28614.m: Genoa is a port city on the Mediterranean.

28615.q: Which city was Genoa’s great trading rival in the Mediterranean in the Middle Ages?
28615.e: Genoa and Venice were both rich maritime republics. They fought several wars over control of trade.
28615.m: Genoa and Venice were rivals in sea trade.

28616.q: Where did Marco Polo dictate the account of his journey?
28616.e: As a prisoner of war in Genoa he told his experiences to a fellow prisoner, who wrote them down.
28616.m: Marco Polo’s travel account was written while he was a prisoner in Genoa.

28617.q: Roughly how long was Marco Polo away from Venice?
28617.e: Marco Polo set off in 1271 and returned in 1295. He spent many of those years at the ruler’s court in China.
28617.m: Marco Polo was away for about 24 years.

28618.q: What did Marco Polo describe in China that Europeans could hardly believe?
28618.e: Marco Polo was amazed that in the Great Khan’s empire people paid with printed paper instead of coins.
28618.m: Marco Polo reported on Chinese paper money.

28619.q: Which people did Genghis Khan unite?
28619.e: Genghis Khan united the quarrelling Mongol tribes. After that he conquered a huge empire.

28620.q: How did Genghis Khan’s warriors mainly travel?
28620.e: The Mongols were excellent riders and archers. With their fast horses they covered huge distances.
28620.m: The Mongols fought as fast horsemen.

28621.q: What is still unknown today about the grave of Genghis Khan?
28621.e: Genghis Khan died on a campaign in 1227. His grave was kept secret and has still not been found.
28621.m: The grave of Genghis Khan has never been found.

28622.q: In what kind of tent did the Mongol nomads live?
28622.e: The yurt is a round felt tent that can be taken down quickly and carried on animals.

28623.q: What makes the Mongol Empire stand out among the great empires?
28623.e: In the 13th century the Mongol Empire stretched from Korea to Eastern Europe.
28623.m: The Mongol Empire was the largest connected land empire in history.

28624.q: How did the Mongol armies move so quickly over long distances?
28624.e: The Mongols were nomadic horsemen. Each warrior had several horses and could cover long distances every day.
28624.m: The Mongols were fast mounted warriors.

28625.e: Around 1206 Genghis Khan united the Mongol tribes. His successors expanded the empire further.
28625.m: Genghis Khan founded the Mongol Empire.

28626.q: What was the Mongol part of the empire called that ruled over Russia for a long time?
28626.e: From the 13th to the 15th century the Golden Horde controlled large parts of Eastern Europe, and Russian princes had to pay it tribute.
28626.m: The Golden Horde ruled over Russia.

28627.q: How was Kublai Khan related to Genghis Khan?
28627.e: Kublai was a son of Tolui, the youngest son of Genghis Khan.
28627.m: Kublai Khan was a grandson of Genghis Khan.

28628.q: Which large country did Kublai Khan rule as emperor?
28628.e: In 1271 Kublai Khan founded the Yuan dynasty in China and ruled as Chinese emperor.
28628.m: Kublai Khan ruled China as emperor.

28629.q: Which present-day capital did Kublai Khan have expanded as his residence?
28629.e: Kublai had the city of Dadu built, which the Mongols called Khanbaliq. It lies in present-day Beijing.
28629.m: Kublai Khan made Beijing his capital.

28630.q: Which country did Kublai Khan try in vain to conquer in 1274 and 1281?
28630.e: Both fleets failed because of resistance and storms, which the Japanese called “kamikaze”, divine wind.
28630.m: Kublai Khan’s attacks on Japan failed.

28631.q: Which famous traveller from Venice lived at the court of Kublai Khan?
28631.e: Marco Polo travelled to China and served Kublai Khan for many years. He also described Kublai’s splendid summer residence, Shangdu.
28631.m: Marco Polo lived at the court of Kublai Khan.

28632.q: Which people did Kublai Khan belong to?
28632.e: Kublai was a grandson of Genghis Khan and became Great Khan of the Mongols in 1260. Later he also ruled over China.

28633.q: What did the flagellants do in their processions?
28633.e: The flagellants whipped themselves in public with leather straps to do penance for people’s sins.
28633.m: The flagellants whipped themselves as penance.

28634.q: During which disaster did the flagellant processions reach their peak in 1348/1349?
28634.e: Many people believed the Black Death was a punishment from God and tried to avert it through penance.
28634.m: The great flagellant processions took place at the time of the plague.

28635.q: Why did the flagellants whip themselves?
28635.e: The flagellants believed that God was punishing people for their sins. Through the pain they wanted to do penance and make peace with God.
28635.m: The flagellants wanted to do penance by punishing themselves.

28636.q: How did the Church react to the flagellant processions in 1349?
28636.e: Pope Clement VI saw the flagellants as a danger to the order of the Church and banned their processions.
28636.m: The pope banned the flagellant processions in 1349.

28637.q: In which country did flagellants first appear in large numbers around 1260?
28637.e: The first flagellant movement began in Perugia in 1260 and spread across the Alps.
28637.m: The flagellant movement began in Italy.

28638.q: The flagellants are named after the Latin word “flagellum”. What does it mean?
28638.e: A flagellum is a whip. That is where the name flagellants comes from.
28638.m: The flagellants are named after the flagellum, a whip.

28639.q: What false accusation was made against Jews during the plague?
28639.e: Without any proof, people claimed that Jews had poisoned wells and so spread the plague.
28639.m: Jews were wrongly accused of poisoning wells.

28640.q: How were the supposed confessions of Jews at Chillon Castle obtained in 1348?
28640.e: The Jews were tortured until they made false confessions. These were sent to many towns and fuelled the persecutions.
28640.m: The confessions of Chillon were forced by torture.

28641.q: What happened to many Jews in Basel in January 1349?
28641.e: The Jews of Basel were locked in a wooden house on an island in the Rhine and burned.
28641.m: In Basel many Jews were murdered in 1349.

28642.q: What did the Pope declare in 1348 about the accusation that Jews had spread the plague?
a: The plague came from the stars
28642.e: Pope Clement VI pointed out that Jews died of the plague just as much, and that the disease also raged where no Jews lived.
28642.m: In 1348 the Pope defended the Jews against the well-poisoning lie.

28643.q: In which direction did many Jews flee after the plague pogroms?
28643.e: The Kingdom of Poland in particular took in many Jews, which is why large Jewish communities later grew up there.
28643.m: Many persecuted Jews fled to Eastern Europe.

28644.q: Why did Jewish families hide their valuables in 1349, for example in the walls of houses?
a: Because they feared persecution and robbery
Because they were going on a journey
28644.e: During the plague pogroms many Jews were murdered and robbed. One such hidden treasure was found in Erfurt in 1998.
28644.m: The Erfurt Treasure is a reminder of the plague pogroms.

28645.q: What is a pogrom, such as the ones in Strasbourg and Basel in 1349?
a: Violence and murder against a persecuted group
28645.e: In a pogrom, a crowd attacks a group of people. In 1349 hundreds of Jews were murdered in Strasbourg.
28645.m: A pogrom is a violent persecution.

28646.q: Which land did the reformer Jan Hus come from?
28646.e: Jan Hus came from southern Bohemia, an area in today’s Czech Republic.
28646.m: Jan Hus was a reformer from Bohemia.

28647.q: In which language did Jan Hus preach to thousands of people in Prague?
28647.e: In the Bethlehem Chapel, Hus preached in the language of the people instead of Latin. That way everyone understood him.

28648.q: What did Jan Hus mainly rely on when he criticised the Church?
28648.e: Like his role model, the Englishman John Wycliffe, Hus saw the Bible as the most important basis of faith.
28648.m: Jan Hus relied on the Bible.

28649.q: What was one thing Jan Hus criticised about the Church?
28649.e: In 1412 Hus spoke out against the selling of indulgences and against the wealth of the clergy.
28649.m: Jan Hus criticised the sale of indulgences.

28650.q: In which city was Jan Hus condemned and burned in 1415?
28650.e: Jan Hus travelled to the Council of Constance. There he was condemned as a heretic and burned on 6 July 1415.
28650.m: Jan Hus died in Constance in 1415.

28651.q: The king had promised Jan Hus safe protection on his journey to the Council. What happened anyway?
a: He was allowed to travel home freely
28651.e: The king had promised him safe conduct. Even so, Hus was arrested and condemned in Constance.
28651.m: The promised safe conduct did not protect Jan Hus.

28652.q: What does the name “Hus” mean in Czech?
28652.e: A legend says Hus declared that today they were roasting a goose, but later a swan would come; people linked this to Martin Luther.

28653.q: What were the followers of Jan Hus called, who fought wars after his death?
28653.e: The Hussites fought in the Hussite Wars from 1419; their symbol was the communion chalice.
28653.m: The followers of Jan Hus were called Hussites.

28654.q: From when to when did the Council of Constance meet?
28654.e: For about four years, bishops, princes and scholars met in the town on Lake Constance.
28654.m: The Council of Constance lasted from 1414 to 1418.

28655.q: Which problem was the Council of Constance mainly meant to solve?
a: There were several popes at the same time
There was no emperor any more
The plague was raging in Constance
28655.e: At that time three men were arguing about who was the true Pope. The Council ended this split in the Church.
28655.m: The Council of Constance ended the split in the Church.

28656.q: What happened at the Council of Constance in 1417?
28656.e: On 11 November 1417, Martin V was elected Pope in Constance. With that, the Church was united again.
28656.m: A new pope was elected in Constance in 1417.

28657.q: Which area did the Swiss Confederates conquer in 1415 in connection with the Council?
28657.e: Duke Frederick IV of Austria helped a deposed pope to escape and was outlawed; the Confederates then occupied the Habsburg Aargau.
28657.m: The Swiss Confederates conquered Aargau in 1415.

28658.q: Which statue in the harbour of Constance reminds people of the Council today?
28658.e: The rotating figure Imperia by the artist Peter Lenk has stood at the harbour entrance since 1993 and mocks the powerful people of the Council.
28658.m: The Imperia statue in Constance harbour recalls the Council.

28659.q: Which preacher from Prague was condemned by the Council of Constance in 1415?
28659.e: Jan Hus was burned in 1415. A year later his friend Jerome of Prague met the same fate.
28659.m: The Council of Constance condemned Jan Hus.

28660.q: According to the decision of the Council of Constance, who should stand above the Pope?
28660.e: In the decree “Haec sancta” of 1415, the Council declared that even the Pope had to obey it.
28660.m: The Council of Constance placed itself above the Pope.

28661.e: The Greek word schisma means split; in the Western Schism the Western Church was divided.
28661.m: A schism is a split in the Church.

28662.q: What was the big problem during the Western Schism?
a: There were several popes at once
There was no pope at all
28662.e: Two and later even three popes claimed to be the rightful Pope. Believers no longer knew whom to follow.
28662.m: In the Schism several popes fought over the office.

28663.q: In which two cities did the rival popes first reside?
28663.e: One pope sat in Rome, the antipope in Avignon in southern France.
28663.m: In the Schism there were popes in Rome and in Avignon.

28664.q: How many popes were there at the same time after the Council of Pisa in 1409?
28664.e: The Council of Pisa deposed both popes and elected a new one; but the old ones did not step down.
28664.m: After 1409 three popes fought over the Church.

28665.q: In which town on Lake Constance was the Western Schism ended by a great council?
28665.e: At the Council of Constance from 1414 to 1418, the quarrelling popes were deposed or stepped down. In 1417 a single new pope, Martin V, was elected.
28665.m: The Council of Constance ended the Schism.

28666.q: What do you call a pope who is not recognised by the Church as rightful?
28666.e: In the Western Schism, besides the Pope in Rome there were antipopes in Avignon and Pisa. Today they are not seen as rightful popes.
28666.m: An antipope is a pope who is not recognised.

28667.q: Roughly how long were the crusaders of the First Crusade on the road before they reached Jerusalem?
28667.e: The army of knights set off in 1096 and only reached Jerusalem in 1099. On the way the crusaders had to survive long sieges, hunger and disease.
28667.m: The crusaders’ journey to Jerusalem took about three years.

28668.q: What did the crusaders found after conquering Jerusalem?
28668.e: The crusaders founded a Christian kingdom with Jerusalem as its capital. The first king was crowned in 1100.
28668.m: The crusaders founded the Kingdom of Jerusalem.

28669.q: Which country did Saladin rule as sultan before he also gained Syria?
28669.e: Saladin took power in Egypt in 1169 and later united Egypt and Syria under his rule.

28670.q: What did Richard the Lionheart die of in 1199?
28670.e: During the siege of Châlus Castle in France he was hit by a crossbow bolt; the wound became infected and he died.
28670.m: Richard the Lionheart died of a crossbow wound.

28671.q: In which legend do the people wait for King Richard the Lionheart to return?
28671.e: In the legend, Robin Hood fights against the unjust Prince John until King Richard returns from the Holy Land.
28671.m: Richard the Lionheart appears in the stories of Robin Hood.

28672.q: Why was Richard the Lionheart away from England for a long time?
a: He was on crusade and then held prisoner
He lived as a monk in Rome
He was also ruling in India
He was at sea with the Vikings
28672.e: Richard went on the Third Crusade to the Holy Land. On the way home he was taken prisoner and was only freed in 1194.
28672.m: A crusade and captivity kept Richard away from England.

28673.q: Which town gate is the famous landmark of Lübeck?
28673.e: The Holsten Gate was built of brick in the 15th century and shows the wealth of the Hanseatic town.
28673.m: The Holsten Gate is the landmark of Lübeck.

28674.q: Which famous sailor came from Genoa?
28674.e: Christopher Columbus was born in Genoa around 1451. In 1492, sailing for Spain, he reached America.

28675.q: Which powerful ruler did Marco Polo work for in China?
28675.e: Kublai Khan was a grandson of Genghis Khan and ruled over China. Marco Polo travelled through the empire on his behalf.
28675.m: Marco Polo served the Mongol ruler Kublai Khan.

28676.q: On which famous trade route did Marco Polo travel to Asia?
28676.e: The Silk Road was a network of trade routes between Europe and China. Silk, spices and other goods were carried along it.
28676.m: Marco Polo travelled along the Silk Road.

28677.q: In which century did Marco Polo travel to China?
28677.e: Marco Polo set off in 1271. That is the 13th century, the time of the High Middle Ages.
28677.m: Marco Polo travelled to China in the 13th century.

28678.q: Which device did Chinese sailors use to find their way at the time of the Song dynasty?
28678.e: The magnetic needle of a compass points north. In the Song period the compass was first used for sailing in China.
28678.m: Under the Song, sailors used the compass.

28679.q: Which people ended the rule of the Song dynasty in 1279?
28679.e: The Mongols under Kublai Khan conquered all of southern China after long fighting. With the naval battle of Yamen in 1279, the Song dynasty came to an end.
28679.m: In 1279 the Mongols conquered the last Song territory.

28680.q: In which country did the Song dynasty rule?
28680.e: The Song dynasty ruled China from 960 to 1279. It was a golden age of trade, technology and art.
28680.m: The Song dynasty ruled in China.

28681.q: Which drink became popular everywhere in China at the time of the Song dynasty?
28681.e: In the Song period people of all classes drank tea. There were teahouses and even competitions in making tea.
28681.m: Tea was very popular in China in the Song period.

28682.q: Which form of money did the state under the Song dynasty issue as one of the first in the world?
28682.e: In the province of Sichuan the state issued official banknotes from 1024. Before that, traders had already used private paper receipts.
28682.m: Under the Song, the Chinese state issued paper money for the first time.

28683.q: Which technique was known in China around 400 years before Gutenberg?
28683.e: Around 1040 a craftsman shaped single characters out of clay and put them together into pages. Gutenberg only printed around 1450 in Mainz.
28683.m: In China people printed with movable type very early.

28684.q: How were state officials mainly chosen under the Song dynasty?
28684.e: The Song greatly expanded the state civil service exams. Anyone who passed the exams on the classical writings could get a post.
28684.m: In the Song period you became an official by passing exams.

28685.q: About how many people lived in the Song empire around the year 1100?
28685.e: Thanks to new kinds of rice and better farming, the population doubled to about 100 million. For comparison: Switzerland has about 9 million inhabitants today.
28685.m: The Song empire had about 100 million inhabitants around 1100.

28686.q: Roughly when did Chinese writings first describe the compass as a help for sailors?
28686.e: A text from around 1111 to 1117 mentions that sailors looked at the magnetic needle in cloudy weather. Before that, magnetic stones had been used mostly for fortune-telling.
28686.m: By around 1100, Chinese sailors were already using the compass.

28687.q: What did the Chinese scholar Shen Kuo notice about the compass needle in 1088?
a: It does not point exactly north
It always points to the sea
28687.e: Shen Kuo was one of the first to recognise the difference between magnetic north and geographic north.
28687.m: Shen Kuo saw that the compass needle differs slightly from true north.

28688.q: What was the compass called in ancient China, because people paid attention to one end of the needle?
28688.e: In China the direction south was considered especially important. That is why people spoke of a needle that points south.
28688.m: The Chinese called the compass a south-pointer.

28689.q: When does the compass first appear in European writings?
a: At the end of the 12th century
At the time of the Romans
28689.e: The English scholar Alexander Neckam described a magnetic needle for sailors around 1190. That was about a century after the first Chinese reports.
28689.m: In Europe the compass is only mentioned around 1190.

28690.q: Which three substances make up gunpowder?
28690.e: Saltpetre supplies the oxygen, while sulphur and charcoal burn very quickly. Together they cause a violent explosion.
28690.m: Gunpowder is a mix of saltpetre, sulphur and charcoal.

28691.q: What were Chinese alchemists probably searching for when they discovered gunpowder?
28691.e: Daoist alchemists mixed many substances to find an elixir of life. In doing so they came across a mixture that burned fiercely.
28691.m: Gunpowder was an accidental discovery by alchemists.

28692.q: In which country was gunpowder invented?
28692.e: Chinese alchemists discovered gunpowder. The oldest known recipe dates from 1044.

a: A tube of powder on a spear
28693.e: A tube of bamboo or paper filled with powder was fixed to a spear. When lit, a flame shot forwards; firearms later developed from this.
28693.m: The fire lance was an early firearm from China.

28694.q: What did firearms change in Europe in the late Middle Ages?
a: Castles and armour gave less protection
28694.e: Cannons could destroy castle walls, and bullets went through armour. The age of knights slowly came to an end.
28694.m: Firearms made castles and knights’ armour less useful.

28695.q: Under which Chinese dynasty did Zheng He make his fleet voyages?
28695.e: The Ming dynasty ruled China from 1368. Its emperors sent Zheng He with large fleets across the Indian Ocean.
28695.m: Zheng He sailed on behalf of the Ming emperors.

28696.q: In which period did Zheng He’s fleet voyages take place?
28696.e: The first voyage began in 1405, the last ended in 1433. That was decades before the Portuguese reached the Indian Ocean.
28696.m: Zheng He was at sea between 1405 and 1433.

28697.q: In which religion did Zheng He grow up?
28697.e: Zheng He came from a Muslim family; his original name was Ma He. This helped him with contacts in Muslim port cities.
28697.m: The admiral Zheng He came from a Muslim background.

28698.q: What did the Chinese emperor mainly want to show with Zheng He’s huge fleets?
a: How to found colonies in Europe
28698.e: The ships brought gifts to foreign lands and returned with envoys and tribute. In this way the whole world was to see China’s greatness.
28698.m: Zheng He’s fleets were meant to show China’s power.

28699.q: About how many ships were in the fleet on Zheng He’s first voyage?
28699.e: According to Chinese reports, over 300 ships with almost 28,000 people set sail. It was one of the largest fleets of the Middle Ages.
28699.m: Zheng He’s first fleet had over 300 ships.

28700.q: Which port city in today’s Kenya did Zheng He’s fleet reach?
28700.e: The fleet sailed as far as the east coast of Africa. In Malindi and other ports, gifts and goods were exchanged.
28700.m: Zheng He’s ships got as far as Malindi in East Africa.

28701.q: Why did China stop the great fleet voyages after 1433?
a: The court thought they were too expensive
28701.e: The voyages cost a great deal of money, and the northern border needed protecting. Many officials thought the voyages were unnecessary.
28701.m: After Zheng He, China turned away from seafaring.

28702.q: What was a samurai called in Japan who no longer had a master?
28702.e: Ronin means something like “wave man”, because he drifted around aimlessly. A samurai became a ronin if his master died or cast him out.
28702.m: A ronin was a samurai without a master.

28703.q: With which weapon did the early samurai mainly fight from horseback?
28703.e: The first samurai were mounted archers. Only later did the sword become the best-known samurai weapon.
28703.m: The early samurai were mainly mounted archers.

28704.q: Which job did many samurai take on in the peaceful Tokugawa period?
a: They became farmers in rice fields
28704.e: From 1603 there were no big wars in Japan for a long time. The samurai remained a class, but often worked in government.
28704.m: In the peace of the Tokugawa period many samurai became officials.

28705.q: In which decade was the samurai class abolished in Japan?
28705.e: After 1868 the Meiji government modernised Japan. In the 1870s the samurai lost their privileges, for example the right to carry swords.
28705.m: The samurai lost their special status in the 1870s.

28706.q: What was a shogun in Japan?
a: A supreme military commander who ruled the country
28706.e: The shogun was the most powerful warrior in Japan. He ruled the country, while the emperor was mainly a symbol.
28706.m: The shogun was Japan’s supreme commander and ruler.

28707.q: What role did the Japanese emperor have at the time of the shoguns?
a: He had hardly any real power
He appointed the lords every year
28707.e: The emperor remained the honoured head in Kyoto. But the real government lay with the shogun and his warriors.
28707.m: In the shogunate the shogun ruled; the emperor was mainly a symbol.

28708.q: Which attackers did Japan fight off in 1274 and 1281?
28708.e: Kublai Khan twice sent large fleets against Japan. Both attacks failed, partly because of heavy storms; the second was only ten years before the Federal Charter of 1291.
28708.m: In the 13th century Japan fought off two Mongol attacks.

28709.q: What did the Japanese call the storms that destroyed the enemy fleets in the 13th century?
28709.e: Kamikaze means “divine wind”. The Japanese believed the gods had protected their land with the storms.

28710.q: In which city did the Tokugawa shogunate have its seat from 1603?
28710.e: The Tokugawa ruled Japan from Edo until 1868. Today Edo is called Tokyo and is the capital of Japan.
28710.m: Edo, today’s Tokyo, was the city of the Tokugawa shoguns.

28711.q: Which warriors served the shoguns in Japan?
28711.e: The samurai were Japan’s warrior class. They swore loyalty to their masters and fought for them.

28712.q: In which country today is Angkor Wat?
28712.e: Angkor Wat is in the north of Cambodia. The temple even appears on the country’s flag.

28713.q: For which religion was Angkor Wat originally built?
28713.e: Angkor Wat was built in the 12th century as a Hindu temple for the god Vishnu. Only later did it become Buddhist.
28713.m: Angkor Wat was first a Hindu temple.

28715.q: Which religion does Angkor Wat mainly serve today?
28715.e: From the late Middle Ages Cambodia became Buddhist. That is why Buddhist monks and believers pray at Angkor Wat today.
28715.m: Today Angkor Wat is a Buddhist shrine.

28716.q: Which people built the temples of Angkor?
28716.e: From the 9th to the 15th century the Khmer had a large empire in Southeast Asia. Angkor was their capital.

28717.q: In which country today was the Khmer Empire with its capital Angkor?
28717.e: The Khmer Empire was in Southeast Asia, in today’s Cambodia. The temples of Angkor are still famous today.
28717.m: The Khmer Empire was in today’s Cambodia.

28718.q: What were the huge water reservoirs, the barays, used for in the Khmer Empire?
28718.e: The Khmer built artificial reservoirs several kilometres long. They stored water for the rice fields and also had a religious meaning.
28718.m: With large reservoirs the Khmer secured their rice harvests.

28719.q: What is the Bayon temple at Angkor famous for?
28719.e: King Jayavarman VII had the Bayon built around 1200. Many of its towers bear giant stone faces.
28719.m: The Bayon has towers with stone faces.

28720.q: From which country today did the attackers come who conquered Angkor in 1431?
28720.e: The Thai from the Kingdom of Ayutthaya took Angkor. After that, the Khmer kings moved their seat to the south.
28720.m: Attackers from today’s Thailand conquered Angkor in 1431.

28721.q: Which city did Mansa Musa pass through on his pilgrimage, causing the price of gold to fall there?
28721.e: Mansa Musa spent and gave away so much gold in Cairo that gold lost value there for years. Arab historians reported this.
28721.m: Mansa Musa’s gold made the price of gold in Cairo fall.

28722.q: What is Mansa Musa still known for today?
28722.e: Mansa Musa ruled over areas with large gold deposits. He is considered one of the richest people in history.
28722.m: Mansa Musa was famous for his gold.

28723.q: Which buildings did Mansa Musa have built in Mali after his pilgrimage?
28723.e: After returning from Mecca, Mansa Musa had mosques built, for example in Timbuktu. They are made of mud and wood.
28723.m: Mansa Musa had mud mosques built in Mali.

28724.q: According to the reports, how large was Mansa Musa’s entourage on his pilgrimage?
28724.e: Arab sources speak of thousands of companions, servants and soldiers. The exact numbers are probably exaggerated, but the journey was huge.
28724.m: Mansa Musa travelled with an enormous entourage.

28725.q: What title did the kings of the Mali Empire have?
28725.e: Mansa means king or ruler. The most famous mansa was Mansa Musa.
28725.m: The kings of Mali were called Mansa.

28726.q: Which great river flowed through the Mali Empire?
28726.e: The Niger was the lifeline of the empire. Goods were carried on it, and important towns lay on its banks.
