28726.m: The Mali Empire lay on the river Niger.

28727.q: Where did the salt come from that was traded for gold in the Mali Empire?
a: From salt mines in the Sahara
28727.e: In the desert, for example in Taghaza, salt was cut in large slabs. Caravans took it south, where salt was scarce.
28727.m: The salt for Mali came in slabs from the Sahara.

28728.q: Which city in the Mali Empire was a famous centre of trade and learning?
28728.e: Caravans from the Sahara met in Timbuktu. There were mosques, schools and many books there.
28728.m: Timbuktu was a rich city of trade and scholars.

28729.q: On the territory of which present-day countries, among others, did the Mali Empire lie?
28729.e: The empire stretched from the Atlantic coast far inland along the Niger. Today’s state of Mali is named after it.
28729.m: The Mali Empire was in West Africa.

28730.q: Who founded Timbuktu around the year 1100?
28730.e: The Tuareg first used the place as a camp near water. It grew into an important trading city.
28730.m: Timbuktu grew out of a Tuareg camp.

28731.q: Which mosque in Timbuktu was a centre of learning and is often called a university?
28731.e: Many scholars taught and studied around the Sankore Mosque. They studied law, religion, maths and astronomy.
28731.m: The Sankore Mosque made Timbuktu a city of scholars.

28732.q: What are the old mosques of Timbuktu mainly built of?
28732.e: The mosques are made of mud with wooden beams sticking out of the walls. After the rainy season the mud is renewed by everyone together.
28732.m: Timbuktu’s mosques are built of mud.

28733.q: Which treasure is still kept in Timbuktu today?
28733.e: Timbuktu has hundreds of thousands of old manuscripts on religion, law and astronomy. In 2012 many were saved from destruction.
28733.m: Timbuktu is famous for its old manuscripts.

28735.q: Why was Timbuktu’s location so good for trade?
a: There was a large seaport here
There were rich gold mines here
28735.e: Timbuktu lay on the southern edge of the desert and close to the Niger. Goods from the camel caravans were loaded onto boats here and the other way round.
28735.m: Timbuktu linked the desert routes with the river Niger.

28736.q: How did many Europeans imagine Timbuktu for a long time?
a: As a mysterious, fabulously rich city
As a small fishing village by the sea
As a city of ice and snow
28736.e: Stories of gold and scholars made Timbuktu famous. Because hardly any European got there, the city remained a mystery for a long time.
28736.m: In Europe Timbuktu was seen as a mysterious city.

28737.q: In which period was Great Zimbabwe mainly built and lived in?
28737.e: Building in stone began in the 11th century. In the 15th century the city lost importance and was later abandoned.
28737.m: Great Zimbabwe flourished from the 11th to the 15th century.

28738.q: Who is now considered to have built Great Zimbabwe?
28738.e: Archaeological finds show that Bantu-speaking ancestors of today’s Shona built the city. They lived from cattle farming, agriculture and trade.
28738.m: African ancestors of the Shona built Great Zimbabwe.

28739.q: About how high is the wall of the Great Enclosure at Great Zimbabwe at its highest point?
28739.e: The wall is up to 11 metres high and about 250 metres long. It is considered the largest ancient stone building in Africa south of the Sahara.
28739.m: The Great Enclosure has walls up to 11 metres high.

28740.q: What material are the famous bird figures of Great Zimbabwe made of?
28740.e: Eight soapstone birds were found on tall columns. The soft stone was easy to carve.
28740.m: The Zimbabwe birds are carved from soapstone.

28741.q: Why did some Europeans in the 19th century believe that Great Zimbabwe had not been built by Africans?
a: Because building plans were in Europe
Because the inhabitants said so themselves
28741.e: Many Europeans did not believe Africans could build such stone structures. These prejudices were wrong and were later disproved by researchers.
28741.m: Prejudice led to false ideas about Great Zimbabwe.

28742.q: How did researchers find out who really built Great Zimbabwe?
a: Through photos from the time of building
28742.e: Archaeologists studied the finds closely. They showed that Africans had built the city in the Middle Ages.
28742.m: Excavations proved that Africans built Great Zimbabwe.

28743.q: Which finds show that Great Zimbabwe had far-reaching trade links?
28743.e: At Great Zimbabwe, Chinese porcelain, glass beads from Persia and coins from Arabia were found. The goods came through the ports on the East African coast.
28743.m: Chinese porcelain proves the long-distance trade of Great Zimbabwe.

28744.q: Which striking structure stands inside the Great Enclosure of Great Zimbabwe?
28744.e: The solid tower is about 9 metres high and not hollow inside. What it was used for is still not known for certain.
28744.m: A mysterious conical tower stands in the Great Enclosure.

28745.q: Who is the town of Lalibela in Ethiopia named after?
28745.e: The town bears the name of King Gebre Meskel Lalibela. The famous rock churches were made under his rule.
28745.m: Lalibela bears the name of its king.

28746.q: Roughly when were the rock churches of Lalibela made?
28746.e: King Lalibela ruled in the late 12th and early 13th century. Most of the churches were carved out of the rock at that time.
28746.m: The rock churches of Lalibela date from around 1200.

28748.q: Which holy city did King Lalibela want to recreate in Ethiopia with his churches?
28748.e: The pilgrimage to Jerusalem was long and dangerous. So King Lalibela is said to have created a “new Jerusalem” in his own country.
28748.m: Lalibela is seen as a “new Jerusalem” in Ethiopia.

28749.q: What is the name of the stream in Lalibela that recalls the Holy Land?
28749.e: Many names in Lalibela recall places in Israel and Palestine. That is why the stream between the groups of churches is called the Jordan.
28749.m: A stream called the Jordan flows through Lalibela.

28750.q: Which church do the rock churches of Lalibela belong to?
28750.e: Ethiopia is one of the oldest Christian countries in the world. The Ethiopian Orthodox Church still holds its services in Lalibela today.
28750.m: Lalibela is a holy place of Ethiopian Orthodox Christians.

28751.q: For which festival do tens of thousands of people make a pilgrimage to Lalibela every year?
28751.e: The Ethiopian Church celebrates Christmas, called Genna, on 7 January. Then pilgrims in white robes come to Lalibela from all over the country.
28751.m: At Genna on 7 January, Lalibela is full of pilgrims.

28752.q: How were the rock churches of Lalibela built?
a: They were carved out of the rock
28752.e: The builders chiselled the churches out of the rock from the top down. Each church is made from a single piece of stone.
28752.m: The churches of Lalibela are carved out of the rock.

28753.q: Which three islands or island groups form the corners of the Polynesian Triangle?
a: Hawaii, New Zealand and Easter Island
28753.e: The Polynesian Triangle covers a huge part of the Pacific. All the islands in it were settled by people with related languages.
28753.m: Hawaii, New Zealand and Easter Island form the Polynesian Triangle.

28754.q: Which large land was the last in Polynesia to be settled, around 1250 to 1300?
28754.e: The ancestors of the Māori only reached New Zealand in the 13th century. That makes it one of the last large land masses to be settled by people.
28754.m: New Zealand was only settled by people in the 13th century.

28755.q: With which boats did the Polynesians cross long distances in the Pacific?
28755.e: Two hulls joined by a platform made the canoes stable. With sails they could carry people, animals and plants far across the sea.
28755.m: Polynesians sailed in large double-hulled canoes.

28756.q: What did Polynesian navigators use to find their way without a compass?
28756.e: The navigators knew where many stars rose and could read the swell of the sea. Seabirds and clouds showed where land was.
28756.m: Polynesians read their way from stars, waves and birds.

28757.q: What did the 1976 voyage of a replica canoe from Hawaii to Tahiti without instruments prove?
a: Polynesians could navigate across the sea on purpose
Hawaii and Tahiti are close together
28757.e: A navigator found the way using only stars, waves and birds. This showed that the settlement of Polynesia was no accident.
28757.m: Polynesians could navigate on purpose without instruments.

28758.q: Which crop from South America was already common in Polynesia before Columbus?
28758.e: The sweet potato comes from South America but grew early on Polynesian islands. This points to contact between Polynesians and South America.
28758.m: The sweet potato shows early contact between Polynesia and South America.

28759.q: What do the Māori call New Zealand in their language?
28759.e: Aotearoa is often translated as “land of the long white cloud”. Today the name is used in New Zealand alongside the English name.
28759.m: Aotearoa is the Māori name for New Zealand.

28760.q: Where did the ancestors of the Polynesians originally come from?
28760.e: Languages and DNA show that the ancestors came from the area of Taiwan and Southeast Asia. Over many generations they moved east from island to island.
28760.m: The ancestors of the Polynesians came from Southeast Asia.

28761.q: What are the moai of Easter Island made of?
28761.e: Most moai were carved from soft tuff stone from an old volcanic crater.
28761.m: The moai are made of volcanic rock.

28762.q: About how tall is a moai on average?
28762.e: Most moai are about 4 metres tall and weigh around 12 tonnes. The largest moai ever put up is almost 10 metres tall.
28762.m: An average moai is about 4 metres tall.

28763.q: What do some moai wear on their heads?
28763.e: Some moai wear a reddish stone cylinder. It probably represents a topknot of hair.
28763.m: Some moai wear a red stone hat.

28764.q: Which way do most moai face?
28764.e: Most moai stand on the coast but look inland. They were probably meant to watch over the people of the villages.

a: The Rapa Nui, the people of Easter Island
28765.e: The Rapa Nui settled Easter Island many hundreds of years ago. They carved the statues out of the rock with stone tools.
28765.m: The moai are the work of the Rapa Nui.

28766.q: Who did the moai probably represent?
28766.e: The moai probably represented important ancestors. People believed that they protected the islanders.

28768.q: What did the discovery of a Viking settlement in North America in 1960 prove?
a: That Vikings were in America before Columbus
That Columbus had Vikings as guides
That the Vikings came from America
That America was joined to Europe
28768.e: A Norwegian couple of researchers found the remains of Viking houses on Newfoundland. This made it clear that the sagas’ stories about Vinland are based on truth.
28768.m: Vikings were in America about 500 years before Columbus.

28769.q: On which island in North America were the remains of a Viking settlement found?
28769.e: On Newfoundland in eastern Canada, the foundations of turf houses and a smithy were found. The site is now a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
28769.m: A Viking settlement stood on Newfoundland.

28770.q: How did researchers find out in which year Vikings cut down trees on Newfoundland?
a: They counted the tree rings in the wood
They read a date on a rune stone
They found a letter from the Vikings
28770.e: In the pieces of wood they found traces of a solar storm from the year 993. From there they counted on through the tree rings and arrived at the year 1021.
28770.m: Tree rings in the wood revealed when the Vikings were in America.

28771.q: From which sources do we know about the voyages to Vinland?
28771.e: The “Saga of the Greenlanders” and the “Saga of Erik the Red” tell of the voyages. They were only written down about 200 years later.
28771.m: The Vinland voyages are recorded in Icelandic sagas.

28772.q: According to the sagas, why did the Vikings not stay in Vinland for good?
a: Because of conflict with the local people
Because there was no wood there
28772.e: The sagas tell of fights with the people who lived there. Also, the way to Greenland was long. After a few years the settlers went back.
28772.m: The Vikings left Vinland again after a few years.

28773.q: What did Leif Eriksson call the land he found in North America?
28773.e: Leif called the land Vinland, meaning “wine land”. It was probably on the coast of today’s Canada.
28773.m: Leif Eriksson called his land in America Vinland.

28774.q: What was the name of Leif Eriksson’s father, who settled Greenland?
28774.e: Erik the Red founded the first settlements on Greenland around 985. His son Leif sailed on westwards from there.
28774.m: Leif Eriksson was the son of Erik the Red.

28775.q: Which faith was Leif Eriksson supposed to bring to Greenland on behalf of the Norwegian king?
28775.e: Around the year 1000, King Olaf Tryggvason gave Leif the task of converting Greenland. His mother had one of the first churches built there.
28775.m: Leif Eriksson brought Christianity to Greenland.

28776.q: On which continent did Leif Eriksson land about 500 years before Columbus?
28776.e: Leif Eriksson reached the coast of North America around the year 1000. Columbus only came to America in 1492.
28776.m: Leif Eriksson was in America long before Columbus.

28777.q: From which large island did Leif Eriksson sail west?
28777.e: Leif lived in the Viking settlement on Greenland that his father had founded. From there he sailed on to America.
28777.m: Leif Eriksson set off for America from Greenland.

28778.q: Which city did the Medici family rule during the Renaissance?
28778.e: For generations the Medici were the most powerful family in Florence and steered the city’s politics. Under them Florence became the centre of the Renaissance.
28778.m: The Medici made Florence the city of the Renaissance.

28779.q: How did the Medici become rich?
28779.e: The Medici founded a bank with branches in many European cities. A large part of their fortune came from money dealings, including with the Pope.
28779.m: The Medici were above all a family of bankers.

28780.q: What nickname did Lorenzo de' Medici, who supported many artists, have?
28780.e: Lorenzo de' Medici supported artists such as Botticelli and the young Michelangelo. Because of his splendour he was called “il Magnifico”, the Magnificent.
28780.m: Lorenzo de' Medici was called “the Magnificent”.

28781.q: Roughly how long did the Medici hold power in Florence?
28781.e: From 1434 the Medici steered Florence, with short breaks. The family only died out in 1737.
28781.m: The Medici shaped Florence for about 300 years.

28782.q: Why did the Medici also have dangerous enemies in Florence?
a: Other rich families wanted power for themselves
They wanted to sell Florence to France
They did not allow churches to be built
28782.e: Other banking families were jealous of the Medici’s power. In 1478 a Medici was even killed in an attack in the cathedral.
28782.m: The Medici’s power stirred up envy and hostility.

28783.q: Which high office did as many as two members of the Medici reach in the 16th century?
28783.e: With Leo X and Clement VII, two Medici became Pope. So the family’s power reached as far as Rome.

28784.q: Which woman from the Medici family became Queen of France in 1547?
28784.e: Catherine de' Medici married the future King Henry II of France. After his death, as the mother of three kings, she had great influence.
28784.m: Catherine de' Medici was Queen of France.

28785.q: On which river is Florence, the home city of the Medici?
28785.e: The Arno flows right through Florence and reaches the sea near Pisa. The famous Ponte Vecchio bridge crosses it.
28785.m: Florence lies on the river Arno.

28786.q: Which era does the master builder Filippo Brunelleschi belong to?
28786.e: Brunelleschi lived in Florence from 1377 to 1446. He took ancient buildings as his model and is considered one of the first Renaissance architects.

28787.q: In which city is Brunelleschi’s famous cathedral dome?
28787.e: Brunelleschi built the dome of Florence Cathedral from 1420. It is still the landmark of the city today.
28787.m: Brunelleschi’s cathedral dome is in Florence.

28788.q: What was especially amazing about how the cathedral dome of Florence was built?
a: It was built without a large supporting frame
It was built in one week
It is made entirely of glass
28788.e: The dome was so big that a wooden frame underneath was hardly possible. Brunelleschi found a way of building in which the bricks held themselves up even during construction.
28788.m: Brunelleschi built the dome of Florence without a large supporting frame.

28789.q: How is the cathedral dome of Florence built so that it is lighter?
28789.e: The dome consists of an inner and an outer shell with a space between them. Stairs inside lead up to the top.
28789.m: The dome of Florence has an inner and an outer shell.

28790.q: Which rich family in Florence gave Brunelleschi important building commissions?
28790.e: The Medici were rich bankers and ruled Florence. They had Brunelleschi rebuild the church of San Lorenzo.
28790.m: The Medici supported artists and builders in Florence.

28791.q: Which trade had Brunelleschi originally learned?
28791.e: Brunelleschi was first registered as a goldsmith in the silk guild. Only later did he turn to architecture.
28791.m: Brunelleschi began his career as a goldsmith.

28792.q: In 1401 Brunelleschi took part in a competition for the doors of the baptistery in Florence. What is a baptistery?
28792.e: The word comes from the Greek word for baptise. The children of the city were baptised in the Florence Baptistery.
28792.m: A baptistery is a church for baptisms.

28793.q: Which rich family in Florence gave Botticelli many commissions?
28793.e: The Medici were rich bankers and ruled over Florence. They supported many artists, including Botticelli.
28793.m: The Medici were important patrons of Botticelli.

28794.q: Which painting by Botticelli shows a garden with goddesses and flowers and has an Italian title meaning “spring”?
28794.e: “Primavera” means “spring” in English. The painting shows Venus and other figures in an orange grove in bloom.

28795.q: In which city did Sandro Botticelli live and work most of the time?
28795.e: Botticelli was born in Florence around 1445 and died there in 1510. Many of his patrons came from the circle of the Medici.

28796.q: In Botticelli’s famous painting, a goddess stands on a large shell. Who is she?
28796.e: The painting is called “The Birth of Venus”. It shows the goddess of love coming ashore from the sea on a shell.
28796.m: Botticelli painted Venus on a shell.

28797.q: In which famous chapel in Rome did Botticelli paint frescoes on the walls around 1481?
28797.e: Pope Sixtus IV brought several painters from Florence to Rome, including Botticelli. They painted the side walls of the chapel long before Michelangelo decorated the ceiling.
28797.m: Botticelli painted in the Sistine Chapel before Michelangelo.

28798.q: What do Botticelli’s paintings mostly show?
a: Scenes from the Bible and old legends
28798.e: Botticelli painted many Madonnas and biblical scenes. But his paintings of ancient gods like Venus are also famous.
28798.m: Botticelli painted Bible scenes and ancient legends.

28799.q: Roughly what does the nickname “Botticelli” mean?
28799.e: The painter’s real name was Alessandro di Mariano Filipepi. The nickname “Botticelli” means something like “little barrel” and probably passed to him from his brother.
28799.m: Botticelli is a nickname meaning “little barrel”.

28800.q: Which era does the painter Raphael belong to?
28800.e: Raphael lived from 1483 to 1520. He was one of the great painters of the Italian Renaissance.

28801.q: Which figures from Raphael’s “Sistine Madonna” are often seen today on postcards and mugs?
28801.e: At the bottom of the painting two little angels rest their heads on their hands. They have become more famous than many whole paintings.

28802.q: With which two artists is Raphael often named as the greatest master of the Renaissance?
28802.e: Leonardo da Vinci, Michelangelo and Raphael lived at the same time in Italy. Together they are seen as the great masters of the High Renaissance.
28802.m: Raphael, Leonardo and Michelangelo are the masters of the High Renaissance.

28803.q: In which ancient building in Rome is Raphael buried?
28803.e: Raphael wished to be buried in the Pantheon. His tomb can still be seen there today.
28803.m: Raphael’s tomb is in the Pantheon in Rome.

28804.q: In which city did Raphael paint large frescoes for the Pope from 1508?
28804.e: Raphael painted several of the Pope’s rooms in the Vatican in Rome. Michelangelo was working there at the same time.
28804.m: Raphael created frescoes for the Pope in Rome.

28806.q: How did Albrecht Dürer sign many of his works?
a: With a monogram of A and D
28806.e: Dürer put a large A with a small D underneath on his paintings and prints. This mark became so well known that others even forged it.
28806.m: Dürer’s mark is the monogram of A and D.

28807.q: Which animal did Dürer paint in 1502 so precisely that you can see almost every hair?
28807.e: The watercolour “Young Hare” shows the animal very true to life. It is now in the Albertina in Vienna.
28807.m: Dürer’s “Young Hare” is a masterpiece of close observation of nature.

28808.q: Which famous drawing by Dürer shows two hands placed together?
28808.e: The brush drawing was made in 1508 as a study for an altarpiece. It is one of the best-known images in German art.
28808.m: The “Praying Hands” are a study by Albrecht Dürer.

28809.q: What is Dürer especially known for, as he was one of the first artists to do it several times?
28809.e: Dürer drew himself when he was only 13 and later painted himself several times. The self-portrait of 1500 in a fur coat is especially famous.
28809.m: Dürer painted himself again and again in self-portraits.

28810.q: With which printing technique did Dürer create the print “Melencolia I” in 1514?
28810.e: In copper engraving, lines are cut into a copper plate, filled with ink and printed onto paper. Dürer achieved very fine details with it.
28810.m: Dürer was a master of copper engraving.

28811.q: Which animal does Dürer’s famous woodcut of 1515 show, even though he had never seen it himself?
28811.e: A rhinoceros had been brought from India to Lisbon in 1515. Dürer drew it only from a description and a sketch, which is why it looks as if it is wearing armour.
28811.m: Dürer’s rhinoceros was made only from a description.

28812.q: Which city did Dürer travel to from 1505 to 1507 to get to know Italian art?
28812.e: Dürer spent about two years in Venice and painted an altarpiece there for German merchants, among other things. Italian art strongly shaped his later work.
28812.m: Dürer brought Renaissance ideas from Venice to Germany.

28813.q: In which Swiss city did Erasmus of Rotterdam live for many years and is buried?
28813.e: In Basel, Erasmus worked closely with the printer Johann Froben. He died in Basel in 1536 and is buried in Basel Minster.
28813.m: Erasmus is buried in Basel Minster.

28814.q: What does the name “Erasmus” stand for at many universities in Europe today?
28814.e: The European Union’s exchange programme was named after Erasmus in 1987. He himself travelled a lot in Europe and studied and taught in several places.
28814.m: The Erasmus programme recalls the travelling scholar.

28815.q: What is the name of Erasmus’s famous satire from 1511?
28815.e: In “In Praise of Folly”, Folly herself speaks and makes fun of monks, scholars and rulers. The book was a great success.
28815.m: In “In Praise of Folly”, Erasmus mocked the powerful people of his time.

28816.q: Which intellectual movement of the Renaissance did Erasmus belong to?
28816.e: Humanists studied ancient texts in Latin and Greek and put human beings at the centre. Erasmus was known as the “prince of humanists”.
28816.m: Erasmus was the most famous humanist in Europe.

28817.q: In which ancient languages did Erasmus read the texts of antiquity?
28817.e: As a humanist, Erasmus studied ancient writings in their original languages. He even published the New Testament in Greek.
28817.m: Erasmus read ancient texts in Latin and Greek.

28818.q: Which painter made famous portraits of Erasmus?
28818.e: Holbein worked in Basel and portrayed Erasmus several times, including while writing. These pictures still shape our idea of the scholar today.
28818.m: Holbein painted Erasmus at his writing desk.

28819.q: What position did Erasmus have in the Church?
28819.e: Erasmus joined a monastery of Augustinian canons when he was young and was ordained a priest in 1492. Later, though, he mostly lived as an independent scholar.
28819.m: Erasmus was a priest and lived as an independent scholar.

28820.q: Which country did Henry the Navigator come from?
28820.e: Henry was a son of the Portuguese king John I. He supported voyages of discovery along the coast of Africa.
28820.m: Henry the Navigator was a Portuguese prince.

28821.q: What is surprising about the nickname “the Navigator”?
a: He hardly went to sea himself
28821.e: Henry sent captains on voyages of discovery but did not go on any himself. He only went to sea for military campaigns in North Africa.
28821.m: Henry the Navigator let others go on voyages of discovery for him.

28822.q: Along which continent’s coast did Henry the Navigator have explorations made?
28822.e: Henry sent captains further and further south along the west coast of Africa. This prepared the way for the later sea route to India.
28822.m: Henry the Navigator had the coast of Africa explored.

28823.q: In which nimble type of ship did the Portuguese go on voyages of discovery in Henry the Navigator’s time?
28823.e: The caravel was light and could sail well against the wind. That made it suitable for voyages along unknown coasts.
28823.m: The caravel was the ship of the Portuguese explorers.

28824.q: What were sailors afraid of on the coast of West Africa in Henry the Navigator’s time?
a: An unknown sea from which no one returns
The edge of the flat Earth in the east
28824.e: Sailors believed that south of a certain cape a dangerous sea began from which there was no return. In 1434 one of Henry’s captains proved that you could sail on.
28824.m: Courage helped the Portuguese overcome their fear of the unknown.

28825.q: Which island in the Atlantic was settled by the Portuguese from about 1420 under Henry?
28825.e: Portuguese sailors reached Madeira around 1419 and soon began settling it. Later sugar cane was grown there.
28825.m: Madeira was settled under Henry the Navigator.

28826.q: Did Henry the Navigator live to see the Portuguese reach the southern tip of Africa?
a: No, that only happened after his death
Yes, it happened in his youth
No, the southern tip was never reached
28826.e: Henry died in 1460. Bartolomeu Dias only sailed round the southern tip of Africa in 1488.
28826.m: The southern tip of Africa was only reached after Henry’s death.

28827.q: From which city did Bartolomeu Dias set off on his famous voyage in 1487?
28827.e: Lisbon was Portugal’s most important port. Most Portuguese voyages of discovery started from there.
28827.m: The Portuguese explorers usually started from Lisbon.

28828.q: What did Portuguese explorers like Dias set up on newly reached coasts?
28828.e: These stone pillars were called “padrões” and carried the Portuguese coat of arms and a cross. They showed that Portugal claimed the area.
28828.m: A padrão marked Portugal’s claim to a coast.

28829.q: What name did Dias originally give to the cape at the southern tip of Africa?
28829.e: Because of the fierce winds, Dias called it “Cabo das Tormentas”. Later it was given the name “Cape of Good Hope”.
28829.m: Dias first named the cape the “Cape of Storms”.

28830.q: What is the cape that Dias first called the “Cape of Storms” called today?
28830.e: The Portuguese king gave the cape a new name. He hoped that the sea route to India would be found from there.
28830.m: The cape at the southern tip of Africa is called the Cape of Good Hope.

28831.q: Why did Dias not sail on to India after rounding the cape?
a: The crew demanded to turn back
The king called him back by letter
28831.e: The sailors were exhausted and supplies were running low. Dias had to give in to his crew’s wishes and turn back.
28831.m: Dias had to turn back because his crew insisted.

28832.q: How did Bartolomeu Dias die in 1500?
a: His ship sank in a storm near the cape
He died of smallpox in Lisbon
28832.e: In 1500 Dias sailed with a large Portuguese fleet towards India. Near the cape his ship ran into a storm and sank.
28832.m: Bartolomeu Dias died near the very cape he had discovered.

28833.q: With how many ships did Dias set off on his voyage around Africa?
28833.e: Dias sailed with two caravels and a supply ship. He left the supply ship behind on the coast along the way.
28833.m: Dias sailed with two caravels and a supply ship.

28834.q: What is the name of the small, nimble type of ship used by the Portuguese explorers in the 15th century?
28834.e: The Portuguese developed the caravel further in the 15th century. It was well suited for exploring along unknown coasts.
28834.m: The caravel was the explorers’ ship of the Portuguese.

28835.q: What shape were the sails of a typical Portuguese caravel?
28835.e: The caravel carried so-called lateen sails, which are triangular. This kind of sail came from the Mediterranean.

28836.q: What advantage did the caravel’s lateen sails offer?
a: You could tack against the wind
28836.e: With triangular sails a ship can sail at an angle into the wind and make progress in a zigzag. So the explorers could get home even against the wind.
28836.m: With lateen sails you could zigzag against the wind.

28837.q: Why could a caravel sail well close to coasts and into river mouths?
28837.e: The hull of a caravel did not sit deep in the water. So it was less likely to run aground in shallow water.
28837.m: A shallow draught allowed voyages in shallow water.

28838.q: Which ship on Columbus’s first voyage in 1492 was not a caravel?
28838.e: The Niña and the Pinta were caravels. The Santa María was a larger, clumsier ship, a so-called nao.
28838.m: The Niña and the Pinta were caravels.

28839.q: How many masts did a caravel usually have?
28839.e: Caravels usually had two or three masts. Later, larger versions could also carry four.
28839.m: A caravel usually had two or three masts.

28840.q: Why were larger ships than caravels later used for long trading voyages to India?
a: They had more room for cargo and supplies
28840.e: Large ships like the carrack could take a lot of cargo and supplies. For long voyages this was more important than being nimble.
28840.m: Large ships were used for heavy cargo.

28841.q: For which two countries did Vespucci make voyages to the New World?
28841.e: Vespucci sailed with a Spanish expedition in 1499 and for Portugal from 1501 to 1502. Both countries were leading the voyages of discovery at that time.
28841.m: Vespucci sailed for Spain and for Portugal.

28842.q: The coast of which present-day country did Vespucci explore from 1501 to 1502 for Portugal?
28842.e: The Portuguese voyage went far south along the east coast of South America. Among other places, it reached the bay of today’s Rio de Janeiro.
28842.m: Vespucci explored the coast of Brazil.

28843.q: Which country is said to have got its name on a voyage Vespucci took part in in 1499, because houses on stilts reminded the sailors of Venice?
28843.e: “Venezuela” means “little Venice”. The houses on stilts in the water reminded the sailors of the lagoon city.

28844.q: What did Vespucci realise about the land Columbus had reached?
a: That it was a new continent
That it was an island off Africa
That it was part of China
28844.e: In his reports Vespucci described a “New World”. Columbus, on the other hand, believed until his death that he had been in Asia.
28844.m: Vespucci realised that America was a new continent.

28845.q: For which Florentine family did Vespucci work as a merchant before he became a sailor?
28845.e: Vespucci worked for a Medici trading house and came to Seville on its behalf. There he also helped to fit out ships.
28845.m: Vespucci was first a merchant working for the Medici.

28846.q: Which job did Vespucci later take on in Spain?
a: He ruled as viceroy in Mexico
He ran a church in Seville
28846.e: From 1508 Vespucci examined and taught the pilots of Spanish ships. He also collected new maps and reports.
28846.m: Vespucci trained ships’ pilots in Spain.

28847.q: Which two countries divided the newly discovered lands between them in the Treaty of Tordesillas in 1494?
28847.e: After Columbus’s voyage, Spain and Portugal argued over the new lands. In the Treaty of Tordesillas they agreed on a dividing line.
28847.m: In 1494 Spain and Portugal divided the world between them.

28848.q: Who was not asked when the Treaty of Tordesillas was made?
28848.e: The two sea powers handed out lands where millions of people lived. Their rights and opinions did not count.
28848.m: The people living in the divided lands were not asked.

28849.q: How was the world divided in the Treaty of Tordesillas?
a: With a line from pole to pole through the Atlantic
With a line along the equator
With a border across the Mediterranean
28849.e: The line ran from north to south west of the Cape Verde Islands. New lands west of it were to belong to Spain, east of it to Portugal.
28849.m: A line from pole to pole divided the world between Spain and Portugal.

28850.q: What is a “legua”, the unit used to measure the Tordesillas dividing line?
28850.e: The legua, or league, was an old Spanish and Portuguese measure of length of a few kilometres. Its exact length was not fixed in the same way everywhere at that time.
28850.m: The legua was an old measure of distance.

28851.q: Which country in South America speaks Portuguese today because of the Treaty of Tordesillas?
28851.e: The eastern part of South America lay east of the dividing line. Portugal took possession of it from 1500, and later the territory grew further.
28851.m: Brazil is the largest Portuguese-speaking country in the world.

28852.q: Why did Portugal want to move the dividing line further west in 1494?
a: To have enough room in the South Atlantic for voyages round Africa
To get access to the Mediterranean
To give up the Canary Islands
28852.e: On the way round Africa, Portuguese ships had to sail far out into the Atlantic to use good winds. A line too close to Africa would have blocked these routes.
28852.m: Portugal needed room in the Atlantic for the route round Africa.

28853.q: Why did Spain and Portugal argue so fiercely over the Moluccas?
a: There were huge gold mines there
28853.e: The Moluccas are also called the Spice Islands. Cloves and nutmeg from there were very expensive in Europe. In 1529 the two countries agreed, and Portugal got the islands.
28853.m: The Moluccas were sought after for their spices.

28854.q: From which Caribbean island did Cortés set off for Mexico in 1519?
28854.e: Cortés had been living on Cuba, which was ruled by Spain. The governor Diego Velázquez tried to stop the voyage at the last moment.
28854.m: Cortés began his conquest from Cuba.

28855.q: Which town on Mexico’s Gulf coast did Cortés found in 1519?
28855.e: Soon after landing, Cortés founded the town of “Villa Rica de la Vera Cruz”. In this way he wanted to make himself legally independent of the governor.
28855.m: Veracruz was founded by Cortés in 1519.

28856.q: What was the name of the Aztec capital that Cortés conquered?
28856.e: Tenochtitlan lay on an island in a lake. After conquering it in 1521, the Spanish built Mexico City on top of it.

28857.q: Which Aztec ruler did Cortés meet in the capital in 1519?
28857.e: Moctezuma first welcomed Cortés as a guest. Later he was taken prisoner by the Spanish and died in 1520.
28857.m: Moctezuma was the Aztec ruler whom Cortés met.

28858.q: What name was given to the area conquered by Cortés as a Spanish colony?
28858.e: The area was called “Nueva España”, meaning New Spain. In 1522 Charles V made Cortés its governor.
28858.m: The Aztec Empire became the colony of New Spain.

28859.q: Which country did the conqueror Hernán Cortés come from?
28859.e: Cortés was born in 1485 in Extremadura in Spain. Many conquistadors came from this poor region.
28859.m: Hernán Cortés was a Spanish conquistador.

28860.q: What did Cortés do with his ships in 1519 so that his men could not turn back?
28860.e: Cortés had the ships on the coast made useless and sunk. That left his men only one way: inland.
28860.m: Cortés took away his men’s chance of going back.

28861.q: Which country did the conqueror Francisco Pizarro come from?
28861.e: Pizarro was born in Trujillo in Spain. He grew up in humble circumstances and looked for wealth in America.
28861.m: Francisco Pizarro was a Spanish conqueror.

28862.q: About how many soldiers did Pizarro take into the Inca Empire in 1532?
28862.e: Pizarro had only about 168 men, about 60 of them on horseback. Guns, horses and the weakness of the empire after a civil war helped him.
28862.m: Pizarro conquered a great empire with very few soldiers.

28863.q: What happened in 1533 to the captured Inca ruler, even though the ransom had been paid?
28863.e: Pizarro feared an uprising and had the ruler executed in 1533. Even at the time, some Spaniards criticised this breaking of his word.
28863.m: Pizarro broke his word and had the Inca ruler killed.

28864.q: What did the captured Inca ruler offer as a ransom?
28864.e: He promised to fill a room once with gold and twice with silver. The ransom was delivered, but he was still not set free.
28864.m: Pizarro had a huge ransom paid to him.

28865.q: Which present-day capital did Pizarro found in 1535?
28865.e: Pizarro founded the city near the Pacific coast so that it was easy to reach by ship. Today Lima is the capital of Peru.
28865.m: Lima was founded by Pizarro in 1535.

28866.q: How did Francisco Pizarro’s life end?
a: He was murdered in Lima in 1541
He died in a sea battle
He was sacrificed by the Inca
28866.e: Followers of his former partner, who had been killed, broke into his palace in 1541 and killed him. Pizarro was over 60 years old at the time.
28866.m: Pizarro was killed in 1541 by enemies from his own side.

28867.q: Which empire in South America did Francisco Pizarro conquer?
28867.e: From 1532 Pizarro conquered the Inca Empire in the Andes. It lay in the area of today’s Peru.

28868.q: Which ingredient of Italian cooking originally comes from America?
28868.e: The tomato was grown in Central America and came to Europe in the 16th century. It only became an important food in Italy later.
28868.m: Without America there would be no tomato sauce.

28870.q: Which plant from the Old World was grown on large plantations in America, often by enslaved people from Africa?
28870.e: Sugar cane comes from Asia and was brought by Europeans to the Caribbean and Brazil. Millions of people were taken from Africa by force for the hard work on the plantations.
28870.m: Growing sugar cane in America was closely linked to slavery.

28871.q: Which plant did the Europeans bring to America?
28871.e: Wheat comes from the Middle East and was grown in America by Europeans. Maize, tomatoes and pumpkins, on the other hand, came from America to Europe.
28871.m: Wheat crossed the Atlantic with the Europeans.

28872.q: Which farm animals did the Spanish bring to America, where they quickly multiplied?
28872.e: Pigs and cattle found plenty of food in America and multiplied quickly. They greatly changed farming and the landscape.
28872.m: European farm animals spread quickly in America.

28873.q: Which plant, whose leaves the native peoples of America smoked, came to Europe in the 16th century?
28873.e: As early as 1492, Columbus and his men saw local people smoking tobacco leaves. In Europe tobacco was first seen as a medicinal plant.

28874.q: Which animal came from America to Europe through the Columbian Exchange?
28874.e: The turkey was bred by the peoples of Mexico and came to Europe in the 16th century. Chickens, sheep and goats, on the other hand, went from Europe to America.

28875.q: From which American plant is the chocolate made that Switzerland is famous for?
28875.e: The Maya and Aztecs already made a drink from the seeds of the cocoa tree. In the 19th century Swiss makers made chocolate world-famous.
28875.m: Without cocoa from America there would be no Swiss chocolate.

28876.q: In which century did Emperor Charles V reign?
28876.e: Charles V was born in 1500 and reigned until 1556. He was emperor at the time of the Reformation.
28876.m: Charles V reigned in the 16th century.

28877.q: Which famous saying is linked to the huge empire of Charles V?
a: The sun never sets on my empire
I came, I saw, I conquered
28877.e: Charles V ruled over Spain, the Netherlands, parts of Italy, the Holy Roman Empire and colonies in America. That is why people said the sun never set on his empire.
28877.m: The sun never set on the empire of Charles V.

28878.q: Which ruling house did Emperor Charles V belong to?
28878.e: Charles V was a Habsburg and a grandson of Emperor Maximilian I. Through clever marriages he inherited many countries.
28878.m: Charles V came from the House of Habsburg.

28879.q: What did Charles V do in 1555 and 1556 that was very unusual for an emperor?
a: He gave up his thrones of his own free will
He became a monk in Rome
28879.e: Charles V was tired and disappointed because he had not been able to stop the split in the Church. He gave up his offices and withdrew to Spain.
28879.m: Charles V gave up his crowns of his own free will.

28880.q: Who became King of Spain after Charles V?
28880.e: Charles V divided his empire: his son Philip II got Spain and the Netherlands. The imperial crown went to his brother Ferdinand I.
28880.m: Philip II inherited the Kingdom of Spain from his father Charles V.

28881.q: Where did Charles V retire to after stepping down?
28881.e: Charles V spent his last years at the monastery of San Jerónimo de Yuste in Spain. He died there in 1558.
28881.m: Charles V spent his last years at a Spanish monastery.

28882.q: Whose troops plundered the city of Rome in 1527 (the “Sack of Rome”)?
28882.e: Mutinous mercenaries from the army of Charles V plundered Rome in 1527 because they had not been paid. Many Swiss Guards died protecting the Pope.
28882.m: In the Sack of Rome, mercenaries of Charles V plundered the city.

28883.q: What was special when the Pope crowned Charles V emperor in 1530?
a: It was the last coronation of an emperor by a pope
It was the first coronation in Switzerland
The Pope crowned two emperors at once
28883.e: Charles V was crowned by Pope Clement VII in Bologna in 1530. After him no emperor was crowned by the Pope again.
28883.m: Charles V was the last emperor crowned by the Pope.

28884.q: In which year did the German Peasants' War reach its peak?
28884.e: In spring 1525 peasants rose up in southern Germany, Thuringia and Austria. They were defeated in the same year.
28884.m: The German Peasants' War reached its peak in 1525.

28885.q: What were the famous demands of the peasants, written down in Memmingen in 1525, called?
28885.e: The Twelve Articles demanded, for example, the right to choose their own priest and lower payments to the lords. They were quickly printed and spread widely.
28885.m: The peasants wrote down their demands in the Twelve Articles.

28886.q: How did the German Peasants' War end in 1525?
a: The princes' armies defeated the peasants.
The peasants took over the government.
All the peasants were set free.
The emperor gave the peasants all the land.
28886.e: The peasants were poorly armed. The princes' armies defeated them, for example at Frankenhausen in Thuringia. Thousands of peasants died.
28886.m: The peasants lost against the princes in 1525.

28887.q: Which kind of dependence did the peasants mainly want to abolish in the Peasants' War?
28887.e: Serfs belonged to their lord and were not allowed, for example, to move away or marry freely. The peasants pointed to the Bible and said that Christ had set all people free.

28888.q: Which knight with the iron hand led a peasant band in the Odenwald for a while in 1525?
28888.e: Götz von Berlichingen had lost a hand in battle and wore an iron artificial hand. He was made captain of a peasant band.
28888.m: Götz von Berlichingen led a peasant band in the Peasants' War.

28889.q: Which reformer wrote a pamphlet against the rebelling peasants in 1525?
28889.e: The peasants appealed to Luther's teaching. But Luther harshly condemned the uprising and took the side of the princes. Thomas Müntzer, on the other hand, led peasants himself.
28889.m: In the Peasants' War Luther took sides against the peasants.

28890.q: Roughly how many rebels were killed in the German Peasants' War?
28890.e: It is estimated that about 70,000 to 75,000 peasants were killed. Many survivors were also harshly punished.
28890.m: Tens of thousands of peasants died in the Peasants' War.

28891.q: In which Swiss city did the first adult baptism of the Anabaptists take place in January 1525?
28891.e: On 21 January 1525 some young men baptised each other in a house in Zurich, although they had already been baptised as children. This was the start of the Anabaptist movement.
28891.m: The Anabaptist movement began in Zurich in 1525.

28892.q: Which Zurich reformer did the first Anabaptists quarrel with?
28892.e: The first Anabaptists were at first followers of Zwingli. But they wanted to reform faster and more radically, especially regarding baptism.
28892.m: The Zurich Anabaptists broke away from Zwingli.

28893.q: What, for example, did the Anabaptists reject in their confession of 1527?
28893.e: In the Schleitheim Confession the Anabaptists rejected, among other things, swearing oaths and military service. Many Anabaptists are still against violence today.
28893.m: The Anabaptists rejected oaths and military service.

28894.q: Who was Menno Simons, after whom the Mennonites are named?
a: A leader of the peaceful Anabaptists
An emperor of the Holy Roman Empire
28894.e: Menno Simons was a former Catholic priest from Friesland. He gathered the peaceful Anabaptists in northern Germany and the Netherlands.
28894.m: The Mennonites bear the name of Menno Simons.

28895.q: The Amish in the USA go back to an Anabaptist from the canton of Bern. What was his name?
28895.e: Jakob Ammann came from Erlenbach in the Simmental. His followers were named Amish after him, and many later emigrated to America.
28895.m: The Amish are named after Jakob Ammann from Bern.

28896.q: Which baptism did the Anabaptists reject?
28896.e: The Anabaptists believed that only people who believe for themselves should be baptised. That is why they baptised adults, even though they had already been baptised as babies.

28897.q: What happened in 1535 to the rule of the radical Anabaptists in Münster?
a: The city was captured and the leaders executed
It became a kingdom of its own for ever
All the inhabitants emigrated to America
28897.e: In 1534 radical Anabaptists took power in Münster. By 1535 the city had been captured and the leaders were executed.
28897.m: The Anabaptist kingdom of Münster only lasted a short time.

28898.q: In which present-day country is the city of Trent?
28898.e: In Italian Trent is called Trento and it lies in Trentino in northern Italy. At that time the city belonged to the Holy Roman Empire.

28899.q: How many sacraments did the Council of Trent confirm for the Catholic Church?
28899.e: The reformers mostly only recognised baptism and Holy Communion. The Council, on the other hand, held on to the seven sacraments.
28899.m: The Catholic Church has seven sacraments.

28900.q: Why did the Catholic Church call the Council of Trent?
a: As a response to the Reformation
28900.e: The Reformation had split the Church. At the Council of Trent from 1545, the Catholic Church renewed itself and clearly set itself apart from the Protestants.
28900.m: The Council of Trent was the Catholic response to the Reformation.

28901.q: In which language did Catholics everywhere continue to celebrate Mass after the Council of Trent?
28901.e: The Council held on to the Latin Mass, although the reformers held services in the local language. Only after the Second Vatican Council in the 1960s did the local language become usual at Mass.
28901.m: After Trent, Latin remained the language of the Mass.

28902.q: Which office did the Council of Trent abolish because there had been too much abuse?
28902.e: Indulgence preachers had collected money for the remission of punishment for sins. The Council kept indulgences but banned the trade and abolished these preachers in 1562.
28902.m: The Council of Trent abolished the indulgence preachers.

28903.q: Which list did the Catholic Church have published in 1564 after the Council of Trent?
a: A list of all the saints
28903.e: The “Index of Forbidden Books” named writings that Catholics were not allowed to read. These included the works of the reformers.
28903.m: After Trent the Church published an index of banned books.

28904.q: Against Luther, what did the Council of Trent teach about how people are made righteous before God?
a: Faith and good works belong together
Only money for the Church counts
28904.e: Luther said that people are made righteous by faith alone. The Council, on the other hand, stressed that people should play their part and do good works.
28904.m: According to Catholic teaching, faith and good works belong together.

28905.q: What is the official name of the Jesuit order?
28905.e: In Latin the order is called Societas Jesu. That is why Jesuits write the abbreviation SJ after their names.
28905.m: The Jesuits are officially called the Society of Jesus.

28906.q: What was an important task of the Jesuits in faraway countries?
a: Looking for gold for the king
28906.e: Jesuits like Francis Xavier travelled as missionaries as far as India and Japan. They wanted to spread the Christian faith there.
28906.m: As missionaries, the Jesuits spread Christianity.

28907.q: What were the Jesuits in Europe especially known for?
28907.e: The Jesuits founded many grammar schools and colleges, including in Lucerne, Fribourg and Solothurn. They gave many young people a good education.
28907.m: The Jesuits were famous for their schools.

28908.q: What happened to the Jesuit order in 1773?
28908.e: Under pressure from several kings, Pope Clement XIV dissolved the order in 1773. In 1814 it was allowed again.
28908.m: The Jesuit order was banned from 1773 to 1814.

28910.q: Who was the first pope to come from the Jesuit order?
28910.e: The Argentinian Jorge Mario Bergoglio became Pope Francis in 2013. He was the first Jesuit in this office.
28910.m: Pope Francis was the first Jesuit pope.

28911.q: What did Jesuits bring to the emperor's court in China around 1600?
a: Knowledge of maths and the stars
28911.e: The Jesuit Matteo Ricci learned Chinese and lived in Beijing. With his knowledge of mathematics and astronomy he won the trust of the scholars.
28911.m: Jesuits brought European knowledge to China.

28912.q: From when to when did the Thirty Years' War last?
28912.e: The war began in 1618 and ended in 1648, after exactly thirty years. It was fought mainly in what is now Germany.
28912.m: The Thirty Years' War lasted from 1618 to 1648.

28913.q: In which country did the Thirty Years' War begin with an uprising of Protestant nobles?
28913.e: In 1618 the Protestant estates in Bohemia rose up against the Catholic Habsburg ruler. This grew into a war across all of central Europe.
28913.m: The Thirty Years' War began in Bohemia.

28914.q: What was the alliance of the Catholic princes in the Thirty Years' War called?
28914.e: The Catholic League was founded in 1609 under the leadership of Bavaria. Its counterpart was the Protestant Union of 1608.
28914.m: The Catholic princes joined together in the Catholic League.

28915.q: Which two religious groups faced each other in the Thirty Years' War?
28915.e: The war began as a quarrel between Catholic and Protestant princes. Later it was also about power between the great states of Europe.
28915.m: In the Thirty Years' War Catholics fought against Protestants.

28917.q: Which peace ended the Thirty Years' War in 1648?
28917.e: The Peace of Westphalia was made in Münster and Osnabrück. It also recognised the independence of the Swiss Confederation from the Empire.
28917.m: The Peace of Westphalia ended the Thirty Years' War in 1648.

28918.q: What were foreign powers fighting over in the Troubles of the Grisons at the time of the Thirty Years' War?
a: the Alpine passes in the Grisons
the watch factories in the Jura
28918.e: Spain, Austria and France wanted to control the important passes in the Grisons. A key figure of this time was the pastor and soldier Jürg Jenatsch.
28918.m: The Troubles of the Grisons were about the Alpine passes.

28919.q: Who was the father of Queen Elizabeth I of England?
28919.e: Elizabeth was a daughter of Henry VIII, who was married six times. Her mother was Anne Boleyn.
28919.m: Elizabeth I was the daughter of Henry VIII.

28920.q: What happened to Anne Boleyn, the mother of Elizabeth I?
28920.e: Henry VIII had Anne Boleyn beheaded in 1536. Elizabeth was not yet three years old at the time.
28920.m: The mother of Elizabeth I was executed in 1536.

28921.q: In which century did Queen Elizabeth I of England mainly reign?
28921.e: Elizabeth I reigned from 1558 to 1603, for 45 years. During this time England became an important sea power.
28921.m: Elizabeth I reigned in the 16th century.

28922.q: Which nickname did Elizabeth I get because she never married?
28922.e: She stayed unmarried, although many princes wanted to marry her.
28922.m: Elizabeth I was called the Virgin Queen.

28923.q: Which Scottish queen did Elizabeth I have executed in 1587?
28923.e: Mary, Queen of Scots, was Catholic and became involved in plots against Elizabeth. After almost twenty years in captivity she was executed.
28923.m: Mary, Queen of Scots, was executed in 1587 on the orders of Elizabeth I.

28924.q: Which famous writer wrote his first plays in the time of Elizabeth I?
28924.e: William Shakespeare worked in London in the Elizabethan age. His works include, for example, “Romeo and Juliet”.
28924.m: Shakespeare worked in the age of Elizabeth I.

28925.q: Which royal family came to an end with the death of Elizabeth I in 1603?
28925.e: Elizabeth had no children. So the Scottish King James from the House of Stuart became her successor.
28925.m: Elizabeth I was the last ruler from the House of Tudor.

28926.q: In which year did the Spanish Armada sail against England?
28926.e: In summer 1588 the great Spanish fleet set off for England. The attack failed.
28926.m: The Spanish Armada attacked England in 1588.

28927.q: Which Spanish king sent the Armada against England?
28927.e: Philip II wanted to conquer Protestant England. He was also angry because England was supporting the rebellious Netherlands.
28927.m: King Philip II sent the Armada.

28928.q: What was the problem with the commander of the Spanish Armada?
a: He had little experience at sea
28928.e: The Duke of Medina Sidonia took command although he had hardly any experience at sea. The experienced admiral had died shortly before.
28928.m: The leader of the Armada had little experience at sea.

28929.q: Which trick did the English use in 1588 to throw the Spanish ships anchored off Calais into confusion?
28929.e: At night the English let burning ships, called fireships, drift towards the Armada. In panic the Spanish cut their anchors and lost their formation.
28929.m: Fireships threw the Armada into confusion off Calais.

28930.q: What destroyed many of the Armada's ships on the way home?
28930.e: The Armada had to sail back around Scotland and Ireland. There many ships were wrecked on the coasts in storms.
28930.m: Storms destroyed many of the Armada's ships.

28931.q: Roughly how many ships made up the Spanish Armada?
28931.e: The Armada had about 130 ships with many thousands of sailors and soldiers. Many ships were lost; experts disagree about exactly how many came back.

28932.q: Which English seafarer and former privateer fought against the Armada in 1588?
28932.e: Francis Drake had earlier captured Spanish ships and sailed around the world. In 1588 he was one of the most important English commanders.
28932.m: Francis Drake fought against the Spanish Armada.

28933.q: What was the notorious book of 1486 that gave instructions for hunting “witches” called?
28933.e: The Hammer of Witches was written by the Dominican Heinrich Kramer. It described how supposed witches should be tracked down and condemned.
28933.m: The Hammer of Witches fuelled the witch hunts.

28934.q: In which Swiss canton was Anna Göldi executed as a “witch” in 1782?
28934.e: Anna Göldi was executed in Glarus in 1782. She is seen as one of the last women in Europe to be killed as a witch. In 2008 she was officially cleared.
28934.m: Anna Göldi was executed as a witch in Glarus in 1782.

28935.q: Roughly how many people were executed as “witches” in Europe?
28935.e: Experts estimate the number of executions at about 40,000 to 60,000. Many more people were accused and tortured.
28935.m: Tens of thousands of people were executed as witches in Europe.

28936.q: How did judges in witch trials usually force a confession?
28936.e: The accused were tortured until they confessed and often named other people too. This led to whole chains of trials.
28936.m: Confessions in witch trials were forced out by torture.

28937.q: Which realisation helped to end the witch trials?
a: Under torture even innocent people confess
You can recognise witches by their red hair
28937.e: Critics like the Jesuit Friedrich Spee showed that people will confess to anything under torture. With the Enlightenment the witch trials gradually stopped.
28937.m: Criticism of torture helped to end the witch trials.

28938.q: Who was most often accused in the witch hunts?
28938.e: The great majority of the victims were women, but men and even children were persecuted too. It often hit people on the edges of society.
28938.m: Most victims of the witch hunts were women.

28939.q: What was the cruel test called in which supposed witches were tied up and thrown into water?
28939.e: People believed that water would reject a witch, so she would float. Anyone who sank was thought innocent, but could drown.
28939.m: The trial by water was a cruel method of the witch hunts.

28940.q: Which empire did Suleiman the Magnificent rule?
28940.e: Suleiman was Sultan of the Ottoman Empire. Under him the empire reached one of its greatest golden ages.
28940.m: Suleiman the Magnificent was an Ottoman sultan.

28941.q: In which century did Suleiman the Magnificent reign?
28941.e: Suleiman reigned from 1520 to 1566, in the 16th century. That was longer than any other Ottoman sultan.

28942.q: Which nickname does Suleiman have in Turkey?
28942.e: In Turkey he is called “Kanuni”, which means the Lawgiver. He had many laws collected and put in order.
28942.m: In Turkey Suleiman is called the Lawgiver.

28943.q: Which kingdom did Suleiman defeat in a great battle in 1526?
28943.e: At Mohács the Hungarian army was destroyed. After that a large part of Hungary came under Ottoman rule.
28943.m: Suleiman conquered large parts of Hungary.

28944.q: Which city did Suleiman besiege without success in 1529?
28944.e: During the first Ottoman siege of Vienna, Suleiman could not take the city. With winter coming he withdrew again.
28944.m: Suleiman besieged Vienna in vain in 1529.

28945.q: Which famous master builder built a great mosque in Istanbul for Suleiman?
28945.e: Mimar Sinan built the Süleymaniye Mosque, which is named after the sultan. He is seen as the greatest Ottoman architect.
28945.m: Mimar Sinan built the Süleymaniye Mosque.

28946.q: What was the name of the influential wife of Suleiman the Magnificent?
28946.e: Roxelana, in Turkish Hürrem, came from what is now western Ukraine. She had great influence at the sultan's court.
28946.m: Roxelana was the wife of Suleiman.

28947.q: Which empire besieged the city of Vienna in 1683?
28947.e: A large Ottoman army under Grand Vizier Kara Mustafa marched on Vienna. The Ottomans wanted to extend their empire further into Europe.

28948.q: How did the siege of Vienna end in 1683?
a: A relief army defeated the Ottomans
The Ottomans left without a fight
28948.e: On 12 September 1683 an army came to help and put the Ottomans to flight at the Battle of Kahlenberg. Vienna was saved.
28948.m: A relief army freed Vienna in 1683.

28949.q: Which country did the king who led the army to rescue Vienna in 1683 come from?
28949.e: King John III Sobieski led Polish and German troops. His cavalry decided the battle.
28949.m: A Polish king saved Vienna in 1683.

28950.q: Roughly how long did Vienna hold out against the siege in 1683?
28950.e: The city was besieged from mid-July to mid-September. Soldiers and citizens defended the walls until help came.
28950.m: Vienna held out against the siege for about two months.

28951.q: What did the emperor do shortly before the Ottomans reached Vienna in 1683?
28951.e: Emperor Leopold I fled with his court to Passau. From there he tried to get help for Vienna.
28951.m: The emperor fled from Vienna in 1683.

28952.q: Which large area did Austria win from the Ottomans by 1699?
28952.e: After Vienna was freed, Austria pushed the Ottomans back. In the Peace of Karlowitz in 1699 it gained almost all of Hungary and became a great power.
28952.m: After 1683 Austria became a great power.

28953.q: According to legend, which drink became popular in Vienna because the Ottomans left sacks of it behind in 1683?
28953.e: The legend says that after the Ottomans left, sacks of coffee beans were found. Shortly afterwards the first coffee houses opened in Vienna.
28953.m: According to legend, coffee came to Vienna after the siege.

28954.q: What did Russian men have to pay a special tax for under Peter the Great?
28954.e: Peter wanted Russians to dress and shave in the Western style. Anyone who wanted to keep his beard had to pay a beard tax.
28954.m: Under Peter the Great there was a beard tax.

28955.q: Which country did Peter the Great defeat in the Great Northern War?
28955.e: Peter fought against Sweden for decades. After his victory Sweden lost its position as a great power, and Russia became strong.

28956.q: Which ruling family did Peter the Great belong to?
28956.e: The Romanovs ruled Russia from 1613 to 1917. Peter was one of their best-known rulers.
28956.m: Peter the Great was a Romanov.

28957.q: Which new title did Peter the Great take in 1721?
28957.e: After the victory over Sweden, Peter called himself Imperator, meaning emperor. Russia thus became the Russian Empire.
28957.m: From 1721 Peter the Great called himself Imperator.

28958.q: Which city was the capital of Russia before Peter the Great moved the seat of government to the Baltic Sea?
28958.e: Until Peter's time the tsars ruled from Moscow. From 1712 the new city on the River Neva became the seat of government.
28958.m: Before Peter the Great, Moscow was the capital of Russia.

28959.q: To which sea was Peter the Great determined to give Russia access?
28959.e: To trade with western Europe, Russia needed ports on the Baltic Sea. That is why Peter fought against Sweden for decades.
28959.m: Peter the Great won access to the Baltic Sea for Russia.

28960.q: Which new city did Peter the Great have built on the Baltic Sea?
28960.e: In 1703 Peter founded a new city at the mouth of the River Neva. Saint Petersburg soon became the capital of Russia.
28960.m: Peter the Great founded Saint Petersburg.

28961.q: Which country did Frederick the Great rule as king?
28961.e: Frederick II was King in Prussia from 1740 to 1786. Under him Prussia became a European great power.
28961.m: Frederick the Great was King of Prussia.

28962.q: Which popular nickname did Frederick the Great get in old age?
28962.e: People affectionately called the king “Old Fritz”. The name “Soldier King”, on the other hand, belongs to his father.
28962.m: Frederick the Great was called Old Fritz.

28963.q: What is Frederick the Great's summer palace in Potsdam called?
28963.e: The name Sanssouci is French and means “without worries”. Frederick had the palace built in the 1740s.
28963.m: Frederick the Great liked living at Sanssouci Palace.

28964.q: Which rich province did Frederick the Great conquer from Austria?
28964.e: Shortly after coming to the throne in 1740, Frederick marched into Silesia. In the Silesian Wars Prussia kept the province.
28964.m: Frederick the Great took Silesia from Austria.

28965.q: Which musical instrument did Frederick the Great love to play?
28965.e: Frederick played the flute very well and also composed his own pieces. He often gave concerts in the palace.
28965.m: Frederick the Great was a talented flute player.

28966.q: Which crop did Frederick the Great promote with orders so that farmers would plant it?
28966.e: Frederick wanted to prevent famines and had the growing of potatoes encouraged. A well-known decree of 1756 is called the Potato Order.
28966.m: Frederick the Great promoted potato growing.

28967.q: How long did the war last that Frederick the Great fought from 1756 against Austria, Russia and France?
28967.e: The Seven Years' War lasted from 1756 to 1763. Prussia only just survived it and kept Silesia.
28967.m: The Seven Years' War lasted from 1756 to 1763.

28968.q: What did the young Frederick try to do in 1730 because he suffered under his strict father?
a: He wanted to become a monk
He wanted to sail to America
28968.e: The escape was discovered and Frederick was imprisoned. His friend Hans Hermann von Katte was executed before his eyes.
28968.m: In 1730 the young Frederick tried to escape from his father.

28969.q: What was special in 1740 about Maria Theresa inheriting the Habsburg lands?
a: A woman took over the rule
28969.e: Normally only sons inherited. But her father Charles VI had decided in the Pragmatic Sanction that a daughter could inherit too.
28969.m: Maria Theresa inherited the Habsburg lands as a woman.

28970.q: Which war broke out in 1740 because several princes did not accept Maria Theresa's inheritance?
28970.e: After her father's death, Prussia, Bavaria and other powers attacked. The War of the Austrian Succession lasted until 1748.
28970.m: Maria Theresa had to defend her inheritance in the War of Succession.

28972.q: Which son of Maria Theresa ruled alone after her death and carried out many reforms?
28972.e: Joseph II had been emperor and co-ruler with his mother since 1765. After her death he quickly pushed through more reforms.
28972.m: Joseph II succeeded his mother Maria Theresa.

28973.q: Of which country was Maria Theresa crowned queen in Pressburg in 1741?
28973.e: In Pressburg, today's Bratislava, she became Queen of Hungary. Afterwards the Hungarian nobility supported her in the war.
28973.m: Maria Theresa was Queen of Hungary.

28974.q: In which year did Maria Theresa die?
28974.e: Maria Theresa died in Vienna in 1780. She had ruled the Habsburg lands for 40 years.

28975.q: What did Maria Theresa have abolished in her hereditary lands in 1776?
28975.e: Under the influence of Enlightenment lawyers, torture in court cases was abolished in 1776. This made Austria one of the early countries in Europe to do so.

28976.q: What were the settlers protesting against at the Boston Tea Party in 1773?
a: taxes from London that they had no say in
28976.e: Great Britain demanded taxes from the colonies, for example on tea. But the settlers had no representatives in the British Parliament. So in 1773 they threw tea into Boston harbour.
28976.m: The Boston Tea Party was a protest against British taxes.

28977.q: Which slogan summed up the American settlers' protest against Great Britain?
a: All for one, one for all
28977.e: The settlers only wanted to pay taxes if they had a say in Parliament.
28977.m: The settlers demanded: no taxation without representation.

28978.q: Who owned the tea that was destroyed at the Boston Tea Party?
28978.e: The tea belonged to the British East India Company. It was a powerful British trading company based in London.
28978.m: The tea of the Boston Tea Party belonged to the British East India Company.

28979.q: Many people taking part in the Boston Tea Party dressed up as whom?
28979.e: Many men dressed up as Mohawks so as not to be recognised. But the disguise was only very simple.
28979.m: The participants disguised themselves as Mohawks.

28980.q: From 1765, what did settlers in America have to buy from the British for newspapers and documents?
28980.e: Under the Stamp Act of 1765, printed paper needed a tax stamp. The settlers protested so strongly that the law was withdrawn in 1766.
28980.m: A tax stamp on paper turned the colonies against Great Britain in 1765.

28981.q: Which war began in 1775, two years after the Boston Tea Party?
28981.e: In 1775 the first fighting between British soldiers and settlers broke out near Boston. This became the American War of Independence.
28981.m: The American War of Independence began in 1775.

28982.q: In which year did the 13 American colonies declare their independence?
28982.e: On 4 July 1776 the colonies declared their independence from Great Britain. Groups like the “Sons of Liberty” had prepared the resistance. Today 4 July is the national holiday of the USA.
28982.m: The USA declared its independence in 1776.

28983.q: In which British colony was the city of Boston?
28983.e: Boston was the most important city in the colony of Massachusetts. Resistance against the British was especially strong there.

28984.q: On which date was the US Declaration of Independence adopted?
28984.e: The Continental Congress adopted the Declaration on 4 July 1776. Since then the USA has celebrated its national holiday on this day.
28984.m: 4 July is Independence Day in the USA.

28985.q: Which famous bell is a symbol of American independence?
28985.e: The Liberty Bell is in Philadelphia. It has a well-known crack and is no longer rung regularly today.
28985.m: The Liberty Bell is a symbol of freedom in the USA.

28986.q: Which pamphlet by Thomas Paine convinced many settlers to support independence in early 1776?
28986.e: Thomas Paine explained in simple language why the colonies should separate from Great Britain. Hundreds of thousands of copies were sold in a short time.
28986.m: Thomas Paine's “Common Sense” argued for independence.

28987.q: From which king did the colonies break away in 1776?
28987.e: The British King George III also ruled over the colonies at that time. The Declaration lists many complaints against him.
28987.m: The Americans broke away from King George III in 1776.

28988.q: Which inventor of the lightning rod was on the committee that prepared the Declaration of Independence?
28988.e: Benjamin Franklin was a printer, scientist and politician. He sat on the five-man committee for the Declaration and later helped to win France as an ally.
28988.m: Benjamin Franklin was an inventor and a Founding Father of the USA.

28989.q: Which body adopted the US Declaration of Independence?
28989.e: The Continental Congress was the assembly of delegates from all 13 colonies. It approved the Declaration in July 1776.

28990.q: Whose signature is written especially large on the Declaration of Independence?
28990.e: John Hancock was President of the Continental Congress and signed in large writing. That is why in the USA people say “John Hancock” for a signature.
28990.m: John Hancock put the biggest signature on the Declaration.

28991.q: Which young French nobleman fought as a general on the American side from 1777?
28991.e: The Marquis de La Fayette was only 19 when he came to America. He became a close friend of George Washington and also fought at Yorktown.
28991.m: La Fayette helped the Americans in their fight for independence.

28992.q: What position did George Washington hold in the War of Independence?
28992.e: The Continental Congress made Washington commander-in-chief in 1775. He led the American troops to victory.
28992.m: George Washington led the army of the colonies.

28993.q: In which city was George Washington sworn in as president in 1789?
28993.e: At that time New York was the first capital of the USA. Washington took the oath of office at Federal Hall on 30 April 1789.
28993.m: In 1789 New York was the first capital of the USA.

28994.q: How many terms did George Washington serve as president?
28994.e: Washington refused a third term and left office in 1797. This set an example that later became law.

28995.q: Which colony did George Washington come from?
28995.e: Washington was born in Westmoreland County in Virginia in 1732. There he was a big landowner and a militia officer.

28996.q: Which capital city is named after George Washington?
28996.e: The capital of the USA is called Washington. It was named after the first president.
28996.m: The US capital Washington bears the name of the first president.

28997.q: On which dollar bill is George Washington shown?
28997.e: Washington's portrait is on the 1-dollar bill. The capital Washington is also named after him.
28997.m: George Washington is on the 1-dollar bill.

28998.q: At which battle did Washington win a decisive victory over the British in 1781?
28998.e: At Yorktown in Virginia the British General Cornwallis surrendered in October 1781. French troops and ships helped.
28998.m: At Yorktown the War of Independence was practically decided.

28999.q: Which country did George Washington fight against in the War of Independence?
28999.e: The 13 colonies no longer wanted to be ruled by Great Britain. Washington led their army, and France helped the Americans.
28999.m: In the War of Independence the Americans fought against Great Britain.

29000.q: What did Thomas Jefferson found in Virginia in 1819?
29000.e: Jefferson planned the University of Virginia himself, even its buildings. He was prouder of it than of his presidency.

29001.q: Which number president of the USA was Thomas Jefferson?
29001.e: Jefferson governed from 1801 to 1809 as the third president. Before him Washington and John Adams held office.
29001.m: Thomas Jefferson was the third president of the USA.

29002.q: Which huge territory did Jefferson buy from France in 1803?
29002.e: In the Louisiana Purchase the USA bought land west of the Mississippi from Napoleon. This roughly doubled the size of the USA.
29002.m: The Louisiana Purchase made the USA twice as big.

29003.q: Which expedition did Jefferson send all the way to the Pacific?
29003.e: Meriwether Lewis and William Clark travelled to the Pacific and back from 1804 to 1806. They explored the land, plants, animals and peoples of the West.
29003.m: Lewis and Clark explored the West as far as the Pacific.

29004.q: What did Thomas Jefferson, who was very interested in architecture, design himself?
29004.e: Jefferson designed his country house Monticello in Virginia himself. Today it is a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

29005.q: On which special day did Thomas Jefferson die in 1826?
a: On the 50th anniversary of the Declaration of Independence
29005.e: Jefferson died on 4 July 1826, exactly 50 years after the Declaration. John Adams died on the same day.

29006.q: Which contradiction is Thomas Jefferson often accused of?
a: He wrote about freedom but owned slaves
He was king and president at the same time
29006.e: Jefferson wrote that all men are created equal. Even so, he held hundreds of enslaved people all his life.
29006.m: Jefferson preached freedom and still kept slaves.

29007.q: In which year was the US Constitution signed?
29007.e: The Constitutional Convention in Philadelphia signed the Constitution on 17 September 1787. It came into force in 1789.
29007.m: The US Constitution was signed in 1787.

29008.q: What is in the US Constitution?
a: How the state is organised and which rights apply
All the recipes in the country
The names of all the citizens
29008.e: A constitution is the most important law of a country. James Madison contributed a lot to the ideas of the US Constitution.
29008.m: The constitution sets out how the state is organised and people's rights.

29009.q: What are the first ten amendments to the US Constitution called together?
29009.e: The Bill of Rights came into force in 1791. It protects basic rights such as freedom of speech, of the press and of religion.
29009.m: The Bill of Rights protects basic rights in the USA.

29010.q: Which two chambers make up the US Congress?
a: National Council and Council of States
House of Lords and House of Commons
29010.e: In the Senate each state has two seats; in the House of Representatives the number depends on the population.
29010.m: The US Congress has a Senate and a House of Representatives.

29011.q: Which part of the Swiss parliament model of 1848 was influenced by the US Constitution?
29011.e: The Federal Constitution of 1848 took over the idea of two equal chambers. The National Council represents the people and the Council of States the cantons, similar to the House of Representatives and the Senate.
29011.m: The Swiss two-chamber system has an American model.

29012.q: According to the US Constitution, how long is one presidential term?
29012.e: The president is elected for four years. Since an amendment of 1951, at most two terms are allowed.
29012.m: A US president is elected for four years.

29013.q: Into how many branches does the US Constitution divide the power of the state?
29013.e: The Constitution separates lawmaking (Congress), government (the President) and the courts. The branches check each other.
29013.m: The US Constitution has three separate branches of power.

29014.q: Which court has the final say on the Constitution in the USA?
a: The Federal Supreme Court in Lausanne
29014.e: The Supreme Court is the highest court in the USA. It can declare laws unconstitutional.
29014.m: The Supreme Court is the highest court in the USA.

29015.q: Which European country ruled Haiti as a colony before independence?
29015.e: Haiti was a French colony. Enslaved people had to grow sugar and coffee on the plantations.

29016.q: Who rose up against the colonial rulers in the Haitian Revolution?
29016.e: The enslaved people on the plantations fought back against their oppression. Their uprising led to Haiti's independence in 1804.
29016.m: In Haiti enslaved people freed themselves.

29017.q: When did Haiti declare its independence?
29017.e: Jean-Jacques Dessalines proclaimed independence on 1 January 1804. He gave the country the name Haiti.

29018.q: What was special about the founding of Haiti?
a: It was the first state to come from a successful slave uprising
It was the first monarchy in America
29018.e: Formerly enslaved people defeated the French troops and founded their own state. After the USA, Haiti was the second independent state in the Americas.
29018.m: Haiti came from a victorious slave uprising.

a: A former slave and leader of the Haitian Revolution
29019.e: Toussaint Louverture was born into slavery and later became free. He led the rebels and governed the colony for a time.
29019.m: Toussaint Louverture led the revolution in Haiti.

29020.q: Which French ruler sent troops against Toussaint Louverture in 1802?
